topic: Enhanced Transcript Monitor (ETM) — Implementation Location
summary:
## Purpose
The Enhanced Transcript Monitor (ETM) is the persistent background daemon that watches active session transcripts, classifies exchanges, and writes structured observations to the km-core store. This insight records its **confirmed** implementation location and the observation-write (flush) trigger anchors. Supersedes the earlier "location unknown / may not exist" discovery notes — the module was located via the graphify code graph on 2026-08-03 against HEAD b6fe9297.

## Architecture
- **Single implementation file**: `scripts/enhanced-transcript-monitor.js` (~5340 lines). Class `EnhancedTranscriptMonitor` at line 155 (constructor line 156). There is no separate "transcript-monitor" module — all orchestration lives in this one file; earlier filename/keyword greps failed only because they searched the wrong terms.
- **Runs as a launchd daemon** (`com.coding.etm`), started via its `.start()` entrypoint (~line 4485). Not spawned per agent session.
- **Poll loop**: `_processAllTrackedTranscripts()` (line 622) discovers and processes tracked transcripts each tick.
- **Three observation-write (flush) triggers**, all in this file:
  1. **Prompt-set completion** (primary) — `processUserPromptSetCompletion()` defined at line 3723; invoked from the poll loop at 668, 709, 789, 1885–1936 and 4319–4343. The next user prompt closes the prior exchange and drives the flush.
  2. **Wall-clock / time-based flush** — `progressElapsedMs`, set in the constructor at line 227, default `5 * 60 * 1000` (5 min, line 229), override env `ETM_PROGRESS_ELAPSED_MS`. Plus a stale-prompt-set safety force-flush after 5 min at lines 637–682 and a no-new-exchange time-based flush at 747–761.
  3. **Token-delta progress fire** — `_maybeFireProgressObservation()` (line 1104) fires a `kind:'progress'` snapshot via `_fireProgressSnapshot` each time output tokens advance by `progressTokenDelta` (constructor line 214; default `DEFAULT_PROGRESS_TOKEN_DELTA = 30_000` from `lib/live-logging/progress-fire.mjs:23`; override env `ETM_PROGRESS_TOKEN_DELTA`). The tokens-vs-elapsed decision is logged at ~line 1145.
- **Why the wall-clock trigger exists**: opencode/copilot/mastra normalized transcripts carry no `usage.output_tokens`, so `sumOutputTokens` is always 0 and the token-delta path is inert for them. The wall-clock fire is the ONLY long-turn observation coverage for those agents (see constructor comment, lines 218–230).

## Key Files
- `scripts/enhanced-transcript-monitor.js` — the entire ETM daemon: class @155, constructor @156, poll loop `_processAllTrackedTranscripts` @622, prompt-set-completion flush `processUserPromptSetCompletion` @3723, token/elapsed progress fire `_maybeFireProgressObservation` @1104, `.start()` @~4485.
- `lib/live-logging/progress-fire.mjs` — `DEFAULT_PROGRESS_TOKEN_DELTA = 30_000` (line 23) and the `progressFireDecision` helper.
- `src/live-logging/ObservationWriter.js` — receives ETM writes into km-core (`writeObservation` / `writeInsight`).

## Usage
- To change stall-detection, flush cadence, or observation-write behavior, edit `scripts/enhanced-transcript-monitor.js` directly — the location is confirmed; do not repeat filename/keyword discovery passes.
- Tune flush cadence via env: `ETM_PROGRESS_TOKEN_DELTA` (token delta) and `ETM_PROGRESS_ELAPSED_MS` (wall-clock); `0` disables either trigger.

## Troubleshooting
- **"Cannot find ETM implementation"** — it is `scripts/enhanced-transcript-monitor.js`; prior discovery failures were search-strategy artifacts, not evidence of absence.
- **Observation gaps during long non-Claude turns** — check the wall-clock trigger (`progressElapsedMs`); the token-delta path is inert when transcripts lack `usage.output_tokens`.
- **Line numbers drift** — anchors verified 2026-08-03 against HEAD b6fe9297 (file ~5340 lines); if the file has grown, re-locate by symbol name rather than trusting the exact line.

topic: Token Usage Dashboard Label Normalization
summary:
## Purpose
Ensures consistent, deduplicated display of provider and model labels in the Token Usage dashboard by canonicalizing variant spellings before aggregation and render — e.g. merging `copilot`/`github-copilot` into `github`, `claude-code`/`anthropic` into `anthropic`, and `claude-opus-4-8` into `claude-opus-4.8`.

## Architecture
- `normalizeProvider` uses a `PROVIDER_ALIASES` map to merge provider name variants into canonical labels.
- `normalizeModel` converts hyphen-digit separators to dot-digit form (e.g. `claude-opus-4-8` → `claude-opus-4.8`).
- Aggregation functions `mergeByProvider` and `mergeByModel` apply normalization before render: pie chart (~line 700), model list (~line 735).
- Normalization is fully implemented and functioning — no code changes have been required across multiple independent verification passes.

## Key Files
- `token-usage.tsx` — dashboard UI; contains `normalizeProvider`, `PROVIDER_ALIASES`, `mergeByProvider`, `mergeByModel`, and render logic
- `models.ts` — contains `normalizeModel` for hyphen-to-dot conversion

## Usage
Normalization runs automatically during aggregation on every dashboard render. The By Provider pie chart and By Model list both consume normalized/merged data before display.

## Troubleshooting
- If duplicate labels reappear, verify `PROVIDER_ALIASES` in `token-usage.tsx` includes the new variant.
- For model label duplicates, check `normalizeModel` in `models.ts` covers the new hyphen pattern.
- No runtime configuration or restart required — normalization is pure UI-layer logic applied at render time.

topic: Cross-Platform Compatibility — Install and Test Scripts
summary:
## Purpose
Ensures `install.sh` and `scripts/test-coding.sh` run reliably on a fresh checkout across macOS, Linux, and Windows so new users and CI runners can bootstrap and self-test the project without platform-specific manual fixes, hangs, or false failures.

## Architecture
- **macOS timeout handling**: stock `macos-latest` runners lack GNU `timeout`/`gtimeout`. All ~20 call sites in `scripts/test-coding.sh` use a **pure-bash bounded timeout** (background process + signal-based kill) instead of an external binary shim — an earlier shim silently fell back to an unbounded wait, hanging the macOS CI leg indefinitely.
- **Windows line endings**: `.gitattributes` enforces LF line endings repo-wide so Windows `git checkout` doesn't inject CRLF, which previously broke shell script execution (symlinks, undefined commands, shell portability issues).
- **Unattended modes**: `--ci` and `--yes` flags drive graceful degradation (skip interactive prompts, skip unavailable tooling) so the script exits cleanly with code 0 when run non-interactively.
- **Test exit semantics**: `TESTS_FAILED` is incremented only inside `print_fail`, guaranteeing `--ci` mode reflects true pass/fail state and doesn't spuriously exit non-zero.
- **Realistic checkout simulation**: baseline/perf runs use `git-archive` extraction (instead of bind-mounting the full host repo) to emulate a genuine fresh user checkout without `node_modules`, giving a fair full-9-phase runtime baseline.
- **CI validation**: a GitHub Actions 3-OS matrix (`ubuntu-latest`, `macos-latest`, `windows-latest`) defined in `.github/workflows/cross-platform-lite.yml` runs `install.sh`/`test-coding.sh` end-to-end on every relevant PR; full stack verification (Docker + auth + private submodules) is out of scope for this lite matrix and requires self-hosted runners.

## Key Files
- `scripts/test-coding.sh` — self-test harness; contains the pure-bash bounded-timeout implementation and `print_fail`/`TESTS_FAILED` logic
- `install.sh` — cross-platform bootstrap/installer with proxy-heal logic and `--ci`/`--yes` unattended modes
- `.gitattributes` — enforces LF line endings repo-wide
- `.github/workflows/cross-platform-lite.yml` — 3-OS CI matrix definition
- `memory/reference_cross_platform_install_test.md`, `memory/MEMORY.md` — persistent notes on this hardening effort

## Usage
Run locally via `./scripts/test-coding.sh --ci` (or with `--yes` for install.sh) to validate a fresh checkout non-interactively; all 9 test phases should complete and exit 0. CI matrix triggers automatically on PRs touching install/test scripts, exercising all three OS targets.

## Troubleshooting
- If the macOS CI leg hangs indefinitely, suspect a `timeout`/`gtimeout` external-binary fallback reintroduced somewhere — replace with the pure-bash bounded-timeout pattern (background process + `kill` signal).
- If Windows CI fails on shell script execution, check for CRLF contamination — confirm `.gitattributes` is present and effective, and re-checkout the branch.
- For a fair runtime baseline or to reproduce install issues from a real user's perspective, use `git archive` to extract a clean tree rather than testing against the live working directory (which includes `node_modules` and dev artifacts).
- Verify `--ci` exit code correctness by checking that failures are only ever registered via `print_fail`; a non-zero exit with no visible `print_fail` output indicates a bug in error propagation, not a real test failure.

topic: System Health Dashboard — Build Staleness from Branch Divergence
summary:
## Purpose
Explains why a running dashboard instance can silently be missing UI features present on `main` (e.g. the Cost tab), and documents the safe diagnostic and remediation procedure when the checkout cannot be freely merged due to concurrent uncommitted work or unresolved merge conflicts.

## Architecture
- The dashboard's runtime UI is served from a **gitignored `dist/` build output**, not source directly. The build reflects whichever branch/commit was checked out at build time — no build error/warning is raised if features are missing.
- A long-lived feature branch (e.g. `feat/graphify-replace-cgr`) can predate a feature merge into `main` (e.g. the Cost tab: GitHub Copilot/Claude Max spend view, cost-by-month chart, pivot table, cadence control, $5/$25 Opus pricing, plus a cadence-daemon refactor). Building from that branch produces a `dist/` lacking these features.
- **Temporary fix (non-invasive)**: rebuild only the gitignored `dist/` output using the cost-feature frontend source pulled from `origin/main`, without touching the checked-out branch or its working tree — this is deliberately chosen over merging or editing source directly when another concurrent session shares the same physical checkout. This fix is inherently unstable: if the shared checkout later rebuilds from its own branch (e.g. the graphify branch, which lacks the cost-tab source), the feature disappears again.
- **Permanent fix**: merge `origin/main` into the stale feature branch. This can be blocked by real merge conflicts (e.g. in `install.sh`, from divergent CGR-era vs graphify-era edits).
- **Pre-merge safety diagnostic**: before attempting the permanent merge, diff files between `main` and the stale branch to identify what the merge would touch, specifically checking that it would not clobber another concurrent session's uncommitted WIP (e.g. `.data/*`, `.claude`, `.github`) that lives only in the shared working tree, not yet committed.

## Key Files
- `dist/` — gitignored build output actually served by the running dashboard instance; the diagnostic target when features appear "missing."
- `install.sh` — known conflict site between `main` and long-lived feature branches (CGR vs graphify-era edits).

## Usage
Consulted whenever a running dashboard instance is missing an expected UI feature that is known to exist on `main`. The temporary `dist/`-only rebuild is the safe default when the working tree is shared with another active session or has unresolved merge conflicts; the permanent branch-merge fix should only be attempted after diffing against `main` to confirm it won't destroy uncommitted parallel-session work.

## Troubleshooting
- If a dashboard feature is missing despite the feature being merged to `main`, first check which branch/commit the running `dist/` was actually built from — do not assume the checked-out branch matches expectations, especially in a shared working tree.
- Rebuilding `dist/` from `origin/main` source is safe and reversible; it does not alter git state and can be repeated whenever the feature reappears missing.
- Before merging `origin/main` into a stale feature branch, diff the two against each other to catalog every file the merge would touch, and cross-check that list against any uncommitted files in the working tree to avoid destroying another session's WIP.
- Expect the temporary fix to regress if anyone (including another concurrent session) triggers a rebuild from the stale branch — treat it as a stopgap, not a resolution.

topic: LLM Proxy Egress Coverage and Bypass Paths
summary:
## Purpose
Ensures all provider API key egress for LLM/embedding calls is confined to the host-side proxy at `:12435`, eliminating structural bypass paths where in-process SDKs or container-injected credentials could reach provider APIs directly. Remediation is tracked across four tiers (T1–T4), worked incrementally across sessions with cross-session handoff via memory files.

## Architecture
- **T1 — Network-level fail-closed isolation (corrected, complete)**: Initially implemented as machine-wide `/etc/hosts` DNS blackholing, which broke bare `claude` CLI invocations outside the coding project. Corrected to scope fail-closed isolation only to invocations via `bin/coding` with `--claude`/`--opencode`/`--copilot` flags, restoring normal direct CLI usage while keeping the daemon the sole in-scope provider access point.
- **T2 — In-process SDK and container credential bypass (closed)**: All raw `*_API_KEY`/`*_TOKEN` env vars removed from container bootstrap (`docker-compose.yml`, `entrypoint.sh`, supervisord config). All in-process LLM/embedding callers rerouted through the host-side proxy on `:12435` — proxy-bridge extended with `POST /v1/embeddings` passthrough and a `/v1/codegraph/chat/completions` shim for telemetry stamping. Fallback to CLI proxies preserved via `LLM_CLI_PROXY_URL`. Verified state: zero credential env vars present in the container, all supervisord programs running normally, and embeddings/codegraph completions confirmed routing through the proxy — `code-graph-rag` now issues its LLM calls via the shim using `claude-haiku-4-5`.
- **T3 — pending**: not yet started as of the last worked session; scope not yet detailed in project memory.
- **T4 — CI-lint task (in progress)**: work began by pulling project memory files for context; no implementation has started yet.
- **Cross-session continuity**: task-specific memory file `project_t2_egress_lockdown_next.md` (see Cross-Session Task Handoff insight) is used to resume this multi-tier effort across sessions when context runs low.

## Key Files
- `docker-compose.yml`, `entrypoint.sh`, supervisord config — container bootstrap files where raw provider credentials were removed
- Proxy-bridge service (hosts `POST /v1/embeddings` and `/v1/codegraph/chat/completions`) — the shim layer for in-process callers
- `project_t2_egress_lockdown_next.md` — cross-session task-state file tracking T1–T4 progress

## Usage
Any in-process LLM or embedding call (including from `code-graph-rag`) must route through the proxy-bridge shim rather than calling a provider SDK directly with an injected credential. `bin/coding` invocations with `--claude`/`--opencode`/`--copilot` are the only code paths where fail-closed network isolation applies; bare CLI invocations outside the coding project are unaffected.

## Troubleshooting
- If a bare `claude`/`copilot`/`opencode` CLI invocation fails to reach providers, confirm no global `/etc/hosts` DNS blackholing was reintroduced — isolation must be scoped to `bin/coding`-launched invocations only, never machine-wide.

metadata.topic: LLM Proxy Egress Coverage and Bypass Paths
metadata.summary:
## Purpose
Ensures all provider API key egress for LLM/embedding calls is confined to the host-side proxy at `:12435`, eliminating structural bypass paths where in-process SDKs or container-injected credentials could reach provider APIs directly. Remediation is tracked across four tiers (T1–T4), worked incrementally across sessions with cross-session handoff via memory files.

## Architecture
- **T1 — Network-level fail-closed isolation (corrected, complete)**: Initially implemented as machine-wide `/etc/hosts` DNS blackholing, which broke bare `claude` CLI invocations outside the coding project. Corrected to scope fail-closed isolation only to invocations via `bin/coding` with `--claude`/`--opencode`/`--copilot` flags, restoring normal direct CLI usage while keeping the daemon the sole in-scope provider access point.
- **T2 — In-process SDK and container credential bypass (closed)**: All raw `*_API_KEY`/`*_TOKEN` env vars removed from container bootstrap (`docker-compose.yml`, `entrypoint.sh`, supervisord config). All in-process LLM/embedding callers rerouted through the host-side proxy on `:12435` — proxy-bridge extended with `POST /v1/embeddings` passthrough and a `/v1/codegraph/chat/completions` shim for telemetry stamping. Fallback to CLI proxies preserved via `LLM_CLI_PROXY_URL`. Verified state: zero credential env vars present in the container, all supervisord programs running normally, and embeddings/codegraph completions confirmed routing through the proxy — `code-graph-rag` now issues its LLM calls via the shim using `claude-haiku-4-5`.
- **T3 — pending**: not yet started as of the last worked session; scope not yet detailed in project memory.
- **T4 — CI-lint task (in progress)**: work began by pulling project memory files for context; no implementation has started yet.
- **Cross-session continuity**: task-specific memory file `project_t2_egress_lockdown_next.md` (see Cross-Session Task Handoff insight) is used to resume this multi-tier effort across sessions when context runs low.

- `docker-compose.yml`, `entrypoint.sh`, supervisord config — container bootstrap files where raw provider credentials were removed
- Proxy-bridge service (hosts `POST /v1/embeddings` and `/v1/codegraph/chat/completions`) — the shim layer for in-process callers

Any in-process LLM or embedding call (including from `code-graph-rag`) must route through the proxy-bridge shim rather than calling a provider SDK directly with an injected credential. `bin/coding` invocations with `--claude`/`--opencode`/`--copilot` are the only code paths where fail-closed network isolation applies; bare CLI invocations outside the coding project are unaffected.

topic: KB Injection Quality Gate
summary:
## Purpose
Provides gated, LLM-judged knowledge base injection into experiment cells for all agents under `kb-on` conditions, making `kb-on`/`kb-off` a genuine experimental axis rather than a confound. Injection only occurs when a relevance judge confirms the retrieved KB content is actually useful for the goal; otherwise zero content is injected, avoiding both noise-from-irrelevant-injection and silent-missing-injection.

## Architecture
- **Entry point**: `lib/experiments/cell-injection.mjs` — unified gated-injection module; fires before agent spawn for every `kb-on` cell regardless of agent type.
- **Retrieval**: fetches KB content via a composite `task_id+goal` query against `src/retrieval/retrieval-service.js`.
- **Relevance judge**: `src/retrieval/relevance-judge.js` — LLM-based judgment routed to Haiku (~1.1s latency), replacing an earlier keyword-list filter that was too permissive/brittle.
- **Fail-closed semantics (experiments)**: inject only when the judge confirms relevance within a 10s budget; otherwise inject nothing. Interactive (non-experiment) mode retains fail-open behavior against the IDF set — the two modes intentionally differ.
- **Root cause this system fixes**: `claude -p` (headless mode) does not fire the `UserPromptSubmit` hook, so before this gate existed, Claude cells received zero KB injection — a silent gap that produced misleadingly clean scores.
- **Per-agent injection channels** (each agent has a distinct delivery mechanism, wired through `cell-injection.mjs`):
  - Claude — via `--append-system-prompt`
  - opencode — writes to `.opencode/knowledge-context.md` in the run's working directory/worktree
  - copilot — via context files
  - mastra — via `.mastra/context.md`

## Key Files
- `lib/experiments/cell-injection.mjs` — gated injection orchestration, per-agent channel dispatch
- `lib/experiments/experiment-runner.mjs` — invokes cell-injection before agent spawn; entry point for cell construction/execution
- `src/retrieval/relevance-judge.js` — LLM-based relevance gate (Haiku)
- `src/retrieval/retrieval-service.js` — composite `task_id+goal` retrieval
- `tests/integration/retrieval-service.relevance-floor.test.js`, `tests/experiments/cell-injection.test.mjs` — regression coverage (16/16, 6/6 passing)
- `compare-fizzbuzz-kbon.yaml` — reference experiment config exercising the kb-on axis
- `memory/reference_kb_injection_quality_gate.md` — living design/reference doc for this subsystem

## Usage
Runs automatically whenever an experiment matrix includes a `kb-on` cell, across all four supported agents (claude, copilot, opencode, mastra). No manual invocation needed — the runner calls `cell-injection.mjs` at cell spawn time. Verified end-to-end for opencode via an ETM-stall goal pattern run inside an isolated worktree, where injection wrote 1131 characters to `.opencode/knowledge-context.md` before the cell reached `terminal_state=complete`.

## Troubleshooting
- **Expected negative case**: trivial/unrelated goals (e.g., fizzbuzz) should show 0 chars injected — this confirms the gate is correctly filtering out irrelevant content, not a bug.
- **Expected positive case**: goals with real matching KB content (e.g., an ETM issue) should show non-trivial injection (observed: 858 chars / 3 insights for Claude; 1131 chars for opencode) — near-zero injection on a goal known to have relevant KB entries indicates the judge or retrieval service is misconfigured or timing out.
- If an agent's cell shows no injected content despite `kb-on`, verify the correct per-agent channel path exists and is writable (e.g., `.opencode/knowledge-context.md`, `.mastra/context.md`) and check that the judge call completed within the 10s budget rather than falling through to fail-closed.
- To inspect a live opencode injection artifact, check `.opencode/knowledge-context.md` inside the run's worktree before cleanup; run metadata/output files (e.g., `etm-stall-notes.md`) can confirm what the agent actually consumed.

topic: Cross-Agent Experiment Harness — Model Resolution and Proxy Routing
summary:
## Purpose
Ensures all agents (claude, copilot, opencode, mastra) can be launched and measured by the experiment harness without HTTP errors caused by model identifier format mismatches between the experiment spec and the proxy routing layer.

## Architecture
- **Model ID format constraint**: The proxy expects hyphen-separated Claude version strings (e.g., `claude-opus-4-8`). Dot-separated variants (e.g., `claude-opus-4.8`) previously caused HTTP 500 on the proxy route, causing opencode cells to be skipped entirely in comparative experiment runs.
- **Shared normalizer**: `hyphenateClaudeVersion` maps dotted model IDs to hyphenated form. It is implemented in two places that must stay in sync:
  - `model-resolve.mjs` in the coding repo — consumed by the `/experiment` operator skill orchestrator.
  - A dedicated normalizer in the proxy repo — applied to incoming requests before routing, so any client sending a dotted model ID is corrected server-side.
- **Fix validated end-to-end**: after the proxy-side normalizer landed, opencode cells complete measured runs with full token accounting instead of being skipped/erroring at HTTP 500.
- **Provider naming consistency**: `github-copilot` vs `copilot` naming inconsistencies in the token-usage pipeline remain a tracked open concern, separate from the model-ID hyphenation issue.

## Key Files
- `model-resolve.mjs` (coding repo) — exports `hyphenateClaudeVersion`; used by orchestrator before dispatching cells.
- Proxy repo normalizer module — mirrors `hyphenateClaudeVersion` logic on the request-ingest path.

## Usage
Invoked automatically whenever the `/experiment` skill or any harness component resolves a model ID before spawning an agent sandbox or routing an API call. Any new agent integration that accepts a Claude model string must pass through this normalizer.

## Troubleshooting
- Opencode cell shows `skipped` or errors with HTTP 500 on the proxy route → check whether the model ID reaching the proxy is dot-separated; confirm the proxy-side normalizer is deployed and active.
- If coding-repo and proxy-repo normalizers diverge (e.g., one updated without the other), symptoms reappear only for the repo missing the fix — verify both repos are on a commit that includes `hyphenateClaudeVersion`.
- Validate the fix by checking opencode's token count in a fresh run — a nonzero token count (vs. prior 0/skipped) confirms the proxy accepts the resolved model ID.

topic: Graphify Dashboard — Reindex Update Mechanics
summary:
## Purpose
Provides dashboard buttons to trigger either an **incremental** (fast, cluster-preserving) or **full** (complete re-extraction) update of the graphify code graph, and displays a "commits behind" freshness indicator comparing the graph's recorded commit against current HEAD. Exists to avoid unnecessary full extraction/visualization regeneration when only a subset of files changed.

## Architecture
- Reindex is driven by `scripts/graphify-reindex.sh`, spawned by the `system-health-dashboard` backend via a child-process spawn/exec call, invoked with different flags depending on which dashboard button is pressed (incremental vs. full mode).
- The HTTP entry point for triggering a reindex from the UI is the `POST /api/cgr/reindex` route. The route name retains the legacy "cgr" prefix from the pre-graphify (code-graph-rag) era even though it now drives graphify.
- **Confirmed handler location**: the `POST /api/cgr/reindex` route handler is implemented in `integrations/system-health-dashboard/server.js` — verified via direct grep for the route string.
- Incremental path is intended to run `update --no-cluster` for speed, but whether this preserves community/cluster data correctly has not been fully confirmed.

## Key Files
- `integrations/system-health-dashboard/server.js` — hosts the `POST /api/cgr/reindex` route handler; spawns the reindex shell script
- `scripts/graphify-reindex.sh` — actual reindex driver script, accepts flags for incremental vs. full mode

## Usage
Triggered by clicking either reindex button in the system-health dashboard UI; consumed downstream by the dashboard's "commits behind" freshness indicator and the code-graph viewer feature.

## Troubleshooting
- If the reindex button appears to do nothing, check server logs around the `/api/cgr/reindex` handler in `server.js` for spawn errors.
- To confirm which script/flags a given button invokes, grep `server.js` for the route string `POST /api/cgr/reindex` and trace the spawned command into `scripts/graphify-reindex.sh`.
- If incremental updates seem to lose cluster/community data, verify whether `--no-cluster` is actually being passed as intended for the incremental button.

topic: Token Usage Dashboard — Cost Tracking and Budget Management
summary:
## Purpose
Extends the token-usage dashboard with per-model/provider pricing, subscription-tier budget tiles, cost trend visualization, and burn-rate warnings so teams can monitor and cap LLM spend. Feature is implementation-complete and UI-verified against live API data.

## Architecture
- **Design principle**: cost is derived at read-time by joining the proxy's SQLite `token-usage.db` against a price table — never stored as a persisted field.
- **Frontend entry point**: `src/pages/token-usage.tsx` (~1050 lines), single entry point with Overview/Evolution/Recent tabs, all fetching from `${PROXY_BASE}/api/token-usage/*`.
- **Backend**: `GET /api/token-usage/cost` on `rapid-llm-proxy`'s `server.js` computes cost from existing token rows against pricing data; lives entirely in the external `_work/rapid-llm-proxy/` tree, absent from the `coding` repo.
- **Confirmed pricing**: Opus seeded at $15 input / $75 output per million tokens — verified correct against spec, no change needed.
- **Verified UI elements** (cross-checked against live API values): Copilot and Claude Max budget tiles; Mar–Aug cost-by-month stacked bar chart (July spike attributed to Opus foreground usage plus cache-reads); a Haiku-routing optimization suggestion surfaced for the `consolidator-insight` task; correct per-task cost breakdown percentages; consolidation cadence control.
- **Commit hygiene**: cost-feature work spans both the `coding` (frontend/planning) and `rapid-llm-proxy` (backend) repos; staging is done selectively per-repo to include only cost-feature files, explicitly excluding unrelated `.data/*` telemetry churn that accumulates during local testing.

## Key Files
- `src/pages/token-usage.tsx` — frontend dashboard, all three tabs.
- `_work/rapid-llm-proxy/server.js` — `GET /api/token-usage/cost` endpoint and pricing join logic.
- `token-usage.db` (SQLite, in `rapid-llm-proxy`) — raw token-usage rows joined against price table at read-time.

## Usage
Consulted by teams monitoring LLM spend across subscription tiers (Copilot, Claude Max) and per-task/per-model breakdowns. Routing-override control and settings dialog allow functional testing of budget behavior; changes made for testing purposes should be reverted afterward to avoid unintended persisted state changes.

## Troubleshooting
- **Pricing mismatch**: if a tile shows unexpected cost, verify the price table entry for the model (e.g. Opus $15/$75 per million input/output) rather than the token-count logic — cost bugs are almost always pricing-table issues, not usage-tracking issues.
- **Unexpected monthly spike**: check for foreground (non-cached) usage of expensive models plus cache-read volume before assuming a tracking bug — a July spike was correctly attributed to Opus foreground usage + cache-reads, not a defect.
- **Committing cost work**: when staging commits, diff both `coding` and `rapid-llm-proxy` repos separately and exclude `.data/*` telemetry files to avoid polluting the PR with local test artifacts.

topic: Performance Measurement Documentation Set
summary:
## Purpose
Produces canonical, evidence-grounded documentation for the Performance Measurement / Experiment system, covering the cross-agent harness, KB-injection quality gate, scoring pipeline, sandbox hardening, grouped Runs table, per-value tooltips, prompt caching, experiment grouping, polling, pagination, and forced scoring. Every claim is anchored to a real live-dashboard screenshot or a rendered PlantUML diagram rather than a hypothetical description.

## Architecture
- **3-agent parallel extraction pipeline** feeds a single intermediate changelog document (`purrfect-dreaming-rainbow.md`), which grows section-by-section across overhaul passes (reached 52 sections during the v7.3 doc pass):
  - LSL changelog agent — extracts recent system changes from LSLs
  - docs/PUML map agent (aka "map measurement docs structure" agent) — inventories existing diagram sources and coverage gaps
  - dashboard tooltip catalog agent — extracts tooltip-derived tips/definitions from the live UI
- **Screenshot campaign**: driven via `gsd-browser` against the live dashboard, producing evidence images (grouped Runs collapsed/expanded, two-run comparison, experiment matrix, Avenues help, probe timeline, fullscreen timeline, context explainer, caching sections, score tooltips, run monitor, score drawer, reconciliation badge, role-delta comparison) saved to `docs-content/images/`.
- **Diagram set**: PlantUML sources rendered to PNG and referenced from pages — `experiment-measurement-architecture.puml`, `experiment-run-sequence.puml`, `kb-injection-axis.puml`, `experiment-identity-model.puml`, `avenue-fork-lineage.puml`, `scoring-rubric-pipeline.puml`.
- **Published pages**: `dashboard-reference.md`, `tutorial.md`, `overview.md`, `architecture.md`, `experiment-skill.md`, `prompt-caching.md`, `release-notes.md`, all navigated via `mkdocs.yml`.
- **Concurrent-monitoring workflow**: streaming run state allows watching multiple experiment cells simultaneously while a docs-mapping agent retries after a transient failure, avoiding repeated ~4-minute full run cycles by reusing previously captured live-window data.

## Key Files
- `purrfect-dreaming-rainbow.md` — intermediate/working changelog aggregating all three extraction agents' output

topic: Judge Rationale and Scoring Explanations
summary:
## Purpose
`judge.mjs` evaluates agent runs and produces per-dimension scores with rationale text. Rationale must be specific, instance-grounded diagnostic explanations tied to actual score deductions — not generic template filler — so users can understand exactly why a run scored below perfect.

## Architecture
- **Score dimensions**: each dimension produces a numeric score plus a rationale string explaining the deduction relative to a perfect score.
- **Judge inputs**: span/trace/evidence from the target run; the judge does **not** have direct access to file contents and reasons from observable evidence only.
- **Corrected prompt structure** separates two concerns:
  1. Per-dimension identified deficiencies — what specifically capped each score below perfect.
  2. Evidence citations grounding each deficiency claim.
- **Prior defect (resolved)**: a single generic `rubric_rationale` used confidence discounts rather than defect-based penalties, producing identical-sounding rationale across runs regardless of actual failure mode.

## Key Files
- `judge.mjs` — core judge; contains the scoring prompt and rationale generation logic
- `scratchpad/prove-judge.mjs` — standalone verification harness; loads archived span/trace/evidence from a target run, calls `runJudge`, and writes raw rationale to a file for inspection without console truncation

## Usage
Called automatically by the experiment runner after each cell completes. The proof harness (`prove-judge.mjs`) can be run manually against any archived run to validate rationale quality before promoting prompt changes to production.

## Troubleshooting
- **Generic rationale across runs**: indicates the old single-`rubric_rationale` prompt is active rather than the per-dimension defect prompt — verify the prompt structure in `judge.mjs`.
- **Slow judge runs**: default routing may use Opus; switch the proof harness to Sonnet (e.g., `claude-sonnet-4.6`) for faster iteration when validating rationale changes.
- **Verify output**: run `scratchpad/prove-judge.mjs` against a known low-scoring run and confirm each dimension's rationale names a specific defect rather than a confidence discount.

topic: Graphify Migration — Deployment and Documentation Rollout Process
summary:
## Purpose
Provides the detection, extraction, and caching engine behind graphify's incremental/full code-graph updates, plus the file-watching orchestrator (`watch.py`) that triggers incremental rebuilds automatically when source files change. The corpus cache exists to avoid re-classifying every file on every reindex.

## Architecture
- **Detection hot path**: `detect()` lives in `integrations/graphify/graphify/detect.py` (~lines 1292–1585); it is the entry point invoked during incremental/full re-indexing.
- **Corpus cache**: `.detect_corpus_cache.json` caches per-file `FileType` classification results plus derived corpus stats (e.g. word counts), keyed by a SHA-256 `_corpus_signature`.
- **Signature composition**: the corpus signature is built from cache version, `follow_symlinks`/`google_workspace` flags, merged ignore rules, and per-file path — plus `mtime_ns`/size for files whose type is determined by content inspection rather than path alone (ambiguous types). Files classified purely by path pattern don't need content-based signature fields.
- **File-watch orchestration**: `watch.py` monitors the working tree for changes; on detecting a change it invokes the incremental rebuild flow. `detect()` is called from within `_rebuild_code` (defined at `watch.py:893`), confirmed repeatedly as the sole caller site during incremental rebuilds — this is the concrete link between "a file changed" and "detect() re-classifies it."

## Key Files
- `integrations/graphify/graphify/detect.py` — `detect()` implementation, FileType classification logic
- `integrations/graphify/graphify/watch.py` — file-watching orchestrator; `_rebuild_code` (line ~893) is the function that invokes `detect()` during incremental rebuilds
- `.detect_corpus_cache.json` — corpus cache artifact, keyed by SHA-256 signature

## Usage
Triggered automatically in watch mode when source files change (via `_rebuild_code` in `watch.py`); also reachable via the dashboard's incremental/full reindex buttons (`scripts/graphify-reindex.sh`, see "Graphify Dashboard — Reindex Update Mechanics") and directly via graphify CLI update commands.

## Troubleshooting
- If incremental rebuilds fail to pick up a changed file, confirm `watch.py`'s `_rebuild_code` is actually firing (check watch-mode process logs) before suspecting `detect()` itself.
- If classification looks stale, inspect `.detect_corpus_cache.json`'s `_corpus_signature` composition — a mismatched flag (e.g. `follow_symlinks`) invalidates the whole cache.
- If rebuilds are correct but slow, the bottleneck is typically filesystem walk speed (e.g. VirtioFS under Docker on macOS), not `detect()` algorithmic complexity — see the Graphify AST-Cache Performance insight.

topic: Code-Graph/Code-Memory Tool Evaluation — Skeptical Verification Research
summary:
## Purpose
Provides a repeatable, multi-agent skeptical-verification process for evaluating external code-graph and code-memory tools before adopting, referencing, or benchmarking against them — countering marketing inflation in tool READMEs, blog posts, and benchmark claims by checking assertions against primary sources (repos, papers, package registries, star-history).

## Architecture
- **Methodology**: parallel research subagents are dispatched per candidate tool, each independently verifying a specific category of claim (star counts, install package name/version, benchmark numbers, license, feature-tier claims, underlying research paper) rather than trusting the tool's own marketing copy.
- **Negative-control testing**: used to distinguish genuinely fabricated claims from real-but-exaggerated ones — applied to confirm DeusData's `codebase-memory-mcp` and its underlying arXiv preprint (2603.27277) are both genuine artifacts, not fabricated.
- **Four parallel evaluation targets** run to completion: Graphify (external, unrelated to this project's vendored `integrations/graphify`), CodeGraph/code-review-graph, Sourcegraph (industry context), and codebase-memory-mcp. Findings feed a final comparative report and benchmark plan (see `kgbench` harness).

## Key Files
- No repo files — this is a research process producing findings/reports, not code. Distinguish from the project's own vendored submodule at `integrations/graphify`, which is a *different, unrelated* tool from the externally-evaluated "Graphify" (npm package `graphifyy`).

## Usage
Run before adopting or benchmarking any third-party code-graph/code-memory tool; findings inform the comparative report and the `kgbench` benchmark plan (queries/arms/reps) used to objectively score candidate tools against the project's own stack.

## Troubleshooting
- **Verifying package identity/version claims**: check actual npm/PyPI registry name and version, not the name used in the article/README (e.g. external "Graphify" installs as `graphifyy` v0.9.32, not `graphify` v0.8.35 as an article claimed).
- **Verifying star counts**: compare live GitHub star count against article's snapshot; large deltas plus a steep growth curve are signs of inorganic/purchased stars (external Graphify: 101,954 live vs. ~63,200 claimed).
- **Verifying benchmark numbers**: attempt independent reproduction on a comparable dataset before trusting a headline multiplier — external Graphify's claimed 71.5× token-reduction reproduced at only ~7.3× on pure code; codebase-memory-mcp's "99%/120×" example is cherry-picked vs. the paper's honest average (~10× tokens, 2.1× fewer tool calls across 31 repos, 66 languages benchmarked vs. 158 claimed).
- **Verifying underlying research papers**: fetch the actual arXiv/paper ID and cross-check stated results/scope; do not assume a citation is fabricated without checking — negative-control testing confirmed 2603.27277 is real.
- **Verifying licensing/tier claims**: check for signed releases (SLSA provenance, cosign signatures, SBOM) and actual license file rather than marketing pages; flag unlaunched "coming soon" tiers presented as available (external Graphify's "Enterprise VPC/on-prem" tier was not yet launched).
- **Security note**: scan third-party tool READMEs/docs for embedded prompt-injection content before feeding them into agent context — one was found in external Graphify's README.

topic: System Health Dashboard — Code Graph Viewer Feature
summary:
## Purpose
Adds an interactive graph-viewer feature ("Code Graph") to the system-health dashboard so users can visually explore graphify's code graph directly in the dashboard UI. The shipped implementation is a bespoke, vendored **vis-network** based viewer reading `graph.json` directly; a planned follow-on integrates graphify's own native HTML exporter as an alternative/complementary rendering path, alongside separate research into a next-generation rendering architecture for scale/LOD limitations.

## Architecture
- **Shipped implementation**: vendored vis-network bundle, client-side rendering, reads graphify's `graph.json` directly rather than relying on graphify's native `graphify export html` exporter.
- **Native exporter pipeline (traced, not yet integrated)**: CLI dispatch in `cli.py` → `to_html()` in `exporters/html.py`. Correct invocation is `graphify export html --graph PATH --labels PATH --node-limit N`; it reads `graph.json` (default path `.data/graphify/graphify-out/graph.json`) and **always** writes `graph.html` alongside it in the same directory — there is no `--out` flag to redirect output.
- **Community reconstruction fallback**: `to_html()` accepts an arbitrary filtered `nx.Graph` plus a community map; if no analysis sidecar exists, communities are reconstructed from node attributes with safe fallbacks, so the exporter degrades gracefully rather than failing.
- **Execution environment (corrects stale docs)**: graphify runs inside the existing `coding-services` container — **not** a dedicated container — via a venv CLI at `/coding/integrations/graphify/.venv/bin/graphify`, matching the same spawn pattern already used by `scripts/graphify-reindex.sh` and `server.js`. Prior CLAUDE.md documentation describing a separate container was stale and should be disregarded.
- **CDN dependency (integration blocker)**: the generated `graph.html` is **not self-contained** — it loads vis-network from `unpkg.com` via an SRI-pinned `<script>` tag, requiring external CDN access. This fails under corporate-proxy SRI validation, so any dashboard integration must vendor/inline the vis-network JS library instead of trusting the exporter's default CDN reference.
- **Render-scale limits**: only the `integrations/graphify` subgraph (6637 nodes) exceeds the exporter's 5k node render cap and requires aggregation; all other subgraphs render at full node-level without aggregation.
- **Candidate redesign under separate research**: a subagent-driven reuse survey compared existing VOKB/VKB viewers (unified-viewer, memory-visualizer, system-health-dashboard) and recommended porting the Sigma.js v3 + graphology WebGL skeleton (`SigmaCanvas.tsx`, `reducers.ts`, `node-renderer.ts`) from unified-viewer for a future-generation rendering architecture — this is independent of the native-exporter integration plan below.

## Key Files
- `integrations/graphify/graphify/cli.py` — CLI entry point dispatching `export html`
- `integrations/graphify/graphify/exporters/html.py` (`to_html()`) — native HTML exporter with community-reconstruction fallback
- `.data/graphify/graphify-out/graph.json` — default input read by the exporter; `graph.html` is written alongside it
- `integrations/system-health-dashboard/server.js` — dashboard backend; planned new `res.sendFile` route to serve exporter output through the existing static-server proxy; reuses the existing reindex spawn/progress pattern
- Planning doc: `floating-fluttering-shannon.md` — documents the integration plan (filtered graph + generated HTML written to `.data/graphify/graphify-out/`, served via dashboard route, vendored vis-network)

## Usage
The bespoke vis-network viewer is the currently live, user-facing Code Graph feature in the dashboard. The native-exporter integration is planned but not yet implemented: once landed, it will write a filtered graph + generated HTML into `.data/graphify/graphify-out/`, served via a new dashboard route, reusing the existing reindex spawn/progress infrastructure.

## Troubleshooting
- If the native `graphify export html` output fails to render externally (blank page, CSP/SRI console errors) behind a corporate proxy, suspect the `unpkg.com` CDN dependency for vis-network — the fix is to vendor/inline the JS library rather than relying on the exporter's default script tag.
- If exporter output is missing or in an unexpected location, remember there is no `--out` flag — it always writes `graph.html` next to the input `graph.json`.
- If CLAUDE.md or other docs describe graphify running in a dedicated container, treat that as stale — graphify runs inside `coding-services` via `/coding/integrations/graphify/.venv/bin/graphify`, matching `graphify-reindex.sh`'s spawn pattern.
- For the `integrations/graphify` subgraph specifically (6637 nodes), expect the 5k render cap to trigger aggregation — other subgraphs should render at node-level without this behavior.

## Purpose
Canonical data flow for token usage tracking — from wire-level capture through storage to dashboard consumption — spanning the `coding` project and the external `rapid-llm-proxy` checkout. Provides accurate cost/usage attribution per process, model, provider, and subscription, and is the foundation all cost/analytics/latency features build on.

## Architecture
- **Source of truth**: `token-usage.db` (SQLite) inside `rapid-llm-proxy`, holding ~213k rows covering ~3 months of history (May–Jul 2026).
- **Write paths**: proxy daemon wire logs plus host-side adapters write usage rows; deduplicated on `tool_call_id` to prevent double-counting.
- **Read paths**: dashboard forwarder never queries SQLite directly — it calls proxy `/api/token-usage/*` endpoints (`getSummary`, `getRecent`, and the `cost` endpoint). New cost/analytics features should be added as additional proxy API endpoints; no dashboard-server changes required.
- **Attribution dimensions**: per process, model, provider, and subscription. Hourly JSON export is currently disabled.
- **Known data-quality issues**:
  - ~5.8% of rows have empty subscription values — must be coalesced/defaulted rather than dropped.
  - Provider names need aliasing (e.g. `github-copilot` → `copilot`) before aggregation to avoid split/duplicate provider buckets.
  - `tokens_estimated` flag marks rows with inferred (not measured) token counts — must be surfaced or excluded depending on accuracy requirements.
  - Rows exist at both per-turn and per-session-aggregate granularity; naive summing across both levels double-counts — aggregation logic must filter/group by granularity first.

## Key Files
- `token-usage.db` — SQLite source-of-truth database, lives inside `_work/rapid-llm-proxy/`.
- `rapid-llm-proxy/server.js` (external checkout) — hosts `/api/token-usage/*` endpoints (`getSummary`, `getRecent`, `cost`).
- Dashboard forwarder (proxy-side, in the `coding` repo) — relays browser requests to the proxy API; contains no direct DB access.

## Usage
Consumed by the Token Usage dashboard tabs (Overview/Evolution/Recent), cost/budget features, and PERF-03 latency observability — all read exclusively through the proxy's HTTP API layer, never the SQLite file directly.

## Troubleshooting
- If usage totals look inflated, check for double-counting from mixed per-turn/per-session-aggregate rows or missing `tool_call_id` dedup.
- If subscription/provider breakdowns show unexpected "unknown"/split buckets, verify the empty-subscription coalescing and provider-alias mapping are applied before aggregation.
- If a new cost/analytics feature needs additional data, first check whether it can be served as a new proxy endpoint against existing `token-usage.db` columns before touching dashboard-server code.

topic: Code-Graph-RAG to Graphify Migration
summary:
## Purpose
Replaces `code-graph-rag` (CGR) — a Python submodule backed by a live Memgraph graph database — with `graphify`, a lightweight stdio/HTTP tool that queries a static `graph.json` file. Goal: eliminate Python venv and database infrastructure (Memgraph container, bolt/lab ports) while preserving all existing code-graph query functionality consumed by MCP servers and agents (`CodeGraphAgent`, UKB workflows, wave-analysis agents, `analyze_code_graph` tool).

## Architecture
- **Audit scope**: 40+ CGR reference points across 8 areas — MCP server config (`claude-code-mcp.json`, `docker-mcp-config.sh`), the Python submodule (`uv`/`pyproject.toml`), `install.sh` clone/env/cache/reindex logic, `scripts/test-coding.sh`, Docker (compose file, Dockerfile, supervisord, entrypoint), Memgraph ports (bolt 7687, lab UI 3100), documentation, and state directories (`.data/code-graph-index/`, `shared-data/`).
- **Critical blocker resolved architecturally**: CGR serves a dual role — standalone MCP server AND the Memgraph-backed query backend behind `mcp-server-semantic-analysis`'s `analyze_code_graph` tool. Memgraph is a live graph DB; graphify is a static `graph.json`-based stdio/HTTP tool (MCP on port 3851). Both roles are satisfied by graphify's `graph.json` query API, removing the live-database dependency entirely.
- **Proposed containerized design**: graphify built directly into the `coding-services` Docker image, with a host shim invoking it via `docker exec` — eliminates Python venvs and database infrastructure on the host.
- **Risk assessment — Memgraph removal is safe**: all CGR-dependent workflows (`CodeGraphAgent`, UKB workflows, wave-analysis agents) already degrade gracefully on connection failure via TCP probes and try/catch; zero tests depend on a live Memgraph instance.
- **Query-layer migration path**: rewrite `runCypherQuery` and `runCodeGraphCommand` in `code-graph-agent.ts` (~8 fixed Cypher patterns) to use graphify's `graph.json` query API, while preserving the public `CodeGraphAgent` interface so downstream callers are unaffected.
- **Config artifact**: `graphify.json` configuration is persisted under `.data/`.

## Key Files
- `code-graph-agent.ts` — implements `runCypherQuery`/`runCodeGraphCommand`; target of the query-layer rewrite (~8 fixed Cypher patterns to reimplement against `graph.json`)
- `install.sh` — CGR clone/env/cache/reindex logic requiring replacement with graphify setup
- `scripts/test-coding.sh` — test adjustments needed for graphify
- `claude-code-mcp.json`, `docker-mcp-config.sh` — MCP server registry entries to reconfigure
- `.data/graphify.json` — graphify configuration
- `.data/code-graph-index/`, `shared-data/` — CGR state directories to retire

## Usage
Migration is planning/audit-phase; no files modified yet as of the audit. Once implemented, `CodeGraphAgent` callers (UKB workflows, wave-analysis agents, `analyze_code_graph` MCP tool) will transparently query `graph.json` via graphify instead of Memgraph, with no interface changes required on the consumer side.

## Troubleshooting
- If `analyze_code_graph` or `CodeGraphAgent` queries fail post-migration, verify `graph.json` exists and is fresh (check `built_at_commit` field) before suspecting the query rewrite logic.
- Since dependent workflows already handle connection failures gracefully, missing/stale `graph.json` should degrade rather than crash — absence of graceful degradation indicates the try/catch paths were not preserved during rewrite.
- Cross-reference the MCP server registry (`claude-code-mcp.json`) if graphify's MCP endpoint (port 3851) is unreachable — confirm it's registered per-agent (see "MCP Server Configuration" insight; registration is not automatically uniform across Claude/opencode/Copilot).

topic: Agent Memory Repository — Remote Sync and Authentication
summary:
## Purpose
Persists agent memory files (task-state notes, reference articles, the `MEMORY.md` manifest) to a dedicated remote git repository, separate from both the outer `coding` project repo and the `.specstory/history` session-log repo, so memory updates survive across sessions and machines.

## Architecture
- The memory directory is its own git repository with its own remote — distinct from the main `coding` repo and from `.specstory/history`.
- **Remote host and auth**: hosted on the company's GitHub Enterprise instance (GHE, e.g. `<company>.ghe.com`), accessed over **HTTPS with token authentication** — not SSH, unlike the main `coding` repo's submodule remotes (which use SSH with `IdentitiesOnly yes`).
- Tracks `origin/main` in a standard local-ahead-by-N-commits / push pattern.
- Each reference-article file (e.g. `reference_graphify_replaces_cgr.md`) is committed alongside an updated `MEMORY.md` manifest entry in the same commit, keeping the manifest and article content in sync.
- No PR/review step is used for memory-repo commits — pushes go directly to `main`.

## Key Files
- `MEMORY.md` — manifest/index of all persisted reference articles.
- `reference_<topic>.md` files — individual self-contained reference articles (e.g. `reference_graphify_replaces_cgr.md`).

## Usage
Updated whenever a session concludes a body of work worth persisting (e.g. after a feature branch merges, like the graphify/CGR replacement) — the agent commits the new/updated article plus the manifest change, then pushes to remote in a standalone step, decoupled from the outer project's own commit/push flow.

## Troubleshooting
- Before pushing, verify the remote URL scheme (`https://` vs `git@`) to confirm HTTPS+token auth is configured rather than SSH — mismatched assumptions here are the most common cause of push failures.
- Confirm ahead-count via `git status`/`git log origin/main..HEAD` before pushing to avoid surprises.
- If push is rejected for auth reasons, check that the stored HTTPS token/credential helper is valid (GHE tokens can expire independently of GitHub.com SSH keys).

topic: rapid-toolkit Repository Maintenance
summary:
## Purpose
`rapid-toolkit` is a local repository tracking `origin/main`. Periodic rebase onto upstream is required to keep local commits current while preserving in-progress local changes, including carryover rebase work spanning multiple sessions.

## Architecture
- Standard stash/rebase/pop workflow: stash local changes → rebase local branch onto `origin/main` → pop stash → verify local commit(s) reapplied cleanly on top.
- `uv.lock` is the primary conflict-prone file and must be stashed/protected before rebasing, since it frequently diverges between local and upstream dependency state.
- Workflow is resumable across sessions: a rebase task interrupted mid-way can be picked up as a carryover and completed by re-running stash/rebase/pop against the latest `origin/main`.
- Confirmed successful pattern (repeated across multiple sessions, including a carryover task completed by reapplying local commit `e169504` onto `origin/main`): local commit(s) reapply cleanly on top of `origin/main`, and after `stash pop`, working-tree changes (including the protected `uv.lock`) are fully restored with no conflicts.

## Key Files
- `uv.lock` — dependency lockfile most prone to rebase conflicts; always stash before rebase

## Usage
Used whenever local `rapid-toolkit` work needs to be synced with upstream `origin/main` without losing uncommitted or committed local changes. Applicable both for routine syncs and for resuming an interrupted rebase from a prior session.

## Troubleshooting
- If rebase conflicts occur on `uv.lock`, ensure it was stashed before starting `git rebase origin/main`; regenerate/resolve via `uv lock` if needed after rebase completes.
- If `stash pop` reports conflicts, resolve manually and verify the local commit(s) are still present and correctly ordered on top of `origin/main` via `git log`.
- For interrupted/carryover rebases, re-run the full stash → rebase → pop sequence against the current `origin/main` rather than assuming prior partial state is valid.

topic: Performance Dashboard — Runs Table and Auto-Attach
summary:
## Purpose
Displays cross-agent experiment run results in a grouped Runs table with correct goal-alignment scoring, automatic active-run discovery on page load, and proper skip-cell exclusion from rubric scoring.

## Architecture
**Auto-attach on page load:**
- `GET /api/experiments/active-run` endpoint in `api-routes.js` allows fresh page loads to discover an in-progress run without manual clicks
- A Redux thunk and selector in `performanceSlice.ts` call this endpoint; `performance.tsx` wires the result into the component lifecycle

**Goal column scoring:**
- `runs-table.tsx` and `corrected-wins.ts` fall back to `goal_aligned_ratio` when `goal_achieved` is null; avoids blank or incorrect goal-column values for runs where the primary field is unpopulated

**Skip-cell exclusion:**
- `measurement-stop.mjs` checks skip-reason before triggering rubric scoring; skipped cells are excluded from scoring to prevent spurious low scores contaminating aggregate metrics

## Key Files
- `api-routes.js` — `GET /api/experiments/active-run` endpoint
- `performanceSlice.ts` — Redux thunk + selector for active-run discovery
- `performance.tsx` — wires active-run discovery into page load lifecycle
- `runs-table.tsx` — goal column display with `goal_achieved` → `goal_aligned_ratio` fallback
- `corrected-wins.ts` — win calculation with same fallback logic
- `measurement-stop.mjs` — skip-reason guard preventing rubric scoring of skipped cells

## Usage
The Runs table is the primary cross-agent comparison surface. Auto-attach fires on every page load. Scoring fallback and skip-guard fire during the measurement-stop lifecycle, not in the UI layer.

## Troubleshooting
- **Active run not discovered on page load**: check `GET /api/experiments/active-run` response; verify `experiment-run.mjs` pre-created the run directory (endpoint depends on directory presence for header discovery).
- **Goal column shows blank or zero for some runs**: confirm `corrected-wins.ts` fallback is active; `goal_achieved` null is expected for some run types — `goal_aligned_ratio` is the correct fallback field.
- **Skipped cells appear in scoring aggregates with low scores**: verify `measurement-stop.mjs` skip-reason guard is present; skipped cells must not reach the rubric-scoring branch.

topic: Graphify AST-Cache Performance on VirtioFS
summary:
## Purpose
Ensures `graphify update` correctly skips re-parsing unchanged files by relying on an effective AST cache and change-detection mechanism. Without this, every update run re-parsed the full file set (~1335+ files observed) even when no source had changed, defeating the purpose of incremental updates and making them nearly as slow as a full extract.

## Architecture
- Change detection lives in `detect()` (`integrations/graphify/graphify/detect.py`, ~lines 1292–1585), which walks the working tree and compares against cached AST/corpus state to decide which files need re-parsing.
- Root cause of the slowness was **not** algorithmic complexity in `detect()` itself but the underlying **filesystem walk speed** — running inside `coding-services` Docker containers on macOS, the bind mount goes through VirtioFS, which is significantly slower for directory-walk/stat operations than a native Linux filesystem.
- Profiling with `cProfile` was abandoned as too slow/noisy to isolate the hot path; the effective diagnostic approach was direct benchmarking of raw filesystem walk speed in isolation, separate from parsing logic.
- **Fix confirmed and shipped**: the patched `detect()` hot path yields a **4.3× speedup** with byte-identical output versus the pre-fix implementation. End-to-end incremental re-index time dropped from **122s to 31s** on the reference workload.
- Verification markers used to confirm the patch was correctly baked into a rebuilt `coding-services` image: `_rel_by_anchor` occurrence count (≥3 threshold) and `GRAPHIFY_CHANGED` signal consumed by `scripts/graphify-reindex.sh` (≥1 threshold).
- The `graphify` submodule was re-pointed to a personal fork (`fwornle/graphify`) after an upstream push of this fix was rejected due to insufficient permissions — see the submodule SSH/fork-fallback pattern documented under "GitHub Submodule Push — SSH vs HTTPS Authentication."

## Key Files
- `integrations/graphify/graphify/detect.py` (~lines 1292–1585) — `detect()` hot path and corpus-cache logic
- `.detect_corpus_cache.json` — per-file `FileType` classification cache keyed by a SHA-256 corpus signature
- `scripts/graphify-reindex.sh` — consumes the `GRAPHIFY_CHANGED` signal to decide whether an incremental update found changes

## Usage
Invoked implicitly every time `graphify update` runs, either from the dashboard's incremental-update button or via manual/CLI invocation. Performance here directly gates how fast the dashboard's "incremental update" button feels versus a full extract.

## Troubleshooting
- If `graphify update` re-parses the full file set on every run with zero source changes, suspect the AST cache/`detect()` change-detection path rather than the parser itself.
- Benchmark raw filesystem walk time first (isolated from parsing) before profiling parse logic — on macOS Docker hosts, VirtioFS-backed bind mounts are a likely bottleneck for directory walks/stat calls, not CPU-bound parsing.
- Avoid `cProfile` for this class of I/O-bound slowness; it adds too much overhead to reliably isolate the hot function.
- After patching, verify the fix is actually present in the running container (not just source) by rebuilding the `coding-services` Docker image, bringing up a fresh container, and checking for expected marker occurrences (`_rel_by_anchor` count, `GRAPHIFY_CHANGED` count) rather than assuming a source-level patch is live.
- Kill any lingering background `find`/`cProfile` processes before re-running timed tests — stale processes contaminate wall-clock measurements.
- If a push of this fix to the upstream `graphify` repo is rejected, re-point the submodule remote to the personal fork (`fwornle/graphify`) rather than blocking on upstream review; consider upstreaming the perf fix as a follow-up PR once merged locally.

- Change detection lives in `detect()` (`integrations/graphify/graphify/detect.py`, ~lines 1292–1585), which walks the working tree and compares against cached AST/corpus state to decide which files need re-parsing.
- Root cause of the slowness was **not** algorithmic complexity in `detect()` itself but the underlying **filesystem walk speed** — running inside `coding-services` Docker containers on macOS, the bind mount goes through VirtioFS, which is significantly slower for directory-walk/stat operations than a native Linux filesystem.
- Profiling with `cProfile` was abandoned as too slow/noisy to isolate the hot path; the effective diagnostic approach was direct benchmarking of raw filesystem walk speed in isolation, separate from parsing logic.
- **Fix confirmed and shipped**: the patched `detect()` hot path yields a **4.3× speedup** with byte-identical output versus the pre-fix implementation. End-to-end incremental re-index time dropped from **122s to 31s** on the reference workload.
- Verification markers used to confirm the patch was correctly baked into a rebuilt `coding-services` image: `_rel_by_anchor` occurrence count (≥3 threshold) and `GRAPHIFY_CHANGED` signal consumed by `scripts/graphify-reindex.sh` (≥1 threshold).
- The `graphify` submodule was re-pointed to a personal fork (`fwornle/graphify`) after an upstream push of this fix was rejected due to insufficient permissions — see the submodule SSH/fork-fallback pattern documented under "GitHub Submodule Push — SSH vs HTTPS Authentication."

## Key Files
- `integrations/graphify/graphify/detect.py` (~lines 1292–1585) — `detect()` hot path and corpus-cache logic
- `.detect_corpus_cache.json` — per-file `FileType` classification cache keyed by a SHA-256 corpus signature
- `scripts/graphify-reindex.sh` — consumes the `GRAPHIFY_CHANGED` signal to decide whether an incremental update found changes

## Usage
Invoked implicitly every time `graphify update` runs, either from the dashboard's incremental-update button or via manual/CLI invocation. Performance here directly gates how fast the dashboard's "incremental update" button feels versus a full extract.

## Troubleshooting
- If `graphify update` re-parses the full file set on every run with zero source changes, suspect the AST cache/`detect()` change-detection path rather than the parser itself.
- Benchmark raw filesystem walk time first (isolated from parsing) before profiling parse logic — on macOS Docker hosts, VirtioFS-backed bind mounts are a likely bottleneck for directory walks/stat calls, not CPU-bound parsing.
- Avoid `cProfile` for this class of I/O-bound slowness; it adds too much overhead to reliably isolate the hot function.
- After patching, verify the fix is actually present in the running container (not just source) by rebuilding the `coding-services` Docker image, bringing up a fresh container, and checking for expected marker occurrences (`_rel_by_anchor` count, `GRAPHIFY_CHANGED` count) rather than assuming a source-level patch is live.
- Kill any lingering background `find`/`cProfile` processes before re-running timed tests — stale processes contaminate wall-clock measurements.
- If a push of this fix to the upstream `graphify` repo is rejected, re-point the submodule remote to the personal fork (`fwornle/graphify`) rather than blocking on upstream review; consider upstreaming the perf fix as a follow-up PR once merged locally.

topic: Opencode-Headless Execution and Early-Exit Behavior
summary:
## Purpose
Explains why headless agent invocations terminate prematurely relative to interactive sessions, and documents the flags/prompt-design levers needed to reach genuine multi-turn completion. Critical for ensuring experiment cells measure real agent capability rather than an artifact of early termination.

## Architecture
**Root cause:** headless agents terminate on toolless "narration" yields (e.g., "Let me read it…") because they lack a loop-until-done continuation mechanism. This is a structural gap in each agent's headless CLI, not a prompt-wording issue.

**Per-agent loop semantics:**
- `claude -p` — auto-continues natively to completion by design; no extra flags required.
- `copilot -p` — single-turn by default; requires `--mode autopilot --max-autopilot-continues N` (N≈20–30) to loop past narration yields. Without this flag: ~2 tool calls and near-empty diffs; with it: ~30 calls and full implementation.
- `opencode run` — has no in-process auto-continuation knob; interactive session required for convergence. Headless `opencode run -m <model> --dangerously-skip-permissions` will terminate early on narration yields with no workaround short of interactive mode.

**Secondary scoring vulnerability:** `exit(0)` is recorded as `complete` even with an empty diff. Explicit EXECUTION directives in prompts are needed to prevent a vacuous-success false positive.

## Key Files
- `memory/reference_experiment_headless_termination_rootcause.md` — canonical findings document with reproduction commands and per-agent analysis

## Usage
Applies to every experiment cell spawned by the experiment runner. Copilot cells must pass `--mode autopilot --max-autopilot-continues N`. Opencode cells requiring multi-turn convergence must use interactive mode or accept lower completion rates in headless runs.

## Troubleshooting
- **Symptom**: near-zero diff with `complete` status — check whether continuation flags are set for copilot; check whether opencode ran headless vs. interactive.
- **Reproduction**: `opencode run -m rapid-proxy/claude-opus-4.8 --dangerously-skip-permissions` reproduces headless early-exit; compare against interactive session to confirm divergence.
- **Empty-diff false positive**: add explicit EXECUTION directives to the prompt to force the agent past narration-only turns before it exits.

topic: Local Session Storage Cleanup
summary:
## Purpose
Keeps local session storage lean by periodically identifying and removing session directories that are throwaway notes or failed debug sessions with no useful transcript/ingested data — commonly caused by interrupted troubleshooting (e.g. blocked model downloads mid-session).

## Architecture
- Session directories are matched by naming pattern to distinguish disposable/failed sessions from legitimate ones.
- Two recurring categories of safe-to-delete sessions:
  1. **Throwaway note sessions** — created for quick notes, with no lasting value.
  2. **Failed debug sessions** — lack transcript files entirely because a model download or similar external dependency was blocked mid-session, preventing normal session completion (a recurring root cause tied to proxy/network restrictions during troubleshooting; see Proxy/Network Configuration Diagnostics and rapidscribe-meeting Setup insights).
- Before deletion, each candidate session is confirmed to contain no ingested data — i.e., nothing already consumed into observations, the KB, or other durable stores — making the deletion safe and non-destructive to project history.
- Deletions are local-only: no source files are modified; changes are limited to local session state and committed as session-state changes, not code changes.

## Key Files
- Session directories matched by naming pattern (throwaway-note and failed-debug conventions) — location is local session storage, distinct from the `.specstory/history/` LSL repo.

## Usage
Run periodically as routine hygiene, typically after a batch of debug/troubleshooting sessions accumulates (e.g. from blocked model downloads during proxy-restricted network conditions). Each cleanup pass: locate candidates by naming pattern → confirm no ingested data → delete → commit the removal.

## Troubleshooting
- If a session directory lacks a transcript file, check whether it correlates with a known blocked-download event (e.g. Hugging Face model fetch failing due to proxy misconfiguration) before deleting — this is the expected, safe-to-delete pattern, not a sign of data loss.
- Always confirm "no ingested data" before deletion; if a session's contents were partially consumed into the KB or observations store, it should be excluded from a bulk cleanup pass.

topic: rapidscribe-meeting Setup and Model Download
summary:
## Purpose
`rapidscribe-meeting` is a meeting transcription tool that captures system and microphone audio and processes it via FluidAudio-based models. First-run setup requires macOS Screen Recording and Microphone permissions, plus a successful model download from Hugging Face — a step highly sensitive to proxy/network configuration.

## Architecture
- Audio capture pipeline confirmed working once permissions are granted, producing `recording.wav`, `system.wav`, and `mic.wav`.
- Model download is performed by a spawned background worker daemon using Swift's `URLSession` (via FluidAudio).
- The daemon runs as a separate process and **does not inherit** proxy environment variables (`http_proxy`, `https_proxy`, `REGISTRY_URL`) from the parent shell — this causes TLS error `-1200` in proxy-restricted environments (corporate/China networks). Fixing this requires explicitly injecting proxy vars into the daemon's launch environment; this fix has not yet been implemented.
- **Workaround path (offline pre-seed)**: install `huggingface_hub[cli,hf_xet]` via `uv tool install` to get the `hf` CLI, then use it to download the model directly into the local Hugging Face cache, bypassing the daemon's broken proxy path entirely. This pre-seeds the cache so the daemon can find the model locally without needing network access at daemon-launch time.
- Two resolution paths remain open: (a) inject proxy env vars into the daemon's launch environment so `URLSession` picks them up, or (b) complete the `hf` CLI pre-seed so the daemon never needs to download at runtime. Path (b) becomes trivial (no proxy needed at all) when the download is attempted from a network without proxy/geo restrictions.

## Key Files
- `recording.wav`, `system.wav`, `mic.wav` — audio capture outputs confirming permissions/capture pipeline works
- Hugging Face local model cache — target of the `hf` CLI pre-seed workaround
- Daemon launch environment (unidentified exact file) — where proxy env var injection would need to occur for the native-download fix

## Usage
Run at first-time setup of `rapidscribe-meeting` on a new machine or after cache/permission resets. If on a proxy-restricted network, prefer the `hf` CLI pre-seed workaround over waiting for the native daemon download to succeed.

## Troubleshooting
- TLS error `-1200` during model download → confirms the daemon is not seeing proxy env vars; do not attempt to fix by exporting vars in the parent shell alone, since the daemon process does not inherit them.
- If on a network without proxy/geo restrictions (e.g. outside a corporate or China network), strip proxy env vars entirely and retry the download directly — test connectivity first with `curl` against the Hugging Face CDN before running the full download to fail fast on network issues.
- If the download still fails after confirming no-proxy connectivity works via `curl`, suspect stale environment state from prior proxy troubleshooting (see "Proxy/Network Configuration Diagnostics" insight) rather than a `rapidscribe-meeting`-specific bug.

topic: Cross-Agent Initial Conditions Parity
summary:
## Purpose
Ensures that claude, copilot, and opencode receive identical initial conditions within experiment cells so that measured performance differences are attributable to agent capability rather than context asymmetry.

## Architecture
**Cell-layer symmetry (confirmed correct):**
- `neutralizeSandboxRules` deletes `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `.github/copilot-instructions.md`, `.cursorrules`, `.windsurfrules` from all three agents inside every cell.
- KB injection is identical across agents and off by default (see KB Injection Quality Gate insight for the `kb-on` path).

**Global-layer asymmetry (confirmed leak, unresolved):**
- opencode loads `~/.config/opencode/AGENTS.md` (contains context7 rules) on every cell invocation — this file lives outside the sandbox and escapes `neutralizeSandboxRules`.
- claude loads `~/.claude/commands/` globally.
- copilot has no global equivalent, creating an out-of-band instruction bias that favors opencode/claude cells over copilot cells.

**Irreducible differences (document, do not attempt to eliminate):**
- Built-in system prompts, toolsets, and permission models are inherent to each agent's design and are precisely what the comparison is meant to measure — these should be documented as known variables, not neutralized.

**Recommended remediation (not yet implemented):** either (a) enforce zero-rules parity by design across all agents, or (b) equalize by writing canonical sanitized rules into each agent's expected global filename and explicitly neutralizing global config directories (e.g., point `HOME`/`XDG_CONFIG_HOME` at an isolated sandboxed location for the duration of the cell run).

## Key Files
- Sandbox setup code implementing `neutralizeSandboxRules` (cell-level rule stripping)
- `~/.config/opencode/AGENTS.md` — external, non-sandboxed global instruction file for opencode (leak source)
- `~/.claude/commands/` — external, non-sandboxed global instruction directory for claude

## Usage
Applies to every comparative (A/B/C) experiment across claude/copilot/opencode; relevant whenever interpreting a performance delta between agents — reviewers should confirm global config leakage has been accounted for before attributing a win/loss to agent capability.

## Troubleshooting
- If opencode consistently outperforms on tasks touching context7-related conventions, check whether `~/.config/opencode/AGENTS.md` is present on the host running the experiment — this is a known confound, not a capability signal.
- To audit parity for a given run, diff the effective instruction files loaded by each agent (both sandbox-local and global) rather than assuming `neutralizeSandboxRules` alone is sufficient.
- Until remediation is implemented, treat any comparison result as provisional if the host's global agent config directories have not been explicitly neutralized or verified empty.

topic: Experiment Operator Skill — /experiment Orchestrator
summary:
## Purpose
Runs A/B/C comparative experiments across agent variants (claude, copilot, opencode) with fully independent per-cell analysis, producing a ranked comparison matrix without shared starting-point or pre-solved-guidance contamination.

## Architecture
- **Parallel cell execution is the default**: the `experiment.md` skill defaults to `--parallel` execution; all agent cells run concurrently with no shared pre-analysis phase, since a prior shared pre-analysis phase was removed for giving all cells a common starting point.
- **Symptom-only goal enforcement**: experiment goals must describe the observable symptom (e.g., "REC indicator flickers black/green") rather than the diagnosed root cause or the fix, preventing the orchestrator from effectively pre-solving the task before dispatching cells.
- **Validation gate**: after all cells complete (exit code 0), a ranked comparison analysis runs via `experiments-compare.mjs`. A unified batch commit of staged changes only happens after full validation passes.
- **Serial re-run support**: cells can be re-run serially for debugging; exit code 0 from a serial re-run is also a valid completion signal before proceeding to validation.

## Key Files
- `experiment.md` — skill definition; controls default flags (`--parallel`) and goal-phrasing rules enforced at spec-synthesis time.
- `lib/experiments/experiment-runner.mjs` — executes per-cell agent runs.
- `experiments-compare.mjs` — ranks completed cells against each other.

## Usage
Invoked via the `/experiment` operator command with a natural-language description of a bug or task. The orchestrator converts the description into a spec, enforcing symptom-only phrasing, then dispatches one sandbox per agent variant.

## Troubleshooting
- If all cells converge on suspiciously similar solutions, check whether the goal sentence leaked implementation details (root cause or fix) instead of describing only the symptom — this contaminates the comparison.
- If a cell hangs or fails to produce a rubric score (shown as `--`), this is typically due to missing structured evidence capture during the run rather than agent failure — the judge intentionally refuses to fabricate a score without evidence.
