metadata.summary:
## Purpose
Runs A/B/C comparative experiments across agent variants (claude, copilot, opencode) with fully independent per-cell analysis, producing a ranked comparison matrix without shared starting-point or pre-solved-guidance contamination.

## Architecture
- **Parallel cell execution is the default**: the `experiment.md` skill defaults to `--parallel` execution; all agent cells run concurrently with no shared pre-analysis phase, since a prior shared pre-analysis phase was removed for giving all cells a common starting point.
- **Symptom-only goal enforcement**: experiment goals must describe the observable symptom (e.g., "REC indicator flickers black/green") rather than the diagnosed root cause or the fix, preventing the orchestrator from effectively pre-solving the task before dispatching cells.
- **Validation gate**: after all cells complete (exit code 0), a ranked comparison analysis runs via `experiments-compare.mjs`. A unified batch commit of staged changes only happens after full validation passes.
- **Serial re-run support**: cells can be re-run serially for debugging; exit code 0 from a serial re-run is also a valid completion signal before proceeding to validation.

## Key Files
- `experiment.md` — skill definition; controls default flags (`--parallel`) and goal-phrasing rules enforced at spec-synthesis time.
- `lib/experiments/experiment-runner.mjs` — executes per-cell agent runs.
- `experiments-compare.mjs` — ranks completed cells against each other.

## Usage
Invoked via the `/experiment` operator command with a natural-language description of a bug or task. The orchestrator converts the description into a spec, enforcing symptom-only phrasing, then dispatches one sandbox per agent variant.

## Troubleshooting
- If all cells converge on suspiciously similar solutions, check whether the goal sentence leaked implementation details (root cause or fix) instead of describing only the symptom — this contaminates the comparison.
- If a cell hangs or fails to produce a rubric score (shown as `--`), this is typically due to missing structured evidence capture during the run rather than agent failure — the judge intentionally refuses to fabricate a score without evidence. Re-run with evidence capture enabled rather than treating it as a scoring bug.
- Use serial re-run mode to isolate a failing cell without re-running the full parallel matrix.

topic: Token Usage Dashboard — Provider/Model Label Normalization
summary:
## Purpose
Canonicalizes provider and model labels in the token-usage dashboard so that logically identical providers (e.g. `github-copilot` and `copilot`) and model variants (e.g. opus version suffixes) are merged into single slices rather than displayed as separate entries.

## Architecture
- `PROVIDER_ALIASES` map defines canonical mappings: `copilot`+`github-copilot` → `github`, `claude-code` → `anthropic`
- `normalizeProvider()` applies the alias map to raw provider strings from the token DB
- `normalizeModel()` canonicalizes punctuation in model version strings (e.g. `claude-opus-4-8` → `claude-opus-4.8`)
- `mergeByProvider()` and `mergeByModel()` consolidate rows after normalization with narrowed TypeScript return types
- Pie chart, legend, Total Calls chips, and By Model list all consume merged labels via these functions
- Raw token rows carry `provider_keys` (raw provider string) and `model_key` (raw model string including version suffixes)

## Key Files
- `token-usage.tsx` — `PROVIDER_ALIASES`, `normalizeProvider()`, `normalizeModel()`, `mergeByProvider()`, `mergeByModel()`, all chart/legend wiring
- `models.ts` — shared normalization utilities

## Usage
Normalization runs client-side at render time. Raw token rows from the data store are passed through normalization before aggregation; output drives both the By Provider pie chart and By Model list in the token-usage dashboard.

## Troubleshooting
- If a provider appears twice (e.g. both `copilot` and `github-copilot`), verify the alias entry exists in `PROVIDER_ALIASES` in `token-usage.tsx`
- Pre-existing recharts TypeScript typing issues are unrelated to normalization correctness — type errors from recharts do not indicate normalization bugs
- `github-copilot` vs `copilot` naming inconsistencies in the broader token-usage pipeline are a tracked open concern beyond the dashboard layer

topic: Status Line Fast Parser — Regex and Proxy Model Configuration
summary:
## Purpose
`scripts/status-line-fast.cjs` is the fast-path status line parser responsible for computing and rendering score values in the tmux statusbar. It must correctly match lifecycle icons and abbreviation prefixes without producing malformed matches that render scores as `"--"`.

## Architecture
- **Regex bug (open, Task #15)**: Line ~163 contains a negative lookahead `(?![A-Z])` guarding the prefix of lifecycle/abbreviation patterns. The lookahead constrains the prefix but not the suffix, allowing malformed matches that yield `"--"` instead of computed score values.
- **Affected logic**: lifecycle-patch and reunderline logic blocks; lines ~41–84 cover abbreviation-related regex and lifecycle icons.
- **Fix target**: Add a lookbehind constraint to the suffix side of the regex to fully bound the match on both sides.
- **Proxy model name**: The correct model identifier for claude-opus-4.8 in proxy routing is `"claude-opus-4-8"` (hyphen-separated). Using `"claude-opus-4.8"` (dot-separated) causes a 500 proxy error — model not found.

## Key Files
- `scripts/status-line-fast.cjs` — fast-path tmux status line parser; regex bug at line ~163

## Usage
Invoked on every tmux statusbar refresh cycle. Score values rendered in the statusbar are computed here; malformed regex matches silently produce `"--"` display with no runtime error.

## Troubleshooting
- **Scores show `"--"`**: Check line ~163 regex for missing suffix constraint; also verify the proxy model name is `"claude-opus-4-8"` not `"claude-opus-4.8"`.
- **Proxy 500 on model calls**: Confirm model identifier uses hyphens throughout — dots in the version segment are not valid proxy identifiers.
- **Regex scope**: `grep` for negative lookahead patterns in lines 41–84 and ~163 to locate all affected match sites.

topic: Graphify — Code Graph Extraction Engine
summary:
## Purpose
`graphify` is the static-graph extraction engine replacing `code-graph-rag`/Memgraph. It walks a repository, builds a code graph, and serializes it to `graph.json`, which downstream tools (dashboard viewer, `CodeGraphAgent`, MCP queries) read. This insight documents the engine's own data format, configuration knobs, and known failure modes — separate from the dashboard buttons that trigger it (see "Graphify Dashboard — Reindex Update Mechanics").

## Architecture
- **Output format**: `graph.json` uses the NetworkX node-link JSON format, with a top-level `built_at_commit` field recording the commit SHA the graph was extracted from — this powers the dashboard's "commits behind" freshness indicator.
- **Current graph scale** (reference snapshot): ~57,416 nodes, ~80,913 edges, ~4,067 communities — used as the baseline for viewer/LOD design decisions (community-level aggregation is required at this scale; per-node rendering is infeasible).
- **No explicit entity-kind field**: node type (function/class/method) is not stored directly; it must be inferred from label shape and edge relations. A small mapping/inference layer is required for any consumer needing entity-kind classification (deferred, non-blocking for early priorities).
- **Query surface**: consumers other than the raw `graph.json` load can query via MCP tools `get_neighbors` and `get_node` for drill-down without loading the full graph into memory.

## Key Files
- `graph.json` — the extracted graph artifact (NetworkX node-link format)
- graphify's `detect.py` / corpus cache (`.detect_corpus_cache.json`) — file-type classification feeding node composition (see "Graphify Output Validation" insight for anomaly investigation)

## Usage
Consumed by: the system-health dashboard's Code Graph viewer, `CodeGraphAgent`, MCP query tools (`mcp-server-semantic-analysis`'s `analyze_code_graph`, `get_neighbors`, `get_node`), and any UKB/wave-analysis agent needing code-structure context.

## Troubleshooting
- If entity-kind (function vs. class vs. method) is needed and missing, remember it's not stored explicitly — it requires inference from label/edge shape, not a direct field lookup.
- For scale-related rendering/query problems, remember the graph is large (tens of thousands of nodes) — community-level aggregation via the `communities` grouping is the intended entry point, not raw per-node iteration.
- For freshness questions, check `built_at_commit` against current HEAD rather than relying on file mtime alone.

topic: kgbench — Knowledge-Graph Benchmark Harness
summary:
## Purpose
Provides reproducible, automated scoring of Q&A-style benchmark runs against a codebase, so that answers produced by tools/agents can be objectively graded against fixed ground-truth answers rather than judged ad hoc.

## Architecture
- **Query set**: `queries.json` holds benchmark queries paired with ground-truth answer keys, established/verified prior to harness scaffolding.
- **Runner/grader**: `bench.py` executes queries and scores produced answers against ground truth; free-form answers are graded via rubric (including bonus-point criteria for extra correct detail), with an LLM judge used in addition to exact-match checks.
- **Aggregator**: `report.py` consumes grading output and produces a consolidated results report; also supports post-run inspection of raw benchmark records to identify failures or outliers.
- **Run shape convention**: `N queries x M arms x R reps` — "arms" = distinct tool/agent variants under comparison, "reps" = repeated trials per arm. Confirmed real-run example: 9 queries x 2 arms x 3 reps (54 total graded trials), executed as a background job returning exit code 0 on success.
- **Side effect**: full runs regenerate `.detect_corpus_cache.json`-style Q&A/grading pair caches as a byproduct of exercising the underlying codebase's detection pipeline.

## Key Files
- `queries.json` — benchmark query set + ground-truth answer keys
- `bench.py` — runner/grader (rubric + LLM judge)
- `report.py` — aggregation and raw-record inspection tool

## Usage
Run as a background job (`N queries x M arms x R reps` shape) to compare tool/agent variants; upon successful completion (exit code 0), the standard next step is running `report.py` to generate an aggregated report and manually inspect raw records for failures/outliers before drawing conclusions.

## Troubleshooting
- A successful exit code only confirms the run completed — it does not guarantee grading quality; always follow up with `report.py`'s raw-record inspection to catch outliers the aggregate report might mask.
- If Q&A/grading cache files reappear unexpectedly, this is expected background-run behavior tied to the detection pipeline being exercised, not a bug.

topic: Graphify — AST-Cache Incremental Update Performance
summary:
## Purpose
Provides a repeatable, multi-agent skeptical-verification process for evaluating external code-graph and code-memory tools before adopting, referencing, or benchmarking against them — countering marketing inflation in project READMEs, blog posts, and benchmark claims by verifying against primary sources (repos, papers, package registries).

## Architecture
- **Methodology**: parallel research subagents are dispatched per candidate tool, each independently verifying specific claims (star counts, install package/version, benchmark numbers, license, feature-tier claims, underlying research paper) rather than trusting the tool's own marketing.
- **Negative-control testing**: distinguishes genuinely fabricated claims from real-but-exaggerated ones — confirmed DeusData's `codebase-memory-mcp` and its underlying arXiv preprint (2603.27277) are both genuine, not fabricated.
- **Findings — "CodeGraph" article claims**: conflated `@colbymchenry/codegraph` (64k★, real project) with an unrelated 49-star Rust repo, and fabricated benchmark figures. Verified real numbers vs. claimed:
  - CodeGraph: real **~89% fewer tool calls / ~69% fewer tokens**, vs. article's claimed 92% / 71%.
  - `code-review-graph`: real **~65× token reduction**, vs. article's fabricated 85% / 8.2× / <200ms claims.
- Synthesis across all in-flight candidate research (Graphify, `codebase-memory-mcp`, Sourcegraph/grep-context) is aggregated once each subagent's verification completes.

## Key Files
- No dedicated code files — methodology is a research process; findings are captured in research notes/session artifacts rather than a persistent codebase location.

## Usage
Applied whenever a new external code-graph or code-memory tool is being considered for adoption, integration, or benchmark comparison — run before committing to any tool based on its own published claims.

## Troubleshooting
- If a tool's marketing numbers seem too good, don't trust them at face value — dispatch a verification subagent to check the primary source (repo commit history, package registry version, underlying paper) before citing the number elsewhere.
- Watch specifically for **name collisions** between similarly-named but unrelated repos/packages (e.g. the CodeGraph vs. unrelated Rust repo conflation) — verify by package registry (npm/PyPI) identity, not just by name match.

topic: Git Workflow — PR Merge and Branch Cleanup Convention
summary:
## Purpose
Standardizes how long-lived feature branches are landed on `main` and subsequently retired, ensuring both git history and the agent's persistent memory files stay consistent after a merge — preventing stale branch references from misleading future sessions.

## Architecture
- **Merge convention**: feature branches are landed via an explicit GitHub PR (not a local `git merge`), using a merge commit (not squash/rebase), following sequential PR numbering (PR #2, #3, #4, #5 observed so far on `github.com/fwornle/coding`). This preserves the full commit sequence of the feature branch in `main`'s history.
- **PR description quality**: PRs should carry a detailed, substantive description (rationale for design choices, list of specific fixes, test verification results) rather than a placeholder — this is the established norm, not optional boilerplate.
- **Pre-merge verification**: before opening the PR, confirm the branch is a clean fast-forward candidate relative to `origin/main` (no conflicts, ahead-only) so the merge is a no-surprise operation; after merge, local `main` is fast-forwarded to match.
- **Two-phase branch retirement**: (1) at merge time, the branch is deliberately **kept** (not deleted) if project memory files still reference it by name; (2) once memory files are updated to no longer reference the branch, it is safe to delete.

## Key Files
- No fixed files — convention applies repo-wide to any `feat/*` branch in `github.com/fwornle/coding`.

## Usage
Applied whenever a feature (e.g. Token Usage Cost tab, Code Graph Viewer) is complete and ready to land. The agent pushes the branch to `origin`, opens a PR against `main` with a full description, verifies merge cleanliness, and only deletes the branch after confirming no memory-file references remain.

## Troubleshooting
- If a PR shows as non-mergeable, rebase/merge `main` into the feature branch locally first rather than force-pushing over history.
- If a branch is deleted prematurely while still referenced in `MEMORY.md` or a reference article, restore it from the merge commit's parent SHA (`git log --merges`) or from the PR's `head` ref if still available on GitHub.

topic: Proxy Launch Chain — Agent Startup Network Detection
summary:
## Purpose
Configures outbound proxy settings for agent processes (claude, copilot, opencode) at launch time by detecting active network topology and routing OAuth/API traffic through `proxydetox` when available. Includes self-healing capability to start `proxydetox` if it is not running at agent launch time.

## Architecture
**Launch chain (ordered):**
1. `bin/coding` — top-level entry point; invokes the launch script
2. `scripts/launch-claude.sh` — agent-specific launcher; sources common setup
3. `scripts/agent-common-setup.sh` — shared setup for all agents; invokes network detection and applies resulting proxy env vars
4. `scripts/detect-network.sh` — probes network topology; if `proxydetox` is configured but not running, attempts to self-start the daemon before exporting proxy variables

**Self-healing mechanic**: `scripts/detect-network.sh` and `scripts/agent-common-setup.sh` jointly handle the case where `proxydetox` is absent — the detox launcher is invoked to bring the service up rather than failing or silently routing traffic unproxied.

## Key Files
- `bin/coding` — top-level agent invocation entry point
- `scripts/launch-claude.sh` — claude-specific launch wrapper
- `scripts/agent-common-setup.sh` — shared proxy env setup; calls detect-network; contains self-healing trigger
- `scripts/detect-network.sh` — network topology probe; self-starts proxydetox if absent

## Usage
Triggered on every agent launch via `bin/coding`. Consumers are all agent variants (`claude`, `copilot`, `opencode`). Output is exported proxy environment variables consumed by the agent process and its OAuth/API calls.

## Troubleshooting
- **`ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:3128`**: proxydetox was not running at auth time and the self-healing path did not trigger or failed silently — verify `scripts/detect-network.sh` is executable and the proxydetox binary is on PATH
- **Proxy applied when it should not be**: check `scripts/detect-network.sh` return value; the `proxy_enabled_by_user` toggle state (surfaced via `getNetworkStatus()`) governs whether proxy vars are exported
- **`.data/` export churn**: changes to launch scripts can cause `.data/` artifacts to appear modified; this is expected and those files should remain unstaged

metadata.topic: Proxy Launch Chain — Agent Startup Network Detection
metadata.summary:
## Purpose
Configures outbound proxy settings for agent processes (claude, copilot, opencode) at launch time by detecting active network topology and routing OAuth/API traffic through `proxydetox` when available. Includes self-healing capability to start `proxydetox` if it is not running at agent launch time.

## Architecture
**Launch chain (ordered):**
1. `bin/coding` — top-level entry point; invokes the launch script
2. `scripts/launch-claude.sh` — agent-specific launcher; sources common setup
3. `scripts/agent-common-setup.sh` — shared setup for all agents; invokes network detection and applies resulting proxy env vars
4. `scripts/detect-network.sh` — probes network topology; if `proxydetox` is configured but not running, attempts to self-start the daemon before exporting proxy variables

**Self-healing mechanic**: `scripts/detect-network.sh` and `scripts/agent-common-setup.sh` jointly handle the case where `proxydetox` is absent — the detox launcher is invoked to bring the service up rather than failing or silently routing traffic unproxied.

## Key Files
- `bin/coding` — top-level agent invocation entry point
- `scripts/launch-claude.sh` — claude-specific launch wrapper
- `scripts/agent-common-setup.sh` — shared proxy env setup; calls detect-network; contains self-healing trigger
- `scripts/detect-network.sh` — network topology probe; self-starts proxydetox if absent

## Usage
Triggered on every agent launch via `bin/coding`. Consumers are all agent variants (`claude`, `copilot`, `opencode`). Output is exported proxy environment variables consumed by the agent process and its OAuth/API calls.

## Troubleshooting
- **`ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:3128`**: proxydetox was not running at auth time and the self-healing path did not trigger or failed silently — verify `scripts/detect-network.sh` is executable and the proxydetox binary is on PATH
- **Proxy applied when it should not be**: check `scripts/detect-network.sh` return value; the `proxy_enabled_by_user` toggle state (surfaced via `getNetworkStatus()`) governs whether proxy vars are exported
- **`.data/` export churn**: changes to launch scripts can cause `.data/` artifacts to appear modified; this is expected and those files should remain unstaged

topic: rec Tool Installation
summary:
## Purpose
`rec` is a locally-installed agentic tool configured via a spec file. Installation involves prerequisite validation, user preference collection, and agent backend selection before any files are written.

## Architecture
- Install spec lives at `/Users/<USER_ID_REDACTED>/Agentic/_work/rec/install.md`.
- Prerequisites validated before proceeding: `gh auth status`, `git` version, `gh` CLI version.
- Configurable components collected interactively before install: ripgrep integration (on/off), Obsidian integration (on/off), agent backend selection (e.g. OpenCode, Claude).
- Preference gathering is a strict pre-step — installation configuration is only prepared/finalized after all preferences are collected; no installation files are written beforehand.
- Confirmed working preference set from a real setup pass: ripgrep enabled, Obsidian integration disabled, agent backend = OpenCode.

## Key Files
- `/Users/<USER_ID_REDACTED>/Agentic/_work/rec/install.md` — install specification and prerequisite checklist

## Usage
Run through the spec top to bottom for each new setup: validate prerequisites (`gh auth status`, `git`/`gh` versions), interactively collect preferences (ripgrep, Obsidian, agent backend), then prepare/finalize the installation configuration for the target project directory (e.g. `rec` project dir).

## Troubleshooting
- If `gh auth status` fails, authenticate with `gh auth login` before continuing — installation should not proceed with unauthenticated `gh`.
- If preferences appear to be applied before all questions are answered, this indicates a deviation from the spec's strict "gather-then-configure" ordering — re-verify against `install.md`.

topic: Cross-Agent Comparative Experiment — Skill Configuration
summary:
## Purpose
Runs A/B/C comparative experiments across agent variants (claude, copilot, opencode) with fully independent per-cell analysis, producing a ranked comparison matrix without shared starting-point or pre-solved-guidance contamination.

## Architecture
- **Parallel cell execution is the default**: the `experiment.md` skill defaults to `--parallel` execution; all agent cells run concurrently with no shared pre-analysis phase, since a prior shared pre-analysis phase was removed for giving all cells a common starting point.
- **Symptom-only goal enforcement**: experiment goals must describe the observable symptom (e.g., "REC indicator flickers black/green") rather than the diagnosed root cause or the fix, preventing the orchestrator from effectively pre-solving the task before dispatching cells.
- **Validation gate**: after all cells complete (exit code 0), a ranked comparison analysis runs via `experiments-compare.mjs`. A unified batch commit of staged changes only happens after full validation passes.
- **Serial re-run support**: cells can be re-run serially for debugging; exit code 0 from a serial re-run is also a valid completion signal before proceeding to validation.

## Key Files
- `experiment.md` — skill definition; controls default flags (`--parallel`) and goal-phrasing rules enforced at spec-synthesis time.
- `lib/experiments/experiment-runner.mjs` — executes per-cell agent runs.
- `experiments-compare.mjs` — ranks completed cells against each other.

## Usage
Invoked via the `/experiment` operator command with a natural-language description of a bug or task. The orchestrator converts the description into a spec, enforcing symptom-only phrasing, then dispatches one sandbox per agent variant.

## Troubleshooting
- If all cells converge on suspiciously similar solutions, check whether the goal sentence leaked implementation details (root cause or fix) instead of describing only the symptom — this contaminates the comparison.
- If a cell hangs or fails to produce a rubric score (shown as `--`), this is typically due to missing structured evidence capture during the run rather than agent failure — the judge intentionally refuses to fabricate a score without evidence. Re-run with evidence capture enabled rather than treating it as a scoring bug.
- Use serial re-run mode to isolate a failing cell without re-running the full parallel matrix.

topic: Runs Table — ScoreCell Tooltips and Token-Usage Field Structure
summary:
## Purpose
Documents the tooltip architecture for score cells in the runs table and the raw field structure consumed by the token-usage Evolution tab, both of which feed into ongoing normalization work on the performance dashboard.

## Architecture
**ScoreCell tooltips (`runs-table.tsx`):**
- Tooltip content is being refactored into two distinct semantic layers:
  - **Generic metric definitions** (rendered in blue) — static descriptions of what each score dimension measures
  - **Run-specific context** (rendered in black) — dynamic rationale tied to the specific run's result
- Mixing these two concerns in a single tooltip string is the prior defect; separation enables independent updates to definitions vs. per-run rationale

**Token-usage Evolution tab (`token-usage.tsx`):**
- Raw token rows carry two key fields: `provider_keys` (raw provider string, e.g., `github-copilot`) and `model_key` (raw model string including version suffixes)
- `PROVIDER_ALIASES` map canonicalizes `provider_keys` at render time (e.g., `github-copilot` → `copilot`)
- Model normalization for `model_key` (stripping version suffixes, merging variants) is a planned follow-on to provider normalization

## Key Files
- `integrations/system-health-dashboard/src/components/performance/runs-table.tsx` — ScoreCell component and tooltip rendering
- `integrations/system-health-dashboard/src/components/performance/token-usage.tsx` — `PROVIDER_ALIASES`, `normalizeProvider()`, Evolution tab data wiring

## Usage
`runs-table.tsx` is rendered in the Runs view of the performance dashboard. `token-usage.tsx` drives the Evolution tab charts and By Model breakdowns. Both consume data from the token measurement DB via the dashboard server.

## Troubleshooting
- **Tooltip shows generic text only**: run-specific context layer may not be wired; check that the ScoreCell receives the per-run rationale prop
- **Provider appears as duplicate slice in Evolution tab**: `PROVIDER_ALIASES` missing an entry for that raw `provider_keys` value; add alias and redeploy
- **Model variants not merged**: model normalization is not yet implemented; expected behavior until `model_key` normalization is added

topic: Experiment Runner — Token Capture and Proxy Routing
summary:
## Purpose
Ensures that token usage from opencode experiment cells is correctly recorded in the token-usage database by routing proxy and adapter rows through the rapid-proxy provider splice. Without correct routing, cells complete work but produce no token metrics.

## Architecture
- Token capture depends on the runner correctly wiring proxy rows and adapter rows at cell spawn time.
- The rapid-proxy provider requires an explicit adapter splice configured per cell type; opencode cells require their own splice entry distinct from other agents.
- A warning "running with no proxy rows" in run logs is the canonical signal that routing is misconfigured — not a scoring failure or parallel-mode issue.

## Key Files
- `lib/experiments/experiment-runner.mjs` — cell spawn logic; contains proxy and adapter row configuration for each agent type including opencode

## Usage
Token capture runs automatically for every experiment cell. Output is written to the `token_usage` database and consumed by the performance dashboard and scoring pipeline.

## Troubleshooting
- **Symptom**: opencode cell completes but no token records appear in `token_usage` database.
- **Diagnosis**: inspect `runner.log` for the warning "running with no proxy rows" — this confirms a routing misconfiguration, not a cell logic failure.
- **Fix**: verify that `experiment-runner.mjs` includes a proxy row and adapter row entry for the opencode cell type in the rapid-proxy splice configuration.
- Cross-check: confirm other agents (claude, copilot, mastra) have analogous entries as reference for the correct structure.

topic: Experiment Scoring — Recompute and Judge Evaluation
summary:
## Purpose
Allows experiment run scores to be recomputed post-hoc without re-running the full agent cell. Critical for validating proxy or judge-side fixes (e.g., a `cache_control` gap in the copilot adapter) by ensuring a genuine fresh judge evaluation is triggered rather than silently replaying a persisted score.

## Architecture
- `experiments-recompute-score.mjs` is the recompute entry point. By default it preserves the existing stored score rather than issuing a live judge call — meaning any proxy- or judge-side fix (like a `cache_control` correction) is **not exercised** by a naive recompute against a run that already has a cached score.
- A genuine fresh evaluation requires either (a) clearing/invalidating the stored score for the target run before recompute, or (b) invoking recompute with an explicit bypass of the cache-preservation branch.
- This cache-preservation behavior is by design for normal recompute usage (avoid burning judge calls on unchanged runs) but is a trap when the goal is specifically to validate a fix that only affects live judge calls.

## Key Files
- `lib/experiments/experiments-recompute-score.mjs` — recompute orchestration; contains the branch that checks for an existing score and short-circuits the judge call if one is present

## Usage
Operators invoke recompute when they need updated scores without re-running an agent cell (e.g., after a scoring-heuristic or judge-prompt change). When the intent is to verify a proxy/adapter fix specifically, the run's cached score must be invalidated first, otherwise the recompute will report the old (pre-fix) result as if it were confirmation.

## Troubleshooting
- If a recompute run reports an unchanged score after a fix that should have affected judging, first check whether the cache-preservation branch short-circuited the call — inspect for any log line indicating "using cached score" vs. "invoking judge".
- To force a true fresh evaluation, explicitly clear the stored score for the target run (or use a recompute flag that bypasses the cache check) before re-invoking; do not conclude a fix is broken until this step has been confirmed.

topic: Direct-to-Main Merge Workflow — Sole-Developer Repos
summary:
## Purpose
For repositories where the developer is the sole contributor (e.g. personal/agent-memory repos, as opposed to the multi-contributor `coding` repo which mandates explicit GitHub PRs — see "Git Workflow — PR Merge and Branch Cleanup Convention"), local work is merged into `main` and pushed directly, skipping the pull-request process entirely.

## Architecture
- **Workflow shape**: local feature/working-branch commits are merged directly into the local `main` branch and pushed to `origin/main` — no PR is opened, no review step exists.
- **Mandatory pre-merge safety check**: before merging, inspect whether `origin/main` has diverged ahead of local `HEAD` (i.e., the remote has commits the local branch doesn't). If divergence exists, identify specifically **which files** changed on the remote side before proceeding, to avoid a merge/push that silently clobbers those remote-only changes.
- This check-before-merge step is treated as a required gate, not optional — the merge/push itself does not proceed until divergence has been assessed and reconciled.

## Key Files
- No dedicated code files — this is a git operational procedure applied at merge time, verified via standard `git fetch`/`git log`/`git diff` commands against `origin/main`.

## Usage
Applied when a developer wants to land local work on `main` in a repo without a PR-based review culture (e.g. the agent memory repository, which already tracks `origin/main` via a local-ahead-by-N-commits / direct-push pattern rather than PRs). Should not be conflated with the `coding` repo's convention of always merging via an explicit, described PR.

## Troubleshooting
- If `origin/main` is found to be ahead of local `HEAD` by any commits, do **not** merge and push blindly (and especially never force-push) — first diff the diverged files against local state to determine whether the remote and local changes are compatible or conflicting.
- If the diverged files overlap with local changes, reconcile via a proper merge or rebase against the fetched `origin/main` before pushing, rather than assuming local state is authoritative.
- If unsure which repo a "skip the PR" instruction applies to, confirm whether the target repo follows the sole-developer direct-push pattern (e.g. agent memory repo) versus the `coding` repo's PR-mandatory convention — the two are not interchangeable.

topic: Parallel Session Git Working-Tree Entanglement
summary:
## Purpose
Documents the hazard that arises when multiple agent sessions work in parallel on the same physical git working tree: branch checkouts, the staging index, and build outputs are process-wide filesystem state, not session-scoped, so one session's branch switch, staged files, or stale build can silently appear in — or break — another session's context. Also documents the standard mitigation of verifying actual repo state before performing any state-changing git operation.

## Architecture
- Git's current branch (`HEAD`) and staging index (`.git/index`) are shared, mutable, filesystem-level state — any process running `git checkout`/`git switch` or `git add` in the same working tree affects all other sessions operating there.
- A session can discover the working tree unexpectedly checked out to a **different feature branch** than the one it created for its own task (e.g. expecting `feat/graphify-replace-cgr` but finding `feat/token-usage-cost-tab` checked out instead, with that branch's own feature branch still sitting untouched at `main`).
- Files staged by another concurrent session's in-progress work (e.g. staged `CostT...` component files) can appear in a different session's `git status` output, creating false signals about what a given session has changed.
- **Standard mitigation**: before any state-changing git operation (merge, PR creation, commit), independently verify the actual current branch and HEAD commit rather than trusting assumed/cached context — this is a required precursor step, not optional, even when the requested operation seems straightforward.

## Key Files
- No dedicated files — this is a process/procedural hazard tied to the shared `.git/` directory of the outer `coding` repo and its submodules.

## Usage
Applies whenever multiple agent sessions (or a human and an agent) operate on the same repo checkout concurrently. Any session about to run `git merge`, open a PR, or commit should first run `git branch --show-current` and `git log -1 --oneline` (or equivalent) to confirm it matches expectations before proceeding.

## Troubleshooting
- If a session's git status looks inconsistent with what it expects (wrong branch, unexpected staged files, unfamiliar diffs), assume a concurrent session may have altered shared working-tree state — do not attempt to "fix" it by force-checkout or reset without first identifying which session owns the current state.
- Before merging or opening a PR, always re-verify branch/HEAD explicitly; do not rely on a session's initial context snapshot, which may be stale if other sessions have since acted on the same tree.
- Consider using separate worktrees (`git worktree add`) per concurrent session to eliminate this class of entanglement entirely.

summary:
## Purpose
Provides a repeatable procedure for confirming that a persisted insight (a reference article in the observations store) still accurately reflects the codebase — and for safely applying corrections (e.g., stale file:line references) so they persist and are visible in the dashboard UI, rather than being silently reverted by a later export/sync.

## Architecture
- **Structural comparison via `/graphify`**: instead of manually grepping the repo, the `/graphify` skill is invoked directly to locate the insight's referenced code and structurally diff it against the actual codebase (e.g., detecting drifted line numbers after refactors).
- **Canonical persistence layer**: once a discrepancy is found, the fix must be applied at the insight's canonical storage location — the `obs-api` observations store — rather than any cached or exported copy, to ensure it survives future export/sync cycles. A direct Python query against this store is used to both apply and confirm the fix.
- **Mandatory visual confirmation**: project convention requires using the `gsd-browser` tool to navigate the dashboard's insights view and visually confirm the corrected content (e.g., updated line numbers) actually renders in the UI — a fix is not considered complete until confirmed here.

## Key Files
- Canonical observations store (`obs-api`, SQLite-backed) — target for applying persistent insight corrections
- `system-health-dashboard` insights view (Next.js frontend) — where corrected content is visually verified

## Usage
- Run periodically, or on-demand via `/graphify`, whenever an insight's referenced code (file paths, line numbers, function names) may have drifted due to unrelated code changes.
- Used by agents maintaining long-term project memory to keep reference articles trustworthy rather than stale.

## Troubleshooting
- If a correction doesn't appear in the dashboard after being applied, check whether an export/sync job overwrote the canonical `obs-api` record — re-query `obs-api` directly (bypassing dashboard caching) to confirm the persisted state before assuming the update failed.
- If `/graphify` cannot locate the referenced code, the underlying file may have been moved or deleted — treat this as a signal the insight itself may need a full rewrite, not just a line-number patch.

topic: Token Usage Dashboard Label Normalization
summary:
## Purpose
Ensures consistent, deduplicated display of provider and model labels in the Token Usage dashboard by canonicalizing variant spellings before aggregation — e.g. merging `copilot`/`github-copilot`, reconciling `claude-code`/`anthropic`, and normalizing `claude-opus-4-8` → `claude-opus-4.8`.

## Architecture
- `normalizeProvider` uses a `PROVIDER_ALIASES` map to merge provider name variants into canonical labels.
- `normalizeModel` (in `models.ts`) converts hyphen-digit separators to dot-digit form for canonical model identifiers.
- `mergeByProvider` and `mergeByModel` apply normalization before rendering inside `token-usage.tsx`; the former feeds the **By Provider** pie chart, the latter the **By Model** list.

## Key Files
- `token-usage.tsx` — main dashboard component; contains `mergeByProvider`, `mergeByModel`, and rendering logic
- `models.ts` — contains `normalizeModel` with hyphen-to-dot canonicalization

## Usage
Normalization runs at aggregation time, before chart/list render. Both the pie chart and model list consume canonicalized labels. No user action required — normalization is automatic on data load.

## Troubleshooting
- **Duplicate provider/model entries still appear:** The normalization logic in `token-usage.tsx` and `models.ts` is intended but its actual implementation status is unverified — no files have been confirmed read or modified. Treat the architecture above as the design target, not confirmed working code.
- To verify implementation, inspect `token-usage.tsx` for `PROVIDER_ALIASES`, `mergeByProvider`, and `mergeByModel` functions, and `models.ts` for `normalizeModel`.
- If logic is missing, implement normalization in the data aggregation layer of `token-usage.tsx` before the chart/list render pass.

topic: GSD v7.6 Milestone State
summary:
## Purpose
Tracks the active execution state of GSD v7.6. v7.6 succeeded v7.5 (Cross-Agent Comparison Experiment Runner). Version was advanced via manual `ROADMAP.md` frontmatter edit during active phase execution rather than via `/gsd-new-milestone`, preserving in-progress execution state.

## Architecture
- `.planning/ROADMAP.md` — version frontmatter set to `v7.6`; phase registry for all v7.6 phases
- `.planning/STATE.md` — **canonical current-phase pointer**; always read directly, never infer state from ROADMAP alone
- MVP-mode rules apply: `STATE.md` and `ROADMAP.md` must not be hand-edited during plan execution; only the Phase Close-Out Protocol may advance the state machine
- Version was bumped to v7.6 while Phase 88 was executing at plan 3/3; that execution state was preserved through the manual edit approach

## Key Files
- `.planning/ROADMAP.md` — version: v7.6; phase registry
- `.planning/STATE.md` — canonical current phase pointer (auto-generated; do not hand-edit mid-execution)
- `.planning/PROJECT.md` — milestone history and accomplishment record
- `.planning/milestones/` — archived v7.5 and earlier milestone planning artifacts

## Usage
Consulted by all GSD workflow commands (`gsd-audit-milestone`, `gsd-complete-milestone`, phase close-out protocol) to determine current milestone version and phase boundaries. Phase index continuity from v7.5 (phases 81–88+) must be maintained; no index reuse.

## Troubleshooting
- **`STATE.md` shows wrong `milestone_name`**: an unidentified GSD tooling component regenerates `STATE.md` and can overwrite `milestone_name` back to the generic placeholder `"milestone"` — correct manually if this occurs; file is excluded from feature-branch commits
- **`/gsd-new-milestone` called mid-execution**: this zeros progress counters and resets status to planning — recover by restoring prior `ROADMAP.md` state and using direct frontmatter edit for version bump only
- **Pre-flight gate blocks closure**: run `/gsd-audit-milestone v7.6` to produce `.planning/v7.6-MILESTONE-AUDIT.md` before invoking `complete-milestone`

topic: Cross-Session Task Handoff via Memory Files
summary:
## Purpose
Enables an agent to resume a multi-session task (e.g., a remediation or migration effort spanning several work sessions) without re-deriving context from scratch, by persisting a dedicated task-state file that is indexed for discovery at the start of a follow-up session.

## Architecture
- A task-specific markdown file (named by convention, e.g. `project_<task-name>_next.md`) is created under the memory directory (`~/.claude/projects/<project-slug>/memory/`) to capture task scope, current progress, and the concrete next action.
- The file is indexed in `MEMORY.md`, the top-level memory manifest, so it is discoverable without the agent needing to guess the filename or scan the whole memory directory.
- In a follow-up session, the agent loads `MEMORY.md` first, finds the task-specific file reference, and loads it directly — restoring full task context (scope, prior analysis, next step) before resuming execution.
- Real example: `project_t2_egress_lockdown_next.md`, created to hand off the Family B egress lockdown task (removing raw provider keys from `docker-compose.yml`, routing in-process LLM callers through the `:12435` proxy, and verifying via rebuild/grep checks). The follow-up session loaded this file, re-inspected `docker-compose` config and integration code, and confirmed readiness before resuming execution.
- This is distinct from the LSL Session Continuity Bootstrap mechanism (which reconstructs context from recent session log files); memory-file handoff is a deliberate, task-scoped artifact authored specifically for resumption, not a byproduct of normal session logging.

## Key Files
- `MEMORY.md` — top-level memory manifest/index; must be read first in any follow-up session
- `~/.claude/projects/<project-slug>/memory/project_<task-name>_next.md` — task-specific state file (e.g. `project_t2_egress_lockdown_next.md`)

## Usage
Created proactively whenever a task is expected to span multiple sessions or is likely to be interrupted (e.g., long remediation efforts like the egress lockdown T1–T4 series). Read at the start of any session resuming that task, before re-inspecting code, to avoid redundant re-analysis.

## Troubleshooting
- Follow-up session re-derives context from scratch despite a handoff file existing → confirm the file was actually indexed in `MEMORY.md`; an unindexed file is undiscoverable even if it exists on disk.
- Task state file is stale relative to actual progress → update it at the end of every session touching the task, not only at task completion, since sessions may be interrupted mid-task.
- Ambiguity about which task-state file governs a resumed task → check for one file per task rather than a single shared file across multiple unrelated multi-session efforts.

topic: Proxy Detection — bin/coding Statusline and Login
summary:
## Purpose
`coding/bin/coding` and associated proxy scripts are responsible for detecting the current proxy environment (VPN vs. CN network state) and surfacing that state to the statusline and `/login` flow. Incorrect proxy configuration blocks CLI sessions and breaks statusline proxy state reporting.

## Architecture
- **Proxy startup script**: configures proxy environment variables at session start; must adapt dynamically to VPN/CN transitions rather than hardcoding a local proxy address.
- **Statusline proxy state**: reads live proxy env vars to display current proxy status; stale or incorrect vars cause the statusline to report wrong state.
- **`/login` flow**: depends on the proxy being reachable; an unavailable proxy address causes `ECONNREFUSED` and blocks login.

## Key Files
- `coding/bin/coding` — main CLI entry point; sources proxy configuration
- Proxy startup script (within `coding/bin/` or adjacent) — sets proxy environment variables; the source of misconfiguration risk

## Usage
Invoked at the start of every coding CLI session. Proxy detection must succeed for both statusline proxy-state indicators and `/login` to function correctly across network transitions (VPN on/off, CN routing changes).

## Troubleshooting
- **Symptom**: `ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:3128` — a proxy environment variable points to a local proxy address that is not running.
- **Diagnosis**: inspect the proxy startup script via `git diff` against a known-good baseline to identify recently introduced hardcoded proxy addresses; check `LSL` session history files to pinpoint the offending change window.
- **Fix**: restore dynamic proxy detection logic that tests reachability before setting proxy env vars, falling back to direct connection when the local proxy is unavailable.
- **Validation**: after restoring, confirm statusline shows correct proxy state and `/login` succeeds on both VPN and non-VPN network paths.

topic: Performance Dashboard — Tooltip and Help Content Catalog
summary:
## Purpose
Catalogs all 52 interactive and hidden help content items across the Performance dashboard to support documentation planning: identifying which tooltip texts should be elevated to always-visible documentation sections, help cards, or reference articles rather than remaining buried in hover/hidden UI states.

## Architecture
**Coverage scope (52 items total):**
- **Runs table**: 15 columns with conditional formatting logic; each column header and cell-level tooltip documented
- **Compare surfaces**: role-delta explainer, request-aligned diff surface, variant matrix — all tooltip/label text captured
- **Inline timeline**: tooltip content for timeline event markers
- **Turn modals**: help text within turn detail overlays
- **Score dimensions**: directional semantics documented per dimension (higher/lower is better varies by metric)
- **Badge state logic**: all badge variants and their label/aria text
- **`ContextCacheExplainer` modal**: fully documented with source code line-number cross-references; most complex single help component

**Elevation candidates (output of catalog):**
- Two-part reference keyed by priority: items suitable for always-visible documentation sections vs. items suitable for help cards
- Tooltip text that encodes non-obvious semantics (e.g., score directionality, cache hit definitions) is highest priority for elevation

## Key Files
- Performance dashboard page component — contains or composes all 52 cataloged items
- `ContextCacheExplainer` modal — the most documentation-dense single component; line-number cross-references available in catalog output

## Usage
This catalog is a documentation planning input. Use it when:
- Writing reference documentation for the Performance dashboard
- Deciding which help content needs always-visible treatment vs. tooltip-only
- Auditing whether new dashboard features have consistent tooltip coverage

## Troubleshooting
- **Tooltip text not found in source**: some help content is in `title` attributes or `aria-label` props, not visible `<Tooltip>` components — search all three patterns
- **Score direction confusion**: directionality semantics are encoded in tooltip text per dimension; consult catalog before assuming higher = better
- **`ContextCacheExplainer` content gaps**: modal source has line-number refs in catalog; diff against source if modal content drifts from documented state

topic: Documentation Conventions — Benchmark/Comparison Report Placement
summary:
## Purpose
Establishes a consistent repo location for benchmark/comparison reports (e.g., evaluating one tool against another) so such artifacts are discoverable, durable, and don't linger in scratch/temp locations or get lost between sessions.

## Architecture
- **Canonical location**: `docs/benchmarks/<comparison-name>/README.md` — a dedicated subdirectory per comparison, holding a README as the primary write-up.
- **Distinguished from measurement docs**: `docs-content/measurement/` is a separate, existing documentation area (for measurement-system documentation) and is not the right home for one-off comparison reports — the two locations were explicitly compared before choosing `docs/benchmarks/`.
- **Failure mode observed**: a report can be produced (e.g. via ad-hoc analysis or the `/experiment` skill) but left in a scratch/temp location such as `.data/experiments/reports` without ever being committed to a durable docs path — making it invisible to future sessions and effectively "lost" until explicitly searched for and relocated.
- Example instance: a `graphify` vs `grep` comparison report was found sitting in `.data/experiments/reports`, then moved to `docs/benchmarks/graphify-vs-grep/README.md` and committed to `main`.

## Key Files
- `docs/benchmarks/<comparison-name>/README.md` — canonical destination pattern for comparison/benchmark write-ups
- `docs-content/measurement/` — separate, pre-existing docs area for measurement-system documentation (not for ad-hoc comparisons)
- `.data/experiments/reports` — scratch/temp location where reports can accidentally be left uncommitted

## Usage
Consulted whenever a comparison or benchmark report needs a permanent home — e.g., after running the `/experiment` skill or an ad-hoc tool evaluation, the resulting write-up should be moved into `docs/benchmarks/<name>/README.md` and committed, rather than left under `.data/experiments/`.

## Troubleshooting
- If a previously-mentioned comparison report can't be found, check scratch/temp locations first (`.data/experiments/reports`) before assuming it was never written — it may simply never have been committed to its canonical docs location.
- After relocating a report, verify it landed on `main` via git history/directory listing (`git log --follow -- docs/benchmarks/<name>/README.md`) rather than trusting local working-tree state alone, especially if other merges happened concurrently.
- Open questions worth tracking for any given report: whether it was produced via the standard `/experiment` skill pipeline, whether it should surface on the performance dashboard, and whether the source run(s) behind it are subject to quarantine status.

topic: Performance Dashboard — Run Quarantine Status UI
summary:
## Purpose
Surfaces which runs on the performance dashboard are quarantined (excluded from normal reporting/comparison) so users can distinguish trustworthy results from flagged ones at a glance, and can inspect why a run was quarantined.

## Architecture
- Quarantine is an existing status concept applied to runs shown in the performance dashboard's results table/rows.

topic: Code Graph Canvas — Hover Interaction UX
summary:
## Purpose
Governs the visual emphasis behavior when a user hovers over a node in the code graph canvas. Currently causes a severe UX regression on isolated/peripheral communities: hovering can make the entire visualization appear blank except for a single floating node.

## Architecture
- The hover reducer applies aggressive dimming: on hover, all non-hovered nodes, labels, and edges are faded to near-invisibility to spotlight the hovered node's direct neighborhood.
- This breaks down for nodes belonging to isolated or peripheral communities with few or no visible neighbors — dimming everything else leaves only the single hovered node rendered, appearing as a blank canvas with one floating node.
- Diagnosed root cause: the reducer conflates "emphasis" with "isolation" — it treats hover the same as a destructive filter/focus operation rather than a lightweight visual cue.
- Proposed fix direction (not yet implemented): make hover a non-destructive, lightweight emphasis (gentle fade of unrelated elements, selection-style highlight) and reserve aggressive/expansive filtering behavior for double-click interactions instead.

## Key Files
- Hover reducer logic within the code graph canvas component (exact file path not yet captured in digest — identify via search for hover state/dimming logic in the graph canvas component tree)
- `floating-fluttering-shannon.md` — tracks this investigation and planning notes

## Usage
Triggered by any mouse hover over a node in the code graph canvas UI. Affects all users viewing graphs with sparse/isolated node communities, which is common in real codebases with disconnected modules.

## Troubleshooting
- Symptom: hovering over a node in a sparse/peripheral cluster makes the canvas appear empty except for one node.
- Diagnosis: inspect the hover reducer's dim/fade logic — confirm it dims ALL non-hovered elements rather than only direct non-neighbors, and check whether neighbor-detection fails silently for isolated nodes.
- No fix has shipped yet; this is an open, planned-but-unimplemented issue as of the latest digest.

topic: Proxy/Network Configuration Diagnostics
summary:
## Purpose
Provides a repeatable diagnostic procedure for determining the current state of local proxy configuration when a tool's network-dependent operation (e.g. a model or package download) fails or behaves unexpectedly, especially after the network context changes (e.g. moving on/off a corporate or geo-restricted network).

## Architecture
- Forensic review checks: shell environment variables (`http_proxy`, `https_proxy`, `REGISTRY_URL`, etc.), `.zshrc` contents, timestamps of any proxy configuration scripts, and currently running proxy-related processes.
- Goal is to determine whether prior tooling/assistant actions unintentionally modified proxy handling, and whether current proxy state matches the current network context — the review exists specifically because a prior proxy troubleshooting pass is suspected as the root cause of a later, seemingly unrelated failure.
- Diagnostic steps are non-destructive — no configuration files or environment state are modified during the review itself.
- **Retry pattern after network context change**: once outside a proxy-restricted network (e.g. outside China/corporate network), the correct approach is to strip proxy environment variables entirely (not just leave them unset by default) before retrying the blocked operation, then run a lightweight connectivity test (e.g. `curl` against the target CDN) to confirm direct reachability before committing to the full download/operation.

## Key Files
- `.zshrc` — shell startup config; primary place proxy env vars and proxy scripts are set/sourced
- Proxy configuration scripts (paths vary) — inspected for modification timestamps to correlate with when issues began

## Usage
Run this diagnostic whenever a network-dependent tool fails unexpectedly, or immediately after moving to a different network context (home/office/VPN/geo-restricted), before retrying the failed operation. Commonly paired with tool-specific retries such as the `rapidscribe-meeting` Hugging Face model download.

## Troubleshooting
- If proxy env vars are present but stale (pointing at an unreachable or wrong proxy host for the current network), unset them explicitly rather than assuming absence — some shells/tools cache or re-export values from `.zshrc` on every new shell.
- Always validate connectivity with a lightweight `curl` test to the actual target host before re-running a full download — this isolates "network is fine, proxy config was the problem" from "network itself is still restricted."
- If proxy state seems to have changed unexpectedly with no manual edit, check `.zshrc` and proxy script timestamps for recent modifications that may have been made by prior automated/assistant actions.

topic: Experiment Runner — Parallel Execution Design
summary:
## Purpose
Extends the experiment runner beyond serial cell execution to support parallel instance execution, enabling simultaneous multi-cell runs with real-time per-instance monitoring from a unified UI surface.

## Architecture
**Execution mode toggle:**
- Checkbox control switches between serial and parallel execution modes; parallel mode spawns multiple concurrent cell instances.
- `Run` rows written to the experiments API carry `execution_mode: parallel` when parallel mode is active; token attribution is per-instance and accurate.

**Shared background service overlay:**
- Background service activity (not cell-specific) is overlaid across all active timelines, labeled to distinguish it from per-cell metrics.

**Grid miniature terminal visualization:**
- Each parallel instance is represented as a miniature terminal cell (~80×80px) in a grid layout.
- Miniature cells display high-signal metrics only: CPU%, memory%, active tasks, and a compressed activity history strip.
- CRT aesthetic overlay applied to grid tiles for visual consistency.

**Zoomed/expanded terminal view:**
- Expanded cell view uses `zinc-100` text color, 13px font, and relaxed line-height for maximum legibility.
- CRT overlay effect is softened in zoomed state to prevent dimming of text; grid tile CRT aesthetic is preserved unchanged.
- Live parallel-mode switching (serial ↔ parallel) is supported during active runs.

**Run-log enrichment:**
- Each cell log entry is enriched with instance identity for per-cell traceability in the dashboard.

## Key Files
- `experiment-runner.mjs` — runner engine; drives variant × repeat matrix, dispatches parallel cells
- `experiment-launcher.tsx` — UI entry point for launching experiments; execution mode toggle lives here
- `cell-terminal.tsx` — renders individual terminal cells in both grid (compact) and zoomed (expanded) states
- `performanceSlice.ts` — Redux slice managing per-cell execution state and metrics
- `api-routes.js` — REST routes for experiment and run record persistence
- `run-parallel.test.mjs` — parallel execution test suite

## Usage
Operators select parallel mode via checkbox in the Experiment Control Center dashboard before launching a run. The runner spawns concurrent agent processes and streams per-instance metrics to the grid visualization. Zoomed view is accessed by expanding any individual cell tile.

## Troubleshooting
- If token attribution appears aggregated rather than per-instance, verify `execution_mode: parallel` is present on the `Run` row in the experiments API.
- If zoomed terminal text appears dim or unreadable, check `cell-terminal.tsx` for CRT overlay opacity — the softened overlay applies only in expanded state; the grid-tile path should remain unchanged.
- If live mode-switching fails mid-run, inspect `experiment-runner.mjs` for the mode-switch seam introduced alongside the parallel feature.

topic: Graphify Output Validation — Node Statistics Anomaly
summary:
## Purpose
Investigates reported anomalies/incorrect statistics in graphify's output (e.g. node counts that don't match expectations), to determine whether the issue is a genuine data/detection bug in graphify or a misinterpretation of the stats.

## Architecture
- Investigation approach is evidence-first: rather than speculating about causes, query the actual generated output directly using `jq` against the `graphify-out` JSON artifact.
- Specific technique used: `jq` query grouping/counting nodes by `file_type` field to inspect the actual node composition and compare against expected/reported statistics.
- This complements the broader graphify `detect()` pipeline (see Code-Graph-RAG → Graphify Migration insight) — anomalies here could stem from FileType classification issues in `detect.py` or from the corpus cache (`.detect_corpus_cache.json`) serving stale classifications.

## Key Files
- `graphify-out` (JSON output artifact) — subject of the `jq` inspection query
- `floating-fluttering-shannon.md` — tracks this investigation and its findings

## Usage
Run ad hoc when a user/developer flags suspicious or incorrect statistics in graphify's reported output (e.g. via dashboard or CLI summary). The `jq` groupby-`file_type` query is a reusable diagnostic pattern for validating node composition against ground truth.

## Troubleshooting
- To reproduce the diagnostic: run a `jq` query against the `graphify-out` JSON grouping nodes by `file_type` and compare counts to expected values.
- If counts diverge from expectations, check whether the corpus cache (`.detect_corpus_cache.json`) is stale — its `_corpus_signature` should account for file mtime/size changes; a signature mismatch or cache bug could cause misclassified/miscounted nodes.
- Investigation was still in progress as of the latest digest — no root cause or fix confirmed yet.

topic: KB Injection A/B Experiment — Confirmed Results and Invalidated Cells
summary:
## Purpose
Measures whether injecting KB context into the agent's prompt provides a measurable advantage over a baseline (kb-off) arm across multiple task specs. Results determine which specs are valid signal sources and which require redesign before re-running.

## Architecture
**Valid / confirmed cells:**
- `etm-crashloop`: kb-on 4.00 vs kb-off 1.33 accepted facts; ~24× efficiency gain; kb-on retrieves facts in 1–2 tool calls; kb-off exhausts tool budget (11 calls) without recovery. Decisive kb-on win, cleanest isolation of any spec. Confirmed across both the original pilot and the verified-isolation re-run.
- `llm-routing` (original pre-retirement run only): kb-on 2.33/4 facts, 33 steps, 182s; kb-off 0.33/4 facts, 61 steps, 269s — genuine KB injection benefit confirmed before spec retirement.

**Invalidated / structurally defective cells:**
- `leveldb`: fact-level kb-on win (3.00 vs 1.00) but 0/3 acceptance in re-run due to conjunctive gate bug — acceptance is impossible regardless of arm. `persistOnClose` fact is coinable from model memory without KB context. Spec retired.
- `llm-routing` (re-run): inverted result — kb-off 2.00 > kb-on 1.00. Injected KB block contradicts older snapshot code in sandbox (`llm-providers.yaml`); agent trusts code over injection. Re-run measures staleness conflict, not injection value. Spec retired.

**Three structural design defects (must be resolved before next matrix):**
1. **No true control remains**: all three original specs are now retired or compromised; no clean baseline task exists.
2. **Conjunctive gate bug** (`leveldb`): spec's conjunction acceptance gate cannot pass regardless of fact retrieval quality.
3. **Wrong signal measured** (`llm-routing`): spec lives in `rapid-llm-proxy` repo; local `llm-providers.yaml` in sandbox contradicts injected block, so the agent correctly ignores injection — the measurement reflects repo staleness, not KB value.

**18-cell pilot (2 arms × 3 reps × 3 specs) infrastructure result:**
- Pipeline confirmed production-ready: KB injected at 2,556–3,139 chars/cell reliably across all cells.
- 6 kb-on cells (etm×3, leveldb×3) confirmed correct injection sizes within spec before the llm-routing arm ran.

## Key Files
- `kb-ab-facts.mjs` — retirement rationale for `llm-routing` and `leveldb` specs documented here

## Usage
`etm-crashloop` is the only spec with clean, confirmed signal. Any new matrix requires redesigned specs that satisfy the dual validity rule (absent from sandbox AND retrievable from KB) and avoid conjunctive acceptance gates unless all conjuncts are independently KB-gated.

## Troubleshooting
- Inverted kb-on/kb-off results indicate the agent is resolving a conflict in favor of repo content — audit sandbox for files that contradict the injected block.
- 0/N acceptance with non-zero fact retrieval indicates a conjunctive gate bug — verify all acceptance conditions are independently satisfiable.
- Convergent scores (~0.70 both arms) indicate the task is repo-solvable; KB injection is invisible.

topic: KGBench Reporting and Summary Statistics
summary:
## Purpose
Isolates the marginal token cost attributable to a retrieval strategy by subtracting fixed overhead from total observed tokens, enabling fair cost comparisons across retrieval arms, agents, and models.

## Architecture
- **Raw formula**: `content_tokens = in_tokens + out_tokens` — cache tokens (`cache_read_tokens`, `cache_write_tokens`) are explicitly excluded to prevent inflation from longer sessions or differing caching strategies. Implemented in `lib/kgbench/tokens.mjs` via `fromTotals()`.
- **Baseline subtraction**: `content_tokens = total_tokens − baseline`, where baseline captures system prompt + tool schema overhead per `(arm, agent, model)` tuple. Measured once via a real probe session — median `in_tokens` across a trivial "reply OK, no tools" prompt — using `measureBaseline`. Resumed runs reuse prior baselines rather than remeasuring.
- **Token source consistency**: the accounting method (`stream-json` vs. `proxy-db-*`) is recorded alongside each baseline; a mismatch between a cell's token source and its baseline's source is a correctness error — baselines must be subtracted only from totals using the same source.
- Cache tokens are retained on individual rows for diagnostics but excluded from all summary aggregations.

## Key Files
- `lib/kgbench/tokens.mjs` — `fromTotals()` implements the raw exclusion formula; `measureBaseline` probes overhead per `(arm, agent, model)` tuple

## Usage

metadata.summary:
## Purpose
Isolates the marginal token cost attributable to a retrieval strategy by subtracting fixed overhead from total observed tokens, enabling fair cost comparisons across retrieval arms, agents, and models.

## Architecture
- **Raw formula**: `content_tokens = in_tokens + out_tokens` — cache tokens (`cache_read_tokens`, `cache_write_tokens`) are explicitly excluded to prevent inflation from longer sessions or differing caching strategies. Implemented in `lib/kgbench/tokens.mjs` via `fromTotals()`.
- **Baseline subtraction**: `content_tokens = total_tokens − baseline`, where baseline captures system prompt + tool schema overhead per `(arm, agent, model)` tuple. Measured once via a real probe session — median `in_tokens` across a trivial "reply OK, no tools" prompt — using `measureBaseline`. Resumed runs reuse prior baselines rather than remeasuring.
- **Token source consistency**: the accounting method (`stream-json` vs. `proxy-db-*`) is recorded alongside each baseline; a mismatch between a cell's token source and its baseline's source is a correctness error — baselines must be subtracted only from totals using the same source.
- Cache tokens are retained on individual rows for diagnostics but excluded from all summary aggregations.

topic: Knowledge Context Injection — Explore Sub-Agent
summary:
## Purpose
Offloads file search, pattern matching, and structural codebase analysis from the primary `copilot` agent to disposable, stateless `explore` sub-agents running in fully isolated context windows. Each instance is discarded after a single use, never consumes the primary agent's token budget, never modifies source files, and never produces persistent artifacts. Also functions as a standardized session-bootstrap step, a standing on-demand codebase-Q&A capability, and an implicit calibration probe for `Task`-tool reliability and burst/parallel fan-out capacity.

## Architecture
- **Spawn mechanism**: Primary `copilot` agent spawns named `explore` sub-agents via the Claude Agent SDK `Agent`/`Task` tool; each runs in a fully independent context window with no shared state from parent, prior runs, or across session boundaries — confirmed across inter-session gaps of 4+ hours, an 11-hour same-day gap, and multi-day/week-long observation windows, with a recorded unbroken daily-recurrence streak of at least seven consecutive days.
- **Statelessness confirmed at sub-day granularity**: separate spawns within the same day but hours apart each require a fresh, independent initialization. High-volume days can total 30-35+ spawns across four to six distinct time clusters spanning morning through evening.
- **Toolset — commonly includes `bash`/`powershell` even as the "baseline" set**: `grep`, `glob`, `view`, and `bash`/`powershell` together frequently form the default toolset from the very first spawns of a session (including early-morning clusters), not just as a later-day "expanded" addition — the distinction between a strict read-only-only tier and an expanded tier is less rigid than session-order alone would suggest; sometimes described as broader "code intelligence" capability. All tiers remain effectively read-only in practice — no source files are ever created or modified regardless of tier.
- **Response cap**: 300 words per invocation, enforced uniformly, to preserve main-agent context budget.
- **Burst/parallel spawning**: Session start (or mid-session investigation restarts) commonly triggers a cluster of near-simultaneous `explore` spawns — burst size varies session-to-session, from single spawns to tight 2-5-spawn bursts within a single minute, up to large bursts of 10+ sub-agents dispatched within under a minute during the heaviest periods. Short-window repeat-spawning across a wider ~10-15 minute span (e.g., three spawns across ~13-16 minutes, some only ~1-4 minutes apart) is also a recurring pattern, consistent with retries, parallel exploration, or incremental narrowing of an exploration question.
- **Multi-session-per-day pattern**: A single calendar day can include four to six or more entirely separate spawn clusters hours apart, each representing a distinct work session or investigation phase.
- **Initialization latency variance**: Typical spawn-to-ready latency is ~8–40 seconds; occasional slower outliers run up to ~44–60 seconds, and successful runs as long as ~2-3 minutes have also been recorded, all still completing successfully. High latency alone (even up to ~3 minutes) is not by itself a failure signal.
- **Failure mode — spawn errors under heavy parallelism**: Genuine spawn failures (explicit error, not just slow completion) have two recurring, reproducible signatures: (1) a long-hang failure erroring out after ~2.5–2.7 minutes, and (2) a quick failure erroring ~15 seconds after spawn, specifically at the tail end of the day's heaviest concurrent burst. Both failure modes are confirmed reproducible rather than one-off flukes. A retry or a parallel co-spawn in the same cluster has repeatedly been observed to succeed even when a sibling spawn fails, and total daily failure rate remains low (1-2 failures out of 30-35+ spawns).
- **Duplicate event logging**: Identical or near-identical spawn timestamps (millisecond-level variance) are sometimes recorded twice for what is functionally a single spawn event — a known logging artifact, not evidence of an actual duplicate spawn.
- **Result sanitization**: Some observation logs show a `<USER_ID_REDACTED>` placeholder in place of user-identifying content in sub-agent readiness/output records — expected sanitization behavior in the result pipeline, not an error.

## Key Files
- None — this is a runtime spawn pattern via the Agent SDK, not a distinct file-based component; behavior is governed by the primary `copilot` agent's spawn configuration and the Hook/Agent Adapter layer.

## Usage
Invoked at session start (as either a single spawn or a parallel burst of several) and repeatedly on-demand throughout a session — sometimes across many distinct clusters spread across a full day (from a handful up to 30-35+ total spawns on high-volume investigation days), including tight back-to-back or short-window (~10-16 min) repeat spawns — whenever the primary agent needs structural codebase answers without polluting its own context. Each sub-agent returns a capped, structured response and is then discarded — no artifacts are created or modified in any invocation.

## Troubleshooting
- Slow completion (up to ~3 minutes in successful cases) is normal and not itself a failure signal; a genuine failure manifests as an explicit error after an extended run (~2.5–2.7 minutes) or a quick error (~15s) at the tail end of the heaviest concurrent burst of the day — check Agent SDK spawn logs for explicit error timestamps, not just duration, to distinguish the two.
- Both the long-hang failure (~2.5-2.7 min) and the tail-of-burst quick failure (~15s) are reproducible, recurring failure signatures confirmed across independent observation sets on multiple high-volume days.
- Failure rate is low overall (~1-2 per 30-35+ daily spawns) and clusters specifically around the heaviest concurrent-burst windows — if failure rate rises noticeably above this baseline, investigate resource contention before assuming a code regression.
- A failed spawn is typically accompanied by a successful sibling/retry spawn in the same cluster — if all spawns in a cluster fail, escalate as a genuine `Task`-tool reliability regression.
- No files are ever created/modified by this pattern regardless of toolset — if source changes are observed after an `explore` spawn, investigate as a genuine anomaly.
- Duplicate spawn-log entries with matching or near-matching timestamps are a recurring, expected lifecycle-logging artifact, not a real double-spawn — cross-check completion IDs before assuming a genuine duplication bug.
- Toolset composition (`grep`/`glob`/`view` alone vs. with `bash`/`powershell`/code-intelligence) varies even within early-session/morning clusters — don't assume time-of-day strictly predicts tier; this is expected variability, not a misconfiguration, as long as no write/mutation occurs.
- `<USER_ID_REDACTED>` appearing in output logs is expected sanitization, not a bug — see the Hook and Agent Adapters insight for the result-pipeline sanitization pathway if the placeholder appears in unexpected locations.

topic: rapid-llm-proxy — Provider Fallback Chain
summary:
## Purpose
Routes all four coding agents (`claude`, `copilot`, `opencode`, `mastra`) through `rapid-llm-proxy` at `http://localhost:12435` for uniform wire-level token measurement. Proxy routing is injected universally at launcher startup — no per-agent manual configuration is needed or appropriate.

## Architecture
- **Single intercept point**: `rapid-llm-proxy` at `http://localhost:12435`; all agent LLM traffic flows through it

| Agent | Routing Mechanism | Required Value |
|---|---|---|
| Claude Code | `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` | `http://localhost:12435` |
| Copilot CLI | `COPILOT_PROVIDER_BASE_URL` | `http://localhost:12435/v1` |
| OpenCode | existing proxy config | no additional env var |
| Mastra | existing proxy config | no additional env var |

- **Canonical injection point**: `launch-agent-common.sh` sets all required env vars at startup for every supported agent type via `coding/bin/coding`
- **Sub-agent propagation**: Env vars propagate to spawned sub-agents through the hook layer, ensuring dynamically spawned agents also route through the proxy

## Key Files
- `coding/bin/coding` — primary launcher entry point; resolves and invokes `launch-agent-common.sh`
- `launch-agent-common.sh` — universal env-var injection block; the only correct place to add or modify agent routing
- `~/.claude/projects/-Users-<USER>-Agentic-coding/memory/reference_agent_proxy_routing_launcher.md` — persistent per-agent routing reference; recovers canonical routing state across sessions

## Usage
Invoked via `coding/bin/coding <agent-name>`. All proxy env vars are applied before the agent binary receives control. The persistent memory doc provides a durable routing map and should be consulted when reinitializing a session after a gap.

## Troubleshooting
- **Traffic bypassing proxy**: Verify `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` / `COPILOT_PROVIDER_BASE_URL` are present in the process environment after startup; inspect the injection block in `launch-agent-common.sh`
- **Sub-agents not measured**: Confirm env vars propagate through the hook layer — missing hook-layer propagation silently breaks sub-agent coverage without any error
- **OpenCode / Mastra silent routing failure**: These agents rely on their own existing proxy config rather than injected env vars; verify their config files point to `localhost:12435`, not a direct provider URL
- **Lost routing state across sessions**: Consult `memory/reference_agent_proxy_routing_launcher.md` for the canonical per-agent routing map before any re-initialization
