topic: a2a-xpr Documentation Tiering (Quick/Deep Tabs)
summary:
## Purpose
Restructures a2a-xpr's MkDocs documentation into a code-along tutorial (8 chapters, Quick/Deep Dive tiers) that walks a reader from an empty directory to a working a2a/AgentStack deployment, while also serving as a dogfooding exercise that surfaces real defects in the platform's own tooling.

## Architecture
- Tutorial is organized as 8 sequential chapters (~2,000 lines across 16 new doc files) added to `mkdocs.yml` nav, with chapter-discovery and `.gitignore` guards added so chapter artifacts aren't accidentally excluded from the docs build.
- Each chapter is dogfooded end-to-end: every command in the tutorial is actually run against a real checkout, verifying all four A2A paradigms (sync, async+input-required, streaming, push) work as documented.
- Defects found via dogfooding are fixed in the underlying codebase (not just documented), each with a regression test, since the tutorial is treated as an executable spec of the platform's UX.
- Builds on the general Quick/Standard/Deep tab pattern established for other pages (shell page + `pymdownx.snippets` include of moved-verbatim original content), extended here to a full tutorial rather than a per-page split.

## Key Files
- `mkdocs.yml` — nav restructured for the 8-chapter tutorial flow.
- `serve.py` — had a missing "push" wiring bug, now fixed.
- `adp-internal-a2a.md` — had stale claims corrected to match current behavior.
- New chapter doc files (16 total, one plan file e.g. `eager-munching-cake.md`) — the tutorial content itself.
- Test suite additions — regression tests for each of the 5 defects found (gitignore masking docs, push not wired, `make demo` entry point, proxy blocking compose names, NL path type mismatch).

## Usage
Consumed by new developers/readers following the "Build it" tutorial from scratch; also used internally as a validation harness — running through the tutorial is now an effective way to catch regressions in the a2a/AgentStack developer experience (69 tests must pass, `mkdocs build --strict` must be clean).

## Troubleshooting
- If `mkdocs build --strict` fails, check for broken snippet includes or nav entries referencing renamed/moved chapter files.
- If a chapter's commands fail against a fresh checkout, suspect drift between documented behavior and actual code — treat as a defect to fix + regression-test, not just a doc typo.
- Mermaid diagrams (e.g. in chapter 5) should be visually spot-checked on the deployed site after merge, since `--strict` build success doesn't guarantee correct rendering.
- PR merge blockers seen previously: branch already merged into main (check `gh pr view`/`git log` before re-attempting), and GitHub CLI auth mismatches between github.com and internal GHE remotes (verify `gh auth status` against the correct host).

- PR merge blockers seen previously: branch already merged into main (check `gh pr view`/`git log` before re-attempting), and GitHub CLI auth mismatches between github.com and internal GHE remotes (verify `gh auth status` against the correct host).

topic: Agent Configuration — Hardcoded Model Names and Dynamic Discovery Gap
summary:
## Purpose
Documents a known architectural gap where model names in agent configuration files are hardcoded string literals rather than dynamically resolved against live provider availability, risking silent substitution or invalid-ID errors at runtime.

## Architecture
- Current state: model names (e.g. `opus-4.6`) are hardcoded literals in the Claude agent config; no dynamic discovery or validation against provider-advertised model lists occurs at config load time.
- Whether a per-provider dynamic discovery mechanism should replace hardcoded names is flagged as needing broader architectural review — investigation remains early-stage with no artifacts or fixes produced yet.
- Comparison across agents: Copilot CLI audit found no equivalent hardcoding concern — its `model`/`effortLevel` fields are inert (see Copilot CLI insight); Pi agent audit also found no hardcoding issues, serving as a clean baseline.
- Related concern (see LLM Routing insight): hyphen-vs-dot naming convention error — `opus-4.6` uses invalid dot notation and would fail catalogue validation regardless of hardcoding.

## Key Files
- Claude agent config file (location not yet fully documented — pending architectural review)

## Usage
Reference this before proposing fixes to Claude model references; any fix should consider whether to also introduce dynamic discovery rather than just correcting the literal string.

## Troubleshooting
- If Claude agent config references a model with dot notation (e.g. `opus-4.6`), this is invalid per the hyphen-only naming convention and should be corrected to hyphen form (e.g. `claude-opus-4-6`).
- Broader fix (dynamic discovery) is unimplemented — do not assume it exists; treat any model list as static/hardcoded until this gap is closed.

topic: Memory File Triage Workflow
summary:
## Purpose
Provides a repeatable process for finding memory files that exist on disk but aren't linked from `MEMORY.md`, validating their continued relevance, and re-indexing keepers while reclaiming token budget in the index.

## Architecture
- Triage steps: (1) enumerate unindexed files identified during prior size-reduction passes, (2) validate each against current system state (e.g. confirming a proxy-related entry still reflects reality), (3) index confirmed keepers, (4) shorten overly verbose titles/hooks to recover byte/token headroom.
- Distinct from the size-trimming pass itself (see MEMORY.md Maintenance insight) — triage focuses on *discoverability* of previously orphaned files, not just compressing existing index entries.

## Key Files
- `MEMORY.md` — target of re-indexing and title shortening
- Previously unindexed memory files — candidates for validation and indexing

## Usage
Run periodically (or after a size-reduction pass surfaces a backlog) to fold orphaned memory files back into the discoverable index without bloating `MEMORY.md` further.

## Troubleshooting
- If a candidate file's content no longer matches current system behavior, do not index it as-is — update or discard rather than propagating stale facts.
- Track byte/token recovery (e.g. via title shortening) to confirm triage is net-positive for index size, not just adding more entries.

topic: Enhanced Transcript Monitor (ETM) Process Management
summary:
## Purpose
Prevents orphaned `enhanced-transcript-monitor` (ETM) processes from persisting indefinitely by detecting and reaping tmux sessions whose underlying agent process has died, was never launched, has no attached panes, or is fully detached. Without this, ETMs/statusline dots pin forever.

## Architecture
- Two session shapes handled: agent-as-pane-process, and agent-as-child-of-launcher; reaper must walk the full process tree under each tmux session, not just check session existence.
- `HEALTH_DEBUG_ETM=1` env var enables per-tick instrumentation logging showing which reap condition decided each entry's fate — primary diagnostic tool for this subsystem.
- Coordinator-spawned ETMs (via launchd) do not inherit `TMUX` env, so `tmux_pane` is null for these entries — a known source of false signals, linked to a session-id collision bug across projects (e.g. `a2a-xpr` vs `coding`). May require widening `REAP_CONTENT_ACTIVE_MS`.
- tmux pane detection parses subprocess stdout using a separator character; a literal TAB separator previously broke parsing when paths containing tabs/ambiguous characters appeared in output. Fixed by using a printable separator and placing the path field last in the output, parsed via regex treating PIDs as invariant.
- Fail-open hardening: when stdout is non-empty but fails to parse, the reaper returns `null` ("could not tell") rather than an empty Set ("nothing alive"), preventing spurious reaps of live processes. This directly fixed false-positive reaping that blocked Coding's ETM and Spawn respawn logic.

## Key Files
- `health-coordinator.js` (tmux pane detection/parsing logic, notably near the separator-handling call site) — core reaper and ETM lifecycle logic.

## Usage
Runs continuously as part of the health-coordinator's monitoring loop; consumed by statusline rendering and process lifecycle management (Spawn respawn, Coding ETM).

## Troubleshooting
- Enable `HEALTH_DEBUG_ETM=1` and inspect per-tick logs to see which reap condition triggered for a given session.
- If ETMs are being reaped incorrectly (false positives), check for parsing failures on tmux pane detection output — verify the separator character is not colliding with content (e.g. paths) and that unparseable-but-nonempty output returns `null` rather than empty.
- If `tmux_pane` is unexpectedly null for coordinator-spawned ETMs, this is expected (no inherited `TMUX` env) — cross-check against session-id collision issues before assuming reaper malfunction.

topic: Health Coordinator — Tmux Pane Detection and Locale-Dependent Format Parsing
summary:
## Purpose
The health-coordinator enumerates live tmux panes to reconcile ETM (Enhanced Transcript Monitor) sessions, spawning trackers for new sessions and reaping orphaned ones. Environment drift between interactive shells and `launchd` contexts (missing `LANG`/locale env vars) previously broke tmux output parsing, causing false churn and excessive reaps.

## Architecture
- Pane discovery uses `tmux -F` format strings; under `launchd`, non-UTF-8-aware locale settings cause tmux to sanitize/alter separator characters in `-F` output, breaking naive splitting.
- Fix: path-last separator strategy — format string `-F '#{pane_pid} #{session_attached} #{session_path}'`, parsed via regex `/^(\d+) (\d+) (.+)$/` so paths containing spaces still parse correctly (path is captured greedily as the final group).
- Parser now returns `null` on parse failure instead of an empty `Set`, distinguishing "couldn't determine sessions" from "confirmed zero sessions" — the former must not trigger reaping.
- Fix hardened both the spawn half and the reap half of the ETM lifecycle logic.
- `HEALTH_DEBUG_ETM` env var enables tracing of spawn/reap decisions for diagnosing future drift issues; left enabled pending further confirmation under real launchd-driven user sessions.

## Key Files
- `health-coordinator.js` — spawn/reap lifecycle logic (~lines 2100+), pane parsing and format-string handling.

## Usage
Runs continuously as part of the health coordinator's session reconciliation loop, invoked whenever tmux panes are enumerated to spawn or reap ETM trackers.

## Troubleshooting
- Symptom: ETM sessions reaped repeatedly (e.g. ~1/30s) despite being healthy/attached — indicates parse failures being misread as "zero sessions" rather than "unknown".
- Fix verification: rollup shows healthy status for real sessions with zero reaps over an extended window (e.g. 90s) once the null-on-failure + path-last parsing fix is active.
- Enable `HEALTH_DEBUG_ETM` to trace spawn/reap decisions when diagnosing recurrence.
- Full test suite (jest + node:test) should be run clean (no concurrent edits) to confirm stability; isolated failures during concurrent runs are often races, not regressions (see Live-Logging Test Suite insights).

topic: Git Workflow: Isolated Doc Update Branches
summary:
## Purpose
Establishes a working pattern for pushing narrow, reviewable changes without dragging in unrelated dirty files, keeping PRs focused and verifiable before push and merge, and ensuring the docs site deploy is triggered only by validated, merged changes.

## Architecture
- Feature branches created off working state with descriptive, scoped names (e.g. `docs/refresh-sdk-check-dates`, `ci/retry-pages-deploy`, `docs/tier-quick-deep`).
- Only files relevant to the specific change are staged/committed; other dirty files are deliberately left uncommitted.
- Before committing/merging, repository state, branch tracking, and CI status are verified via GitHub CLI (`gh pr checks`, `gh pr view`) to confirm build and security scans passed and no work is duplicated.
- Once CI is green, PR is merged into `main` via GitHub CLI or UI, which — per the Docs Site Publishing Pipeline — is the only event that triggers a live redeploy of the docs site.
- Merging is treated as a deliberate, sometimes deferred step, separate from PR creation and CI validation.

## Key Files
- `.github/workflows/docs.yml` — build+deploy workflow triggered on merge to `main`
- Feature branch history — scoped commits per topic, deleted after merge confirmation

## Usage
Used by agents/developers resuming interrupted work (e.g. after an API usage limit reset) to quickly determine remaining work via `gh pr checks` before duplicating effort, then merge and let the deploy pipeline publish changes.

## Troubleshooting
- If CI checks are pending/failing, do not merge — inspect `gh pr checks <PR#>` output for specifics.
- If a PR is merged but the live site doesn't reflect changes, confirm the deploy workflow actually ran (pull_request events do not trigger redeploy, only push/merge to main).
- If resuming after an interruption, always check CI/PR status first rather than assuming prior state.

topic: Session Context Recovery Workflow
summary:
## Purpose
Provides a repeatable method for recovering session context and establishing work continuity after a break, by reconstructing state from historical session logs and git history rather than relying on memory or mtime metadata.

## Architecture
- Source data: `.specstory/history/*.jsonl` (current format) and legacy `.md` files, organized in year/month subdirectories, separate per project/repo.
- `.specstory/history/` is itself an independent git repo distinct from the outer project repo; its remote URL follows a `<project>-history` naming convention.
- Ordering rule: parse entries by filename ordering (`YYYY-MM-DD_HHMM-HHMM_<hash>`), not file mtime — mtimes can be corrupted by tooling/sync and produce incorrect chronological reconstruction.
- Reconstruction surfaces: merged commit list, incomplete/blocked work items, untracked files, open PR status, and test-suite pass/fail/skip counts.
- Workflow is resumable across interruptions: a session-limit interruption mid-review can be retried after usage reset without losing reconstructed context, since it re-derives from the same durable log/git sources.

## Key Files
- `.specstory/history/*.jsonl` — session log source of truth (current format)
- `.specstory/history/*.md` — legacy format, still parsed for older history
- `git log` — cross-checked against LSL history to confirm merged work items

## Usage
Invoked at the start of a new session (see also the `/sl` skill) to answer: what was recently merged, what's still in-flight, and what should be verified before starting new work (e.g. checking ETM service health status).

## Troubleshooting
- If summary generation is interrupted by a session/usage limit, restart the same workflow after reset — it is idempotent and re-derives from persistent logs, not in-memory state.
- Cross-check reconstructed continuity against `git log` to confirm which items are actually merged to main vs. still open.
- Confirm test-suite health (pass/fail/skip counts) as part of the continuity check before starting new work.

topic: Git Worktree Setup and Merge Workflow
summary:
## Purpose
Documents the manual setup steps required for git worktrees in this project to avoid module-resolution errors, and the safe workflow for merging shared-tree edits without collisions.

## Architecture
- Worktrees do not automatically inherit `node_modules`, `dist`, or the `@fwornle/km-core` package — these must be manually symlinked into each new worktree.
- Missing these symlinks causes `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` errors when running code from a worktree.
- Merge collisions on shared trees stem from lack of pre-edit announcement — contributors editing the same tree concurrently without communicating risk overwriting each other's changes.
- Safe workflow: merge first, then run full test suite, then push — never push directly after merge without verification.

## Key Files
- Worktree directories (per-branch) — require manual symlinks for `node_modules`, `dist`, `@fwornle/km-core`
- Feature branches (e.g. `fix/install-gsd-browser`) — deleted after their fixes are confirmed merged into `main`

## Usage
Applied whenever creating a new git worktree for parallel branch work, and whenever merging a feature branch that touches shared files/paths also being edited elsewhere.

## Troubleshooting
- `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` after switching/creating a worktree → check for missing symlinks (`node_modules`, `dist`, `@fwornle/km-core`) and recreate them.
- Merge collisions on shared files → announce edits before starting work on files others may be touching concurrently.
- After merging, always run the full test suite before pushing; do not rely solely on CI to catch merge-induced regressions.

topic: gsd-browser Tooling and Mermaid Shadow DOM Rendering
summary:
## Purpose
Covers the `gsd-browser` tool's installation, path resolution, and the fresh-install/merge verification workflow used to confirm fixes work for both new and existing users.

## Architecture
- `gsd-browser` resolves its binary/profile by checking both legacy (`${TMPDIR}/chromiumoxide-runner`) and current (`~/.gsd-browser/browser-profile`) locations, falling back gracefully if one is absent.
- `GSD_BROWSER_BIN` env var provides an explicit override/fallback for locating the binary, used when `install.sh` cannot auto-provision it.
- `install.sh` performs fresh-install provisioning but currently has no `.gsd-browser`-specific references for missing-binary cases; this is a known gap deferred as a product decision rather than a bug.
- `verify_installation` includes warning-level coverage for cases where the binary/profile isn't found in either expected location.
- Test suite (Jest + node:test) validates regex-based guard conditions across bounded windows (e.g. 300-char scan windows) rather than unbounded matches, avoiding false negatives/positives in pattern checks.

## Key Files
- `install.sh` — fresh-install provisioning script, missing `.gsd-browser` binary handling (deferred item)
- Jest test files — verify guard-condition regex patterns across bounded windows
- Path-resolution logic (binary lookup) — checks legacy `${TMPDIR}/chromiumoxide-runner` then `~/.gsd-browser/browser-profile`

topic: Repository Rename: a2a to a2a-xpr
summary:
## Purpose
Documents the rename of the main platform repo from `a2a` to `a2a-xpr` on GitHub Enterprise, and tracks ongoing follow-up work to eliminate stale references.

## Architecture
- Rename performed via GitHub API against `DATAPRO/a2a`, resulting in `DATAPRO/a2a-xpr`.
- Local git remote URLs updated to point at the new repo name.
- Hardcoded references to `DATAPRO/a2a` / `datapro-a2a` may still exist across config files (`mkdocs.yml`, `README.md`, workflow files) and require ongoing auditing — a recurring, not fully complete task.
- GitHub Pages remained functional post-rename; the live docs site only redeploys on merge to main, so stale `repo_url`/`repo_name` values persist in the deployed site until a correcting PR is merged (see Docs Site Publishing Pipeline insight).
- Sibling repo `a2a-xpr-history` is being published separately under the same naming convention (see Repo Publishing insight).

## Key Files
- `mkdocs.yml`, `README.md` — contain repo name/URL references requiring periodic verification
- `.github/workflows/*.yml` — CI/deploy configs that may reference old repo name

## Usage
Consulted whenever auditing the codebase for stale `a2a` references post-rename, or when onboarding new automation that needs the correct repo slug.

## Troubleshooting
- Search for `DATAPRO/a2a` and `datapro-a2a` string literals across `.md`, `.yml`, `.toml` files to find unfixed references.
- If docs site still shows old repo name, confirm the fixing PR has been merged to `main` (pull_request events do not trigger redeploy).

topic: SDK Version Tracking Documentation
summary:
## Purpose
Maintains an up-to-date record of external SDK dependency versions (`agentstack-sdk`, `a2a-sdk`) and their pin status, so the team can quickly confirm whether dependencies are current without re-deriving this from package manifests each time.

## Architecture
- Documentation (markdown) contains a "last checked" date marker (around line 192 of the main doc) recording when SDK version info was last verified against upstream sources (PyPI, main branch).
- Verification is a manual process: search project files (md, puml, toml, txt, yml) for SDK references, compare against actual published/current versions, then update the checked-date marker.
- `open-items.md` maintains its own independent "checked date" marker updated separately — do not conflate with the main doc's marker; treat as pending fresh verification unless explicitly refreshed.
- Latest confirmed state: `agentstack-sdk` at 0.7.1 on PyPI / 0.7.2 on main; `a2a-sdk` pinned at 0.3.24; both confirmed unchanged/current as of the most recent check.

## Key Files
- Main documentation file with SDK version section (~line 192 checked-date marker).
- `open-items.md` — separate, independently-tracked checked-date marker.

## Usage
Consulted whenever someone needs to confirm current SDK pin status before starting SDK-dependent work (e.g. code generation, dependency upgrades). Updated by searching the repo for SDK name mentions and comparing versions.

## Troubleshooting
If SDK versions appear stale, re-run the search across md/puml/toml/txt/yml files for the SDK name, verify against PyPI/main branch, and update the checked-date marker in the main doc. Do not assume `open-items.md`'s marker reflects the same verification — check it separately.

topic: Documentation Deployment Pipeline
summary:
## Purpose
Ensures documentation changes render correctly and are pushed to `main` ahead of the automated `deploy-docs` CI workflow, avoiding races between manual verification and automated deployment.

## Architecture
- Verification is performed by building/serving docs via `mkdocs` locally and visually inspecting rendered pages (e.g. admonitions, note boxes) before committing.
- Verification may involve browser automation (e.g. headless Chrome); stale automation processes from prior sessions can interfere and need to be cleaned up before a fresh verification pass.
- Once visual correctness is confirmed, affected documentation files are staged, committed, and pushed directly to `main`, consistent with the project's no-PR workflow — ahead of or alongside the `deploy-docs` GitHub Actions workflow.

## Key Files
- `mkdocs.yml` — build config driving local preview
- pages under `docs/` and `docs-content/` — source of rendered content being verified

## Usage
Run by a developer immediately after editing documentation pages, before relying on the CI `deploy-docs` workflow to publish.

## Troubleshooting
- If `mkdocs serve`/build hangs or automation fails to capture screenshots, check for and kill stale headless Chrome processes left over from prior verification sessions.
- If rendering looks wrong only on the published site but correct locally, confirm the CI `deploy-docs` workflow ran after the latest push (see CI Documentation insight for workflow details).

topic: System Health Dashboard — Release Workflow
summary:
## Purpose
Captures the standard merge procedure used when landing system-health-dashboard feature work (e.g. timezone display fixes) to `main`.

## Architecture
- Changes are developed on a dedicated feature branch and merged to `main` via non-fast-forward merge, preserving branch topology in history.
- `.data/` and `dist/` directories are deliberately excluded from commits — these are runtime-generated/build artifacts not tracked in version control for this integration.
- Feature branch is deleted after merge and the merge commit is pushed to `main`, consistent with the project's broader no-PR git workflow.
- Confirmed example: routing-times timezone fix (commit `af17b0ade`) followed this exact procedure — feature branch merged non-fast-forward, deleted, pushed.

## Key Files
- `integrations/system-health-dashboard/` — root of the affected integration

## Usage
Followed by any developer landing dashboard UI changes; ensures consistent history and avoids committing generated artifacts.

## Troubleshooting
- If `.data/` or `dist/` accidentally appear staged, unstage before commit — they should never be tracked.
- If merge fails as fast-forward, explicitly pass `--no-ff` to preserve branch history.

topic: Statusline Gauge Session Attribution — Cache Fix
summary:
## Purpose
Ensures the tmux statusline's context-window gauge correctly attributes cached session data to the right session, rather than showing stale/mismatched values due to a caching bug.

## Architecture
- A cache mechanism used for session attribution in the statusline gauge was the root cause of incorrect gauge readings, confirmed via diagnostic commands and a measured ~14% accuracy improvement after the fix.
- Fix landed on a dedicated feature branch touching context-attribution-related files (7 files changed, +354/−2), merged to `main` via standard no-fast-forward merge and pushed, per the project's no-PR git workflow.
- Distinct from the ongoing GSD color-rendering wrapper work and from the unresolved statusline documentation sync gap — this addresses data correctness, not rendering or docs.
- Fix is fully landed on `main`; no outstanding work tracked for this specific cache bug.

## Key Files
- Context-attribution-related files touched by the fix (exact paths not itemized across digests)

## Usage
Runs automatically as part of the statusline gauge rendering pipeline for every session; consumed by any developer viewing the tmux statusline.

## Troubleshooting
If gauge values appear mismatched between sessions again, check the attribution cache invalidation logic first — this was the confirmed root cause previously; use the same diagnostic commands/metric (accuracy delta) used originally to confirm regression.

topic: a2a-xpr / a2a PoC Fix Backporting
summary:
## Purpose
Tracks the effort to backport fixes developed in `a2a-xpr` (a fork/derivative PoC) into the original a2a PoC codebase, so bug fixes aren't siloed in one branch/repo.

## Architecture
- Uses prior session history (LSL - likely "last session log") as context to identify which fixes are relevant and transferable.
- Known transferable fix categories: framework disambiguation (clarifying confusion between the beeAI framework and deployment frameworks like langraph/crewai) and a dark mode rendering fix.
- Transfer is not automatic — requires diagnostic inspection of git state and agentstack references in the target codebase to determine applicability, since the two codebases have diverged architecturally.
- Fixes are only partially transferable; deeper analysis of architectural differences is required before applying changes wholesale.

## Key Files
- Not yet finalized; investigation focused on agentstack-related references and git diff/state inspection in the original a2a PoC repo.

## Usage
Relevant to developers maintaining both a2a-xpr and the original a2a PoC in parallel, wanting to keep bug fixes in sync without blindly copying code across divergent architectures.

## Troubleshooting
- Before applying a fix, confirm whether the referenced framework/module (e.g. agentstack, beeAI) is structured the same way in both codebases — do not assume 1:1 portability.
- If unsure which fixes apply, review prior session's diagnostic notes/LSL history first rather than re-deriving from scratch.
- Treat as an ongoing, multi-session task — full backport is not yet complete.

topic: Repo Sync Hygiene — Exports, Agent Instructions, Planning State
summary:
## Purpose
Ensures machine-generated artifacts (observation exports, regenerated `CLAUDE.md`/agent instructions, planning/task state files) don't silently drift from their source inputs by committing them together as a single, verified sync point.

## Architecture
- Standard pre-commit check: run `git status` / `git diff` to confirm only expected/generated files changed before committing — guards against unintended drift slipping into a "sync" commit.
- Ties into the standing pre-commit rule requiring generators to be re-run before commit; this sync pattern is the concrete instance of that rule being applied.
- Typical commit message pattern: `chore: sync exports, agent instructions, and planning state`.
- After committing, local `main` may sit ahead of `origin/main` by one commit; push is a separate, deliberate step, allowing a final manual review window before publishing.

## Key Files
- Generated exports under `.data/` (or equivalent export directories)
- `CLAUDE.md` (regenerated via agent-instruction generator)

## Usage
Run whenever generated artifacts (exports, instructions, planning state) have been regenerated and need to be committed together as a coherent snapshot, typically at the end of a work session before pushing.

## Troubleshooting
- If `git status` shows unexpected files changed beyond the known generator outputs, stop and investigate before committing — likely indicates a stale generator or manual edit drift.
- If push is skipped, local `main` remains one commit ahead of `origin/main` intentionally until manually reviewed.

topic: CLAUDE.md Context-Size Budget and Documentation Maintenance
summary:
## Purpose
Explains and manages context-size warnings triggered by oversized `CLAUDE.md` files, and preserves command/skill definition integrity during trimming passes.

## Architecture
- Two distinct `CLAUDE.md` files exist: global `~/CLAUDE.md` (~4.5k chars) and project-specific `<repo>/CLAUDE.md` (e.g. `/Users/<USER>/Agentic/coding/CLAUDE.md`, can grow to ~47k+ chars). Context-size warnings target the project-specific file, not the global one — manual counts of the global file alone will not match the warning (confirmed discrepancy: 4.5k manual count vs 47.6k/47.8k warning value, resolved by identifying the correct target file).
- The project file accumulates legacy documentation and "war stories" from past work (e.g. km-core, proxy-routing, ETM) over time, pushing it past budget thresholds.
- Recommended mitigation: migrate accumulated documentation out of `CLAUDE.md` into persistent memory files (see Agent Memory insight) rather than deleting it outright.

## Key Files
- `~/CLAUDE.md` — global instructions, small and stable
- `/Users/<USER>/Agentic/coding/CLAUDE.md` — project-specific instructions, grows over time and is the actual warning target
- `scripts/generate-agent-instructions.sh` — generator that produces the project file from numbered topic entries

## Usage
Consulted whenever a context-size warning appears; used to confirm which physical file is responsible before attempting any manual character-count verification.

## Troubleshooting
If a manual char count doesn't match the warning value, check for the existence of a second, project-scoped `CLAUDE.md` — the warning almost always targets the larger project file, not `~/CLAUDE.md`. Resolve oversized files by migrating war-story/legacy content into memory files or by excluding numbered topic entries from the generator (see "CLAUDE.md Size and Content Maintenance" insight).

topic: Agent Memory — Standing Workflow Rules
summary:
## Purpose
Standing workflow rules are stored in persistent memory files scoped to the Claude `Agentic-coding` project, so they survive across sessions and are automatically consulted at the start of each work cycle without requiring manual re-instruction.

## Architecture
- Memory files live under `/Users/<USER>/.claude/projects/-Users-<USER>-Agentic-coding/memory/`.
- Files are Claude project-scoped memory artifacts — read automatically by the agent at session bootstrap for this project path.
- Scoped to the `Agentic-coding` project; rules do not apply globally to other Claude projects.
- **Active standing rule**: always run the generator before committing code (regenerate observation exports, type stubs, compiled output, etc.).

## Key Files
- `/Users/<USER>/.claude/projects/-Users-<USER>-Agentic-coding/memory/feedback_regen_agent_instructions_before_commit.md` — standing pre-commit generator rule

## Usage
Consulted automatically by the agent at session bootstrap for this project; no manual invocation needed.

## Troubleshooting
- If a pre-commit generator step appears skipped, check whether this memory file was read at session start; if missing, re-add the rule to the memory directory.

topic: Network Switching / CN Egress Robustness Investigation
summary:
## Purpose
Investigates whether the network-switching issue — CN firewall/egress re-decision causing ~30s delays — is genuinely resolved, and whether copilot-api's endpoint-checking approach for detecting network state is architecturally sound. Remains an open diagnostic effort; no fix confirmed.

## Architecture
- Diagnostic focus: egress interval timers and copilot probe mechanics that decide when to re-evaluate network routing during a CN firewall transition.
- Live LLM-based monitoring (asking a model to observe/report state) is fundamentally unreliable during the transition itself — chat sessions stall precisely when the firewall re-decision happens, so an in-band probe cannot observe its own outage.
- Proposed alternative: a shell-only, file-based recorder process, independent of any LLM session, that writes a timestamped timeline log during the switch — intended as passive forensics for post-transition review rather than a real-time reactive fix.
- No live fix implemented yet; diagnostic inspection has not reached a conclusion across multiple sessions.

## Key Files
- copilot-api endpoint-checking/probe module (exact path not yet confirmed)
- Proposed but unimplemented: shell-based timeline recorder script

## Usage

topic: EF-412 Feedback Filing — Incomplete/Low-Content Meeting Handling
summary:
## Purpose
Provides principled rules for filing feedback notes when a meeting recording is incomplete or contains mostly non-substantive content (e.g. pre-meeting small talk, partial capture), avoiding both false claims of a missing recording and inflated/speculative feedback content.

## Architecture
- EF-412 Feedback skill rules require notes be shareable, concise, and free of speculation — informal small talk must not be promoted to substantive feedback content.
- Interacts with the `meeting-recording` skill's invariant: an agent must never declare a recording "absent" without verifying its actual presence on disk.
- Resolution approach: check the person's existing feedback folder and vault house style first, to decide whether to log a minimal entry, update Status/Next-actions fields only, or defer filing entirely until more content exists.
- Core tension is between two competing invariants (no speculative content vs. no false "missing recording" claims) rather than a simple bug — requires case-by-case judgment grounded in verified facts (recording duration, actual content) rather than assumptions.
- Applies generally to any short/partial meeting capture, not just specific individuals — the pattern (10 of N minutes recorded, mostly small talk) recurs across different people's feedback folders.

## Key Files
- Vault feedback folders (per-person, under second-brain vault) — checked for existing house style before filing.
- `meeting-recording` skill and `ef-412-feedback` skill definitions under `~/.claude/skills/`.

## Usage
Invoked whenever a feedback meeting recording is short, incomplete, or low-content. Agent must verify recording length/content on disk first, then decide filing approach based on vault house style, never inventing feedback content nor declaring the recording missing without verification.

## Troubleshooting
If uncertain whether to file: check disk for actual recording presence/duration before making any claim about the recording's status. If content is genuinely too thin for substantive feedback, prefer a minimal Status/Next-actions update over fabricated narrative content.

topic: Deploy Documentation CI — Freshness/No-op Detection
summary:
## Purpose
Ensures the Deploy Documentation CI workflow correctly skips build/deploy steps as a no-op when a commit contains no documentation changes, avoiding unnecessary rebuilds and false failure signals.

## Architecture
- The workflow's freshness/gate check inspects changed paths and determines whether docs content requires rebuilding.
- On markdown-only or non-doc commits unrelated to `docs/`/`docs-content/`, the gate correctly identifies "no doc changes" and skips build/deploy — this is expected, correct behavior, not a failure.
- No user notification is warranted when this no-op skip occurs.

## Key Files
- Deploy Documentation workflow definition (GitHub Actions, path not confirmed in this digest — see related `deploy-docs` insight for gate/freshness job structure)

## Usage
Runs automatically on every push; developers should not be alarmed by a "skipped" build/deploy status when no doc-relevant files changed.

## Troubleshooting
If a doc change fails to trigger a rebuild, verify the change touched a path covered by the gate (both `docs/` and `docs-content/` must be watched — see `deploy-docs CI/CD Workflow` insight for the known path-filter gap where `docs-content/`-only changes via `docs/` symlinks can be silently skipped).

topic: Token Usage Database — Query Access Patterns
summary:
## Purpose
Provides an empirical, ground-truth method for verifying LLM proxy token consumption and request counts by querying the SQLite database directly, rather than relying on dashboard screenshots or UI rendering which may lag or misrepresent underlying data.

## Architecture
- Database file: `.data/llm-proxy/token-usage.db`, a SQLite database populated by `rapid-llm-proxy` as it processes requests.
- Direct SQL queries (e.g. filtering by time window, agent, or task) are used to cross-check dashboard-reported figures against raw stored rows.
- This pattern complements — but is distinct from — the read-only `aggregateByTaskId` experimental utility (see Token Aggregator Experiment insight), which is a programmatic, lock-free wrapper for the same DB.
- Also underlies investigation of `prompt_preview` backfill correctness and the unresolved "highlighted rows" visualization question (see related insights).

## Key Files
- `.data/llm-proxy/token-usage.db` — primary SQLite store of per-call token usage, timing, and routing metadata
- `lib/experiments/token-*` — experimental read-only query helper (see Token Aggregator Experiment insight)

## Usage
Used by developers needing to verify actual token/request activity for a given agent or time window (e.g. "how many tokens did fg-chat/pi consume in the last 40 minutes") when dashboard visuals are suspect or unavailable. Typically invoked via ad hoc `sqlite3` CLI queries against the DB file.

## Troubleshooting
- Always query directly against the DB file rather than trusting cached dashboard state when precision matters.
- Ensure queries use `readonly` mode or avoid write locks if the live proxy is running concurrently, to prevent lock contention with the active writer process.
- If row counts seem inconsistent with dashboard totals, check for index/filter mismatches (e.g. `LIKE` vs literal `tool_call_id` filters) — see Token Usage Database — prompt_preview Column insight for a documented pathological full-scan case.

topic: Token Usage Dashboard — Routing Flow Visualization
summary:
## Purpose
Visualizes LLM provider/model routing decisions as a directed graph within the Token Usage dashboard, giving users an at-a-glance view of which routes are actively used in the foreground versus collapsed background traffic, and the relative volume flowing through each.

## Architecture
- `token-usage-flow-tab.tsx` renders routing decisions as a directed graph:
  - 4 foreground routes shown individually (distinct nodes/edges per route)
  - 31 background routes collapsed into 3 aggregate targets to avoid clutter
  - Edge thickness proportional to token volume routed along that edge
  - Fallback routes rendered as dashed edges to distinguish from primary routes
  - Hover tooltips provide per-edge detail on demand
- Supporting edits in `providers.ts`, `token-usage.tsx`, and `token-usage-settings-dialog.tsx` feed routing/provider data into the tab and integrate it into the existing dashboard page.

## Key Files
- `token-usage-flow-tab.tsx` — main graph component
- `providers.ts` — provider data feed
- `token-usage.tsx` — dashboard page integration
- `token-usage-settings-dialog.tsx` — settings wiring

## Usage
Used by developers/operators to visually audit routing distribution without querying the DB directly. Complements the Recorded Call Scrubber and LLM Routing Dashboard decision-ladder view for deeper per-call inspection.

## Troubleshooting
If edge volumes look wrong, verify aggregation counts against `token_usage` DB directly. If graph is too cluttered, check the foreground/background route split threshold (currently 4 foreground / 31 background collapsed to 3 targets).

topic: Health Coordinator — Network State Detection (CN/Corporate Proxy)
summary:
## Purpose
Determines and reports the current network context (open/internet vs. corporate/CN network) so downstream routing and health displays can select the correct proxy pin and behavior.

## Architecture
- Network state is tracked as an explicit state machine field in `health-coordinator.js`, distinct from proxy health.
- On corporate networks, the coordinator pins to a corporate proxy host (e.g. `proxy.muc:8080`); state transitions must reflect this pin accurately rather than defaulting to "open".
- State transition timeline logic determines when to flip between `open` and `corporate` states based on probe results against known endpoints.

## Key Files
- `scripts/health-coordinator.js` — contains netState/threshold logic and state transition timeline

## Usage
Consumed by the coordinator's status output (port 3034) and by LLM routing logic that needs to know whether to route via corporate proxy or direct internet access.

## Troubleshooting
If the coordinator reports "open" while actually on a corporate network, check the netState/threshold logic and state transition timeline for stale or incorrectly-weighted probe results. Verify proxy pin matches actual active proxy (e.g. `proxy.muc:8080`) before concluding a bug.

topic: Opencode Daemon — Session Tracking and Temp File Lifecycle
summary:
## Purpose
Tracks live coding sessions and emits periodic heartbeats reflecting genuinely active (not phantom/stale) session state, with a cursor mechanism preserving position across daemon restarts.

## Architecture
- **Restart mechanism**: managed via `launchctl kickstart`; on restart, the daemon resumes from a preserved cursor position rather than reprocessing from scratch.
- **Session registry**: heartbeats report `registered: N` reflecting only live sessions; a prior cursor bug allowed stale, weeks-old phantom sessions to pollute this count — now fixed, confirmed via restart validation (fast first-heartbeat latency, correct session count).
- **Temp file naming**: previously not unique per-process, creating a cosmetic concurrency edge case during shutdown/startup overlap (state self-corrects on next cycle, so left low-priority). Fixed by making temp paths PID-unique to avoid collisions.
- **Listing convention**: fg-chats (claude, copilot, opencode, pi) are grouped and listed first, followed by services grouped by function.

## Key Files
- Opencode daemon process (managed via launchctl plist) — exact source path not documented in digests

## Usage
Restarted via `launchctl kickstart` when validating fixes to cursor/session-tracking logic or recovering from a stuck state. Heartbeat output (`registered: N`, latency) is the primary observability signal.

## Troubleshooting
If `registered` count includes stale/weeks-old sessions, verify the cursor-fix is active and check temp file naming for PID-uniqueness. Minor overlapping temp file names during shutdown/startup are cosmetic and self-correct within one cycle — do not treat as a blocking bug.

topic: Live-Logging Test Suite — ESM Jest Global Injection
summary:
## Purpose
Ensures live-logging test files running under Node's experimental VM modules (ESM) correctly receive the `jest` global and per-test timeout configuration, matching the pattern used by sibling ESM test suites in the repo.

## Architecture
- Under ESM mode (`node --experimental-vm-modules`), the `jest` global is not automatically injected into test files the way it is under CommonJS Jest execution.
- Test files that rely on `jest.setTimeout()` or other `jest.*` APIs must explicitly `import { jest } from '@jest/globals'` (or equivalent) at the top of the file.
- This pattern must be applied consistently across all files in `tests/live-logging/` that use ESM syntax, mirroring already-fixed sibling suites.

## Key Files
- `tests/live-logging/sweep-sub-agents-dispatcher.test.js` — required explicit `jest` import and `jest.setTimeout()` call after lacking the injected global under ESM
- `tests/live-logging/live-copilot-events-tail.test.js` — sibling ESM suite used as the reference pattern

## Usage
Run via `npm test` (full suite) or in isolation with `node --experimental-vm-modules` for targeted debugging of dispatcher/CLI import reliability issues.

## Troubleshooting
If a live-logging ESM test fails with "jest is not defined" or similar, check for a missing explicit `jest` import — this is not auto-injected under `--experimental-vm-modules`. Cross-check against `live-copilot-events-tail.test.js` for the correct import/timeout pattern.

topic: Pi Agent — Terminal Renderer and HTML Tag Handling
summary:
## Purpose
The `pi` terminal renderer converts markdown to ANSI-styled terminal output. It does not handle raw HTML tags emitted by upstream models, displaying them as literal text instead.

## Architecture
- **Renderer behavior**: correctly processes markdown syntax (e.g. `**bold**`) but treats unrecognized HTML tags (e.g. `<u>`) as literal text — no HTML-to-ANSI translation or tag-stripping occurs
- **Root cause of visible HTML artifacts**: upstream model (e.g. Sonnet-5) emitting raw HTML tags instead of markdown syntax; the renderer's behavior is correct given its markdown-only contract
- **Fix scope**: any fix (mapping HTML tags to ANSI escape codes, or stripping unknown tags) belongs in the upstream `pi` package, not in project code

## Key Files
- `pi` package renderer (upstream dependency) — markdown-to-ANSI conversion; HTML handling absent by design

## Usage
Used whenever the `pi` agent renders model responses in the terminal. Artifact visibility depends entirely on whether the upstream model outputs HTML vs. markdown.

## Troubleshooting
- **Raw HTML tags visible in terminal output**: not a project bug; caused by model emitting HTML instead of markdown. Workaround: prompt the model to use markdown formatting. Long-term fix requires patching or replacing the upstream `pi` renderer.

topic: Generator Provenance Line and Model Name Configuration
summary:
## Purpose
Tracks the correct model name and generator provenance line used in generated artifacts. The provenance line identifies which model produced an artifact and must be present and accurate in all generator outputs.

## Architecture
- Active model name is defined in the `gh-copilot` provider block — source of truth for which model variant is in use (e.g. `claude-sonnet-4.6` vs `claude-sonnet-5`)
- The generator provenance line was removed at some point and requires restoration; its exact prior location is determined by inspecting the provider block configuration directly
- Configuration truth is read from the provider block rather than inferred from assumptions or memory

## Key Files
- `gh-copilot` provider block config — authoritative source for active model name and provenance metadata

## Usage
The provenance line appears in generated artifacts (observation exports, type stubs, compiled output, etc.) to identify the generating model. Consumed by any workflow that audits or traces artifact origin.

## Troubleshooting
- If the provenance line is absent from generated artifacts, locate the `gh-copilot` provider block and verify the model name matches the intended variant before restoring the line
- Do not assume the model name — read it directly from the provider block config to avoid embedding a stale or incorrect value

topic: Observations Database and Backfill Pipeline
summary:
## Purpose
Manages writes to the observations and insights database and provides recovery mechanisms for missing or mis-indexed Qdrant vectors. The backfill pipeline keeps the vector store in sync with km-core source counts across all four collections.

## Architecture
**`writeInsight` return contract:**
- Returns an **object `{legacyId, mintedId}`** — never a scalar `row.id`
- All callers must destructure this shape; treating the return as a scalar silently yields `undefined` for both identifiers

**`legacyId` architectural role:**
- `legacyId` is exclusively a **SQLite→km-core migration bridge field**; it is NOT an application-level idempotency key
- All insight km-core keys are native UUIDs; `legacyId` must never appear in deep-links, display logic, or any public API response
- The canonical public identifier is always `mintedId`

**Backfill idempotency — correct behavior:**
- `content_hash` check must be scoped **per item ID**, not globally across the collection
- A global hash check causes the pruning step to delete correctly-indexed items that happen to share a hash with another item, producing silent data loss
- Per-item scoping is the only safe default; validate collection counts against km-core source after every backfill run

**Collection state (post-repair):**
- insights: 709, digests: 3,450, observations: 8,026, kg_entities: 1,948 — all match source counts exactly

## Key Files
- `backfill.ts` — backfill/reindex pipeline; idempotency logic (per-item hash scoping)
- `src/embedding/listener.ts` — preview cap configuration (1,200 chars)
- `knowledge-injection.md` — calibration notes on content distribution and token utilization
- `kb-ab-etm-crashloop.yaml` — related operational config updated during reindex

## Usage
Run manually to recover from count mismatches between Qdrant and km-core, or after any schema/preview-length change that invalidates existing vectors. Requires obs-api to be stopped for live-mode execution (LevelDB lock contention).

## Troubleshooting
- **Missing items after backfill**: verify `content_hash` check is per-item, not global; a global check silently skips items and then prunes them
- **`legacyId`/`mintedId` mismatch in backfill path**: ensure backfill resolves IDs via km-core native UUIDs, not legacy SQLite row IDs
- **Count mismatch after run**: compare Qdrant point counts per collection against km-core entity counts; re-run backfill with pruning enabled to remove stale vectors
- **LevelDB lock error**: stop obs-api before running live mode; `--dry-run` does not open LevelDB and is safe to run while obs-api is live

topic: Knowledge Context Injection — Embedding Pipeline
summary:
## Purpose
Provides semantic vector search over observations, digests, insights, and KG entities to enable context injection into agent prompts. Backs the standalone retrieval HTTP service (port 3848) consumed by all agent adapter layers.

## Architecture
- **Embedding service** (`src/embedding-service.ts`): uses `fastembed` for local, platform-native text embedding; cache pre-warmed during Docker builder stage and baked into the production image (~90 MB); `local_cache` directory is NOT bind-mounted at runtime
- **Preview generation** (`src/embedding/listener.ts` lines 80–130): **1,200-character cap** for injection-path previews; calibrated against actual content distribution (median ~2,246 chars; decisive facts appear at offsets 520–769; median token utilization 81%, up from 28% at the former 200-char cap)
- **Binding constraint**: moved from a compile-time constant to a **request-time budget**, allowing future tuning without re-indexing
- **Keyword-search path** (`src/retrieval/keyword-search.js` lines 50–80): returns full summaries but yields zero candidates in production — the legacy SQLite store was migrated to km-core, so all traffic flows through the Qdrant path
- **Collection counts (post-reindex)**: insights 709, digests 3,450, observations 8,026, kg_entities 1,948

## Key Files
- `src/embedding-service.ts` — fastembed engine, cache management
- `src/embedding/listener.ts` — preview truncation (1,200-char cap, lines 80–130)
- `src/retrieval/keyword-search.js` — legacy keyword path (inactive in production)
- `backfill.ts` — backfill/re-index pipeline with idempotency logic

## Usage
Triggered on write events for any of the four collections. Output vectors are stored in Qdrant and queried at request time by the retrieval service on port 3848. Agent adapters consume retrieved context via that HTTP endpoint.

## Troubleshooting
- **Stale vectors**: run backfill with per-item hash scoping; a global hash check silently skips valid items and causes the pruning step to delete correctly-indexed entries
- **Zero keyword-search results**: expected — the SQLite source was migrated; all candidates flow through Qdrant
- **Preview too short / decisive facts missing**: the cap is now a request-time budget; adjust without re-indexing; verify offsets 520–769 are within cap
- **Collection count mismatch**: compare Qdrant counts against km-core source; 4,600 stale observation vectors were cleaned in the last full reindex — rerun backfill if counts diverge

topic: Constraint Monitor — no-ukb-bash-command Rule
summary:
## Purpose
Prevents execution of the removed `ukb` binary by flagging shell commands that invoke it. The rule requires careful scoping to avoid false positives on legitimate operations that merely reference the string `ukb` textually (e.g., in `grep` searches, assertion strings, or documentation).

## Architecture
- **Rule location**: `.constraint-monitor.yaml` — contains the `no-ukb-bash-command` pattern
- **Known defect**: the pattern `\s+ukb\s` matches anywhere in command text, not just at command-position; this causes false positives on grep searches and string literals that reference `ukb` without invoking it
- **Required fix**: tighten the pattern to match `ukb` only in command-invocation position (e.g., start of command token after optional path prefix)
- **Launcher contradiction**: the coding launcher's startup reminder instructs agents to run a command that the constraint rule itself blocks — the reminder must be updated to align with the rule
- **Stale MCP server references**: documentation and shell scripts still reference removed MCP servers (`semantic-analysis`, `constraint-monitor`) and require cleanup in MkDocs, install/uninstall scripts, and test scripts

## Key Files
- `.constraint-monitor.yaml` — constraint rule definitions including `no-ukb-bash-command`
- `pattern-test.js` — unit tests for constraint rule patterns
- `verify-rule.sh` — shell-level rule verification script

## Usage
The constraint monitor evaluates bash commands against rules in `.constraint-monitor.yaml` at agent tool-use time via the `preToolUse` hook. The `no-ukb-bash-command` rule fires on any `Bash` tool invocation whose command text matches the pattern.

## Troubleshooting
- **False positive on grep/assertion**: the pattern is too broad; tighten to command-position-only matching before filing as a real violation
- **Launcher startup failure**: if the coding launcher's startup reminder triggers the constraint, update the reminder text to not include the blocked invocation pattern
- **Stale references in docs/scripts**: audit MkDocs source under `docs-content/`, install scripts, and test scripts for references to `semantic-analysis` and `constraint-monitor` MCP servers that no longer exist

topic: llama.cpp Local Inference — Performance Measurement
summary:
## Purpose
Captures how to measure and interpret llama.cpp inference performance, separating one-time initialization cost from steady-state per-turn latency for realistic user-experience profiling.

## Architecture
- **bench.sh harness**: drives `llama-bench` across a matrix of prefill sizes (e.g. 4K, 32K, 128K tokens); each cell is an independent `llama-bench` subprocess
- **Prefill cell cost scaling**: 32K prefill cell runs ~5 min; 128K prefill cell is substantially longer and is commonly skipped to conserve resources
- **Internal timing breakdown**: `llama.cpp` reports three distinct phases — **load** (one-time model initialization), **prompt-eval** (prefill/context ingestion), **generation** (token emission); wall-clock time conflates all three and should not be used as the primary metric
- **Capped prompt test**: a 500-token coding prompt with seed 42 and 8K context is a reproducible real-world latency probe; seed fixes token sequence for comparability across runs

## Key Files
- `bench.sh` — top-level benchmark driver; spawns `llama-bench` per cell; must be terminated before the next cell spawns to skip it cleanly

## Usage
Run `bench.sh` for full prefill matrix results. To capture a partial run, let the current cell finish, then kill `bench.sh` before the next cell spawns. After termination, check for surviving `llama-bench` child processes and kill them manually.

## Troubleshooting
- **Orphaned processes**: terminating `bench.sh` mid-run leaves child `llama-bench` processes running; enumerate and kill them explicitly after script termination
- **Skipping 128K cell**: kill `bench.sh` immediately after the 32K cell completes to prevent the 128K cell from spawning
- **Comparing runs**: use `llama.cpp`'s internal `prompt-eval` and `generation` timing fields, not wall-clock; load time is a one-time cost and should be excluded from per-turn latency comparisons
- **Confirmed reference point**: 32K prefill throughput of ~79.96 tok/s on the optimized system

topic: KB Injection A/B Experiment — Background Writer Services Lifecycle
summary:
## Purpose
The `auto-measure-foreground` and `measurement-reconciler` launchd services write measurement data in the background and must be stopped during active kb-ab experiment task sequences to prevent interference with controlled cell execution.

## Architecture
- Both services are managed via `launchd` and can be queried for state at any time.
- Services are intentionally stopped while any task in the kb-ab sequence is active — this is expected, not a failure condition.
- An EXIT trap handler in the kb-ab sequence script automatically restores both services upon completion of the full task sequence (confirmed to fire on clean code-0 exits), requiring no manual intervention.
- **Completion triggers (dual)**: a direct monitor on the `RE4 COMPLETE` signal plus a fallback process-death detector on the runner PID — whichever fires first delivers the completion ping with smoke-spec verdict and final metrics.
- A process-death backstop runs alongside a `RE4 COMPLETE` log watcher to prevent false "still running" states from blocking the completion ping under hard-kill scenarios.
- The 4-task `kb-ab` pipeline (`kb-ab-etm-crashloop` × 6 cells, `retrieval-service`, `smoke-spec-snapshot-restore-km-core-blockers`, plus report generation) runs sequentially under the EXIT-trap wrapper.

## Key Files
- kb-ab sequence script — contains EXIT trap that restores both launchd services on exit
- launchd plists for `auto-measure-foreground` and `measurement-reconciler`

## Usage
Triggered whenever the kb-ab experiment pipeline executes. The dual completion trigger setup (RE4 signal + process-death fallback) is configured once per run session; no additional setup is required.

## Troubleshooting
- If services appear stopped outside of an active kb-ab run, check whether a prior run exited uncleanly (EXIT trap may not fire on SIGKILL).
- If no completion ping arrives, verify both triggers are active: check the RE4 log watcher and confirm the runner PID is still registered with the process-death detector.
- Services can be manually restarted via `launchctl` if the EXIT trap failed to restore them.

topic: LLM Proxy Dependency (Port 12435)
summary:
## Purpose
The LLM proxy on port 12435 is a required runtime dependency for two subsystems: the coding agent launcher and the kgbench benchmark harness. Both route LLM requests through this proxy; neither has a confirmed fallback or retry mechanism.

## Architecture
- `launch-agent-common.sh` — shared launch script for the coding agent; references port 12435 for LLM proxy connectivity.
- kgbench benchmark harness — also depends on port 12435; full call chain not completely traced.
- The proxy must be live before agent or benchmark processes start; no confirmed fallback or retry logic exists.

## Key Files
- `launch-agent-common.sh` — agent launch entry point; contains port 12435 references

## Usage
Both the coding agent (via `launch-agent-common.sh`) and the kgbench harness route LLM requests through `localhost:12435`. Any benchmark run or agent session requires the proxy to be running first.

## Troubleshooting
If the coding agent or kgbench fails to start or hangs on LLM calls, verify the proxy is running on port 12435 before launching either subsystem. The full dependency chain from kgbench to port 12435 is not completely traced; if failures are observed in kgbench, trace call sites referencing port 12435 in the benchmark harness source.

topic: Project Git Workflow — Forward-Revert Strategy
summary:
## Purpose
Defines how to undo published changes on `main`, covering both the preferred forward-revert approach and the exceptional hard-reset path used when revert leaves the repo in an inconsistent state.

## Architecture
- **Forward-revert (default)**: changes already pushed to `main` are undone via `git revert` (a new commit), never via force-push. After revert, working tree is compared byte-for-byte against the target baseline to confirm full revert.
- **Hard reset (exceptional)**: when `git revert --no-commit` leaves an inconsistent state (e.g. broken submodule pointers), switch to `git reset --mixed <target>` to preserve live service files in `.data/` while removing unwanted commits from history. Force-push with `--force-with-lease`. Rebuild `dist/` after reset.
- **No-PR workflow**: all changes — including reverts and resets — are committed and pushed directly to `main` without pull requests.
- **Recovery artifact**: before any hard reset, save removed commit SHAs to `scratchpad/removed-commits.txt` for potential recovery.
- **Submodule alignment**: after any reset, verify submodule pointers are correct and re-trigger docs deploy if documentation is affected.

## Key Files
- `.git/` — standard git metadata
- `scratchpad/removed-commits.txt` — removed commit SHAs saved before hard resets
- `memory/` — stale memory files (e.g. `memory/feedback_mkdocs_two_image_dirs.md`) may need updating after large reverts

## Usage
Apply forward-revert for routine published-commit rollbacks. Use hard reset only when revert produces an inconsistent tree (broken submodule pointers, unresolvable conflicts). Always verify tree state post-operation and retrigger CI/docs deploy as needed.

## Troubleshooting
- **Inconsistent state after `git revert --no-commit`**: abort with `git revert --abort`, then use `git reset --mixed <baseline-commit>` instead.
- **Submodule pointers broken after reset**: run `git submodule update --init --recursive` and commit corrected pointers.
- **Docs not reflecting reset**: manually retrigger the `deploy-docs` workflow; confirm `dist/` is rebuilt before push.
- **Need to recover removed commits**: consult `scratchpad/removed-commits.txt` for SHAs, then use `git cherry-pick` or `git show` to recover content.

topic: Opencode Early-Exit Bug — Benchmark Impact
summary:
## Purpose
Documents opencode's known early-termination defect, its tool-call trace undercount bug, and the structural dependency on continuation budget — all of which affect benchmark cell validity and cross-agent comparisons.

## Architecture
- **Early-exit failure mode**: opencode exits the task loop on any model turn containing only text and no tool calls, leaving benchmark cells incomplete or with no answer file.
- **Autopilot fix**: integrated into the kgbench adapter; confirmed present for current runs.
- **Trace undercount bug**: caused by `readAnswerFile`'s `no_result` branch failing to carry tool execution records, so `mergeToolTraces()` discarded trace data. A secondary timing bug caused `tail -f` to run before the log file existed. Both are fixed. Corrected mean tool calls: **4.62** (vs. previously reported ~1.25). The original trace showed 20 calls where 66 actually occurred (3.3× undercount).
- **Tool call pattern**: opencode relies heavily on `bash` calls (40/66 in corrected trace) rather than structured search or `write` calls — structurally distinct from Claude and Copilot.
- **Continuation budget**: 13/16 cells at checkpoint required continuation, establishing budget as essential to agent performance measurement. Runs without continuation budget understate opencode capability.

## Key Files
- `readAnswerFile` (test helper) — was missing `await` and dropped tool records in `no_result` branch; both fixed
- `mergeToolTraces()` — discards trace data if upstream records are absent; depends on correct upstream collection
- `docs/benchmarks/coding-v1/` — published report with corrected opencode token counts and provenance

## Usage
All opencode benchmark cells must use the fixed trace collection path. Efficiency comparisons based on ~1.3 tools/question or "20 grep calls across 16 questions" are retroactively invalid. Use corrected figures (4.62 mean tool calls, bash-dominated mix) for cross-agent analysis.

## Troubleshooting
- **Symptom: low tool call counts for opencode**: verify `readAnswerFile` carries tool records through the `no_result` branch and that `mergeToolTraces()` receives non-empty input.
- **Symptom: missing log file on tail**: ensure log file is created before `tail -f` is invoked in the test helper.
- **Duplicate monitor processes**: consolidate to a single watcher; duplicate monitors can cause double-counting or conflicting state.

topic: Production Telemetry Pipeline — Live Data Collection
summary:
## Purpose
Confirms the production telemetry pipeline is active and collecting data. The primary observable artifact is `results.jsonl`, which serves as the live output of the telemetry collection system.

## Architecture
- The pipeline writes collected telemetry records to `results.jsonl` in append/streaming fashion
- Scratchpad state and `results.jsonl` are the two inspection surfaces for verifying pipeline liveness
- No source artifacts are modified during verification; inspection is read-only

## Key Files
- `results.jsonl` — primary telemetry output file; non-empty content confirms active data collection

## Usage
Inspect `results.jsonl` directly (e.g. `tail -f results.jsonl` or `wc -l results.jsonl`) to confirm the pipeline is live and records are being appended. Scratchpad state inspection provides a secondary signal.

## Troubleshooting
- If `results.jsonl` is empty or missing, the telemetry pipeline is not writing output — check the obs-api client write path (see "obs-api Client — Observation Write Path" insight) and confirm the pipeline process is running.
- Scratchpad state showing no recent entries alongside a stale `results.jsonl` indicates the pipeline has stalled rather than simply being idle.

topic: Pi-Agent Routing and ETM Registration
summary:
## Purpose
Documents the verification procedure for confirming that the pi-agent's routing path is correctly established after ETM registration or session recovery, and the diagnostic approach for identifying which provider is serving inference requests.

## Architecture
- **Session baseline**: active tmux sessions and VS Code windows must be audited before assuming the `pi` session needs restarting; an existing clean session may not require relaunch. Sessions are named `coding-pi-<PID>` (e.g. `coding-pi-35390`).
- **VS Code workspace reload risk**: a VS Code workspace reload kills any associated tmux session; mitigated by configuring a `folderOpen` task in `.vscode/tasks.json` to auto-relaunch pi in an integrated terminal, eliminating the need for manual restarts.
- **Routing verification**: post-ETM-registration routing is confirmed via a test inference query (e.g. "There are 3 r's in 'strawberry'") — successful tool response confirms connectivity is restored.
- **Provider identification**: determined via log inspection after the routing test; provider identity is not directly visible from the inference response alone. Confirmed providers include `gh-copilot` backed by `claude-sonnet-5` (~3.4s response times after quota window rollover).
- **Health endpoint**: `localhost:3034/health/state` — use to confirm pi has recovered and is serving.

## Key Files
- `.vscode/tasks.json` — `folderOpen` task that auto-relaunches pi in the integrated terminal; prevents session loss on workspace reload

## Usage
Run after any ETM registration event, VS Code workspace reload, or session restart to confirm the pi-agent's routing and provider are correctly established.

## Troubleshooting
- If pi is unresponsive after a VS Code reload, check whether the tmux session still exists before relaunching; the `folderOpen` task should handle recovery automatically if configured.
- Verify health via `curl localhost:3034/health/state`; a successful response confirms pi is serving.
- If quota is exhausted, pi will recover on the next quota window rollover — monitor response times (~3.4s is normal post-recovery).
- Provider identity is not visible from the inference response; inspect logs to confirm which backend is active.

summary:
## Purpose
Enables sharing a sanitized version of the second-brain repository with department colleagues while fully protecting confidential staff records, meeting recordings, staff discussions, and feedback entries (e.g., EF-412 feedback) — both in current files and in git history.

## Architecture
- **Classification-first prerequisite**: before any split is executed, the full repository structure, git history, and config files must be mapped to classify every file/directory as either confidential or shareable. This classification pass is a standalone task distinct from the actual split implementation.
- **Confidential content**: staff roster, feedback records, personal recordings, named assignments, meeting transcripts, EF-412 feedback entries.
- **Shareable content**: generic function matrices, department setup docs, schema/template files.
- **Tooling enforcement**: `install.sh --private` provisions the confidential vault; `scripts/hooks/pre-commit` (leak-guard) prevents accidental confidential commits to the public repo.

## Key Files
- `second-brain/EF-412/` — confidential; contains all staff feedback folders
- `second-brain/EF-412/staff-roster.md` — confidential HR grading data
- `funktionsmatrix-software-engineering.md` — candidate shareable content
- `scripts/hooks/pre-commit` — leak-guard hook
- `install.sh` — supports `--private` flag for dual-vault provisioning

## Usage
Triggered when preparing a department-facing fork or sanitized clone. Requires a completed classification map before any git history rewriting or repo forking is performed.

## Troubleshooting
- **Classification map missing**: the split effort has been re-initiated from scratch across multiple sessions with no persistent classification artifact — produce and commit a classification map file (e.g., `docs/content-classification.md`) before proceeding to avoid repeated rework.
- **History exposure risk**: current file removal alone is insufficient; git history must also be rewritten (e.g., `git filter-repo`) to remove confidential content from all past commits.

topic: Code-Graph Backend Configuration
summary:
## Purpose
Documents which CodeGraph environment variables are deliberately pinned (and why), and clarifies that responsibility for keeping the code-graph index fresh belongs to external orchestration, not the code-graph backend itself.

## Architecture
- Pinned environment variables and their rationale are documented in a source referred to as `CodeGraphRagConfiguration.md` (or equivalent config-documentation file within the project's docs/insights tree) — searched for repeatedly during KGBench investigations into "why is variable X pinned."
- **Index freshness ownership**: the code-graph backend (Graphify) does not自动ically refresh its own index; freshness is the responsibility of an external orchestration layer (e.g. a scheduled reindex trigger or manual invocation such as the System-Health Dashboard's `POST /api/cgr/reindex` route) that calls into `scripts/graphify-reindex.sh` to rebuild the index on demand.
- This division mirrors the general project pattern of separating passive backend serving (Graphify MCP endpoint) from active index-maintenance orchestration (dashboard-triggered or scheduled reindex).

## Key Files
- `CodeGraphRagConfiguration.md` (or equivalent) — documents pinned env vars and rationale
- `scripts/graphify-reindex.sh` — actual reindex execution, invoked by external orchestration (see System-Health Dashboard CGR Reindex Route insight)
- `config/code-graph.json` — active backend/env configuration surface

## Usage
Consulted when answering questions about why a specific CodeGraph environment variable has a fixed/pinned value, and when explaining who/what is responsible for triggering a fresh reindex of the code graph (answer: not the backend itself — an external caller must invoke the reindex).

## Troubleshooting
- If asked "does the backend keep its own index fresh," the correct answer is no — freshness requires an explicit external trigger (dashboard button, script invocation, or scheduled job), not automatic backend-side refresh.
- If a pinned environment variable's rationale is unclear, check the documentation source (`CodeGraphRagConfiguration.md` or equivalent) rather than inferring intent from the variable name alone — pins often exist for compatibility/stability reasons not obvious from the code.

topic: GSD Worktree Cleanup — Stale Branch Pruning
summary:
## Purpose
Prevents unbounded accumulation of stale `worktree-agent-*` branches and their worktree directories after GSD parallel-wave work has already been squash-merged into `main` under different commit SHAs than the original branch tips.

## Architecture
- After a GSD wave merges (see GSD Multi-Worktree Merge Procedure), individual `worktree-agent-*` branches often survive on disk even though their content is already upstream — because squash-merge produces new SHAs on `main`, a plain branch-merged-check (`git branch --merged`) will not detect them as merged.
- **Patch-equivalence verification**: `git cherry <upstream> <branch>` is used to confirm a branch's commits are patch-equivalent to commits already on `main`, even though the SHAs differ — this is the correct check for squash-merged branches, not `--merged`.
- Each candidate worktree is also checked for uncommitted changes before deletion, to avoid silently losing unmerged work.
- Not all worktrees are cleanup candidates: branches with genuinely unique, not-yet-upstreamed work (e.g. `avenue/exp-*` branches) must be preserved; other worktrees (run-restore scaffolding, detached-HEAD states) are left untouched as they serve other purposes.

## Key Files
- `.claude/worktrees/` — directory holding per-branch worktree checkouts for the `coding` project

## Usage
Run periodically (or after a GSD wave closes) to prune branches whose work is confirmed already merged. Deleted branch SHAs should be recorded before deletion/garbage collection, to allow recovery via `git reflog` or `git cat-file` if a branch was pruned in error.

## Troubleshooting
- If a branch appears unmerged via `git branch --merged main` but its work is known to be upstream, re-check with `git cherry <main> <branch>` — squash-merges break the standard merged-branch detection.
- Before deleting a worktree, run `git status` inside it to confirm no uncommitted changes; abort deletion if any are found and investigate first.
- If a deleted branch's work turns out to be needed, recover via the recorded commit SHA (`git branch <name> <sha>` or `git checkout <sha>`) as long as garbage collection has not yet run.

topic: Specstory History File Privacy & Migration
summary:
## Purpose
Prevent `.specstory` AI session-history transcripts from being tracked in project repos readable by all internal GHE users. History must live in a dedicated private `<repo-name>-history` repository per project, physically nested inside the working repo's `.specstory/history/` path but backed by its own separate git remote, and must never enter the parent project's git history.

## Architecture
- **Convention**: each project's specstory history pairs with a private repo named `<repo-name>-history`, nested as its own git repo at `<working-repo>/.specstory/history/.git`. Example: for `a2a`, this is `Frank-Woernle/a2a-history` (developer's personal namespace, separate from the org-owned parent repo).
- **Migration script phases** (`scripts/migrate-history-to-private.sh`):
  - **Phase A** — untrack `.specstory/history/` from the working repo and add it to `.gitignore` (non-destructive).
  - **Phase C** — push existing transcript content to the private history repo remote.
- **Guardrails hardened after the a2a leak incident**: the coding project's `.gitignore`, "Guard 3a" check, and the migration script were all updated to unconditionally ignore `.specstory/history/` (regardless of prior tracked state) and to tolerate pre-existing in-tree changes rather than failing/skipping — closing the gap that allowed transcripts to be committed to `a2a` in the first place.
- **Known gap**: this migration is not automatically triggered by the standard project workflow — infrastructure exists but isn't invoked by default tooling (e.g. `bin/coding`), so it must be run manually per project.

## Key Files
- `scripts/migrate-history-to-private.sh` — migration script (Phase A untrack/ignore, Phase C push-to-private-remote).
- `.gitignore` (per project) — must unconditionally include `.specstory/history/`.
- Guard/constraint check ("Guard 3a") — validates `.specstory/history/` is not tracked.
- `MEMORY.md`, `specstory-history-per-project.md` — cross-project memory docs tracking this convention and its status per repo.

## Usage
Run when setting up a new project repo, or when auditing an existing repo for accidental transcript leaks, to ensure `.specstory/history/` is untracked, ignored, and mirrored only to its private `<repo-name>-history` companion repo.

## Troubleshooting
- If transcripts show up in a repo's git history despite this convention, check whether `.gitignore` was added *after* the first commit of `.specstory/history/` — untracking alone doesn't remove already-committed history; a `filter-repo` purge is required (see A2A PoC GitHub Enterprise Migration insight for the full remediation procedure).
- If the private history repo doesn't get pushed to, verify Phase C of the migration script actually ran and that the nested repo's remote is correctly configured.
- Because the migration isn't auto-triggered, proactively run the script for each new project rather than assuming default tooling handles it.
